Chapter             T

                   Frankish

     T
         he era known as the Carolingian Renaissance is a brief
         period of cultural and economic revival in western
         Europe. The arts and the economy briefly flourish, and
      many state reforms are made. Charlemagne is unique among
      medieval rulers in feeling sincerely responsible for the welfare
      of his subjects and peace in his empire. He is the first monarch
      to record the laws of his peoples. Each distinct territory has its
      own laws, and he himself edits many pieces of new legislation,
      known as “capitularies.”
        Throughout his 46-year rule there are relatively few inter-
      nal wars or revolts. Only the last years of Charlemagne’s reign are
      relatively anarchic: many counts, even at court, defy the emper-
      or. His sons rule in their father’s stead, as Charlemagne’s health
      declines.
      The  King
      Spiritual Kingship

     T
         he Franks, as the direct descendants of the Trojans, are a
         people chosen by God to rule over others. The Frankish
         King is both the supreme military chief and a spiritual
      leader. Indeed, being consecrated and anointed by the Pope, the
      king is the bearer of salvation for his people. As Gregory the
      Great solemnly put it: “He who is elevated to the summit of power
      receives the sacrament of unction. (…) The head of the king should
      be anointed because the soul of the master must be filled with spir-
      itual grace.”
        Carolingian kings are both crowned and anointed as king.
      Christianity is what holds the Franklands together, shown in the
      numerous cathedrals built during this age. The Pope established
      the duty of the Franks to choose their king from the Arnulfings,
      so all descendants of Pepin the Short are anointed and given a
      diadem, a ring and a staff; emblems of their double function of
      king and bishop (the emperor’s symbols are the scepter, the apple
      and a purple tunic). As such, Charlemagne is the living embodi-
      ment of the divine magic and power which sustains the universe,
      and has a monopoly on God’s truth.

Thirteen:

h  Society

     Charlemagne acknowledges no limitations to his rule. To
  him, the religious and the political are but one. His power ex-
  tends over everything, including the Church. Charlemagne pre-
  sides over Church councils (synods), gives advice to the Pope,
  appoints bishops and abbots and deals with them as he does
  with his counts, deposing them if he feels like. He is the defend-
  er of the Church and his will is sacred, for he acts under divine
  guidance. Charlemagne is the servant of God, not of the Pope.
  Indeed, Charlemagne is invested with clerical powers: he may
  baptize, forgive the sins committed by knights, bless and absolve
  them, administer the extreme unction, and he has the legal pow-
  er to marry people.
  Charlemagne blesses a vassal:
    The king said: “In Jesus’ name and mine.”
    With his right hand he absolved him and blessed him.
       — Song of Roland, XXVI
     Charlemagne is the ultimate moral authority, and the king
  is conscious that he must be a model for his subjects. For the
  first time in history, a king considers it his sacred duty to protect
  widows, orphans and the poor, to defend the land, to keep the
  peace within the borders and to distribute his treasure among his
  vassals to ensure their loyalty. On the other hand, as he is anoint-
  ed and holds religious power, all free Franks must swear an oath
  of fidelity to the king when they become adults. This oath must
  be sworn on relics, in a public place, and before royal officials:
    “To our lord and most pious emperor, Charlemagne, son
    of King Pepin and Queen Bertrada, I am a faithful ser-
    vant, as a man lawfully ought be to his lord, in the ser-
    vice of his kingdom and righteousness. This oath which
    I pledge, I shall keep, and I do intend to keep, to the best
    of my knowledge and understanding from this day for-
    ward, so help me God, who created heaven and earth
    and these relics of the saints.”
       — Capitulary, anno 800

leftColumn:
kingdom, whether ecclesiastic or layman, and each one
       according to his vow and occupation, should now promise
       to him as emperor the fidelity which he had previously
       promised to him as king; and all of those who had not yet
       made that promise should do likewise, down to those who
       were twelve years old. And that it shall be announced to
       all in public, so that each one might know, how great and
       how many things are comprehended in that oath; not
       merely, as many have thought hitherto, fidelity to the
       lord emperor as regards his life, and not introducing any
       enemy into his kingdom out of enmity, and not consent-
       ing to or concealing another’s faithlessness to him.
           — Capitulary, anno 802
      Mundane   Rule

        In reality, Charlemagne’s power is based on his loyal follow-
      ers, whom he rewards with gold and silver, but even more so with
      lands, abbeys and bishoprics.
        Before Charlemagne, many local land holders (counts,
      bishops and abbots) tried to become independent of the king.
      Individual nobles kept armed entourages that were prepared to
      defend their interests and who had an appetite for adventure.
      Whoever collected the largest following naturally held sway
      over the others. For them, might made right. As power is almost
      exclusively measured in terms of landed wealth, this sometimes
      generated an atmosphere of brutal acquisitiveness among the up-
      per classes, resulting in feuds and internecine wars.
        Politics before Charlemagne amounted to what is called
      “feudal anarchy.” Clashes between great lords were characteristic
      of life. The local castle (a motte and bailey) was the center of
      power — an imitation of a king’s court.
        Basically, three factors undermine the basis of royal pow-
      er: in rewarding his vassals by giving them land, the king weak-
      ens his own economic power; when he appoints an indigenous
      count, this nobleman is often more loyal to his clan than to the
      king, since he may even be entirely dependant on his family to
      stay in power; if, on the other hand, the king appoints a stranger,
      the count will surely be very loyal to the king, but the local mag-
      nates will view him as a rival and an intruder.
       A kingdom is just like a body and it can be struck down
       by this or by that illness unless its health is guarded by re-
       ceiving counsel and courage as if from doctors, so the king
       bound the bishops to him. He set up counts and abbots
       through all of the land, and many others too who are com-
       monly called vassals. They were Franks whose wisdom and
       courage would be able to keep him safe from any cunning
       or force. He committed the care of the kingdom to them as
       far as he judged beneficial, likewise the safety of the fron-
       tiers and the revenues of the royal country estates.
           — The Astronomer, I.4

Feudalism

  The  Rise of Feudalism

  T
      he disintegration of the Roman Empire was followed by
      the decline of central authority and administration, and
      the disappearance of an army-of-the-state. The growing
  need for well-equipped warriors could no longer be sustained by
  a lord’s household alone. In order to organize local defenses effi-
  ciently, Charles Martel began giving his loyal followers titles and
  grants of land from the royal domain. In return, the beneficiary
  of a land grant, the vassal, promised to perform personal services
  for his king.
     The petty local lords became little kings on their own do-
  mains, creating a landed aristocracy, a class of nobles. What they
  needed to defend themselves were skilled warriors on horseback.
  But equipping those was expensive, so some fighters were given
  land, which generated the necessary income to pay for their high
  expenses. With the professionalization of the warrior class, peas-
  ants and fighters became more and more separated.
     The fighting power of a lord depends on his body of follow-
  ers, linked by oaths of loyalty. To sustain himself in horses and
  equipment, such a follower needs income from lands. First dis-
  tributed as allods (see Allodial Fief, page 218), they become more
  and more permanent grants in Charlemagne’s time. He pro-
  motes vassalage, because it strengthens social order, and his in-
  cessant demands for military service create the conditions which
  force poor freemen to seek the protection of the magnates. Thus
  the poor become tied to the rich, and the rich are tied to the
  royal counts as vassals, themselves subservient to the king. In the
  end, all administrative districts are ruled by counts. In some re-
  gions of the kingdom a number of counts are placed under the
  command of a duke. This is the emergence of feudalism.
  The  Feudal Pyramid
     Feudalism begins with the belief that everything belongs to
  the king, as highest lord of the land. All rights derive from the
  king, who has distributed some of his rights and responsibilities
  among his lords who, in turn, distribute some of them to their
  knights. All obligations are personal, dependent on the relation-
  ship between a lord and his followers. The followers swear to
  obey the lord, and afterward are known as vassals of that lord.
     The lord ensures the loyalty of his favored followers by giv-
  ing them land, the single most valuable, and permanent, com-
  modity in the realm. To receive silver is a slightly dubious honor,
  since even a peasant can be bribed with silver, but a transfer of
  land is sacred.
     Two types of land transfer are common: A gift is given for
  the duration of the recipient’s life but reverts to the lord on his
  death; A grant is given for the life of the recipient and his heirs.
  A vassal does not own the land, he owns all the granted benefits
  collected from that land. The vassal receives his grant in return
  for loyalty and services.

title: Loyalty
leftColumn:
As long as the knight’s obligations are satisfied, the benefits
      are legally his and cannot be justly taken away. Typically, a knight’s
      obligations are to serve loyally in his lord’s military campaigns and
      to advise his lord on important matters. In return, the lord owes
      his vassal protection, sustenance, and livelihood. Thus there is a
      reciprocal, but non-equal, agreement between lord and vassal.
        Obligations may be changed only if both parties agree.
      Usually they are only changed when one person has done some-
      thing significant for the other. If the vassal rescued the king on the
      battlefield he might receive his former gift as a permanent grant. If
      the knight violates his loyalty he can lose his land. Typical reasons
      for land to revert to the lord are treason, failure to support the
      lord, or the lack of an heir when the grant holder dies (daughters
      may inherit their father’s grants only if there are no male heirs).
        Ranks of feudal vassalage begin with those closest to the
      king, both in friendship and in wealth. In Paladin, they are the
      counts, bishops, abbots and office holders. In turn those men
      appoint their own vassals. Knights (and squires, as knights-in-
      training) are the lowest class of noble vassals. They may hold
      their land from the king, a count, a lower lord, or even from an-
      other knight.
        Church officials and monasteries rely upon land grants to
      knightly vassals in return for loyal service. Monasteries often be-
      come powerful landowners, with their own knights to protect
      them.
      Homage  and Fealty
        Almost everyone but the king is someone’s vassal. Everyone
      who has a lord has taken an oath of loyalty, a ritual composed
      of homage and fealty, pledging two people to an unbreakable,
      permanent bond of loyalty.
        Homage is an act of submission. It is the personal oath of
      an underling to his lord. The vassal kneels before his lord and
      raises his clasped hands to his lord, who encloses them in his
      own. The vassal gives a brief oath promising aid and counsel.
      Aid means military assistance, while counsel means support of
      the lord in his business and giving advice. Then the lord gives
      a similar promise of leadership and of support expressed as a
      beneficium (“gift”). The beneficium is usually a fief (land grant).
      After swearing, the vassal rises, and both men kiss once to seal
      the oath. This finishes the act of homage.
      To protect his own honor, Count Ganelon announces in pub-
      lic at court that he wishes to avenge himself on his son-in-law,
      Roland, which he is entitled to do. He delivers Count Roland
      into the hands of the Moors. However, in doing so, he also
      puts his liege, King Charlemagne, in danger, committing the
      unforgivable crime of high treason. Here is the final verdict
      against Ganelon, addressed to the king:
       Whatever Roland may have done to Ganelon,
       The act of serving you should have protected him;
       Ganelon is a traitor in that he betrayed him;
       He committed perjury against you and wronged you.
           — The Song of Roland, CCLXXVII

  sworn upon saints’ relics. Fealty’s most common clause includes
  a promise never to attack the lord. Unlike homage, which can be
  sworn only once, a fealty oath is sometimes re-sworn to remind
  someone of his place, or whenever felt to be necessary by the lord.

  man.” He is also sometimes called “a man of hands and mouth.”

  court, but the most popular solution offered to the problem
  of multiple lords is the practice of having a liege lord. That is,
  among all of one’s lords, one is selected to be liege, and he has
  priority to the vassal’s loyalty in case of conflict.

  yond the family. All members of society except the mad hold loy-

  important because it is the foundation of military organization
  and the basis of survival in battle.

  one would consider it fair or just to perform hostile acts against
  the person who supports them with food, protection, and com-
  fort. Moreover, loyalty to a leader extends a person’s influence
  outside of his own family, giving him a place in the larger world.

  establish the relationship between two people. As noted above,
  feudal loyalty is an agreement between two parties: a leader and
  a follower.

  ciety, never trusted by right-thinking people. As with the laws of
  hospitality and kinship, the supernatural powers that watch over
  man may intervene to bring an oath-breaker to a terrible end.

title: Social Classes
leftColumn:
3–2: Dishonorable Acts in Chapter 3 lists the things which every-
      one agrees are dishonorable actions for a knight. Performing any
      of these deeds (killing a woman, for example) always diminishes
      honor. Knights have agreed not to do these things.
        However, the concept of a personal definition of honor is
      important. It means two things. First, some aspects of honor are
      determined by the individual, not by common social consent.
      Secondly, “personal” is used to separate honor from the other
      sworn or innate social obligations, including the unwritten laws
      of society or any others, which are determined socially.
      Social  Classes

       My God, what mistake the good warrior makes
       Who arms as a knight the son of a villain,

       And makes him his seneschal and councilor
       As did Girart with the cursed Richier
       To whom he gave good lands, a noble wife.
       As it was Richier who betrayed the city
       Of Roussillon into Charles Martel’s hands!
       My God, how inconsiderate the count had been!

       The city gates would not have been so badly guarded.
           — Girart de Roussillon, LXIII
      The Trifunctional Model

      F
         rankish society is organized according to a trifunctional
         model: the peasants are protected by the warriors, whose
         sins are forgiven by the prayers of the clergy, and all are
      fed by the peasants. People are born into a specific class and en-
      ter the same occupation as their parents. People do not expect
      to change their status, though it remains possible. A commoner
      might attain knighthood through prowess of arms displayed on
      the battlefield. The clergy fill their ranks from people of all class-
      es. Exceptional commoners usually join the church, or become
      personal employees of a nobleman. Exceptional members of the
      ruling class may become monks, hermits, or even saints.
      The Noble  Class
        The nobility consists of rich men owning huge tracts of land,
      often in many different regions. Some of them hold their land di-
      rectly from the king (a baron, who may be a great count or duke, or
      a knight with a single manor), some from a local abbot, count or
      other noblemen (vavasour, or vassal’s vassal). The nobility includes
      the professional household warriors of the vassals as well. One of
      the prerogatives of nobles is the right to command armed men.
      Rich commoners may never have private troops at their service.
        Special rules dictate how to address noblemen: the king is
      “very glorious king,” a royal officer like the seneschal is a “mag-
      nificence,” other court officials are simply “noble sirs,” a count is
      an “illustrious lord,” a duke is a “glorious lord,” and a bishop or an
      abbot is a “venerable father.”
rightColumn:
The noble is a horse-riding comrade at arms, and compan-
  ion in peace, of a lord, and has acquired grants of land or taken
  them for himself. His family descends from a noteworthy fore-
  bear, whose name is passed down from one generation to the
  next. A nobleman is marked as well by his way of life (in war,
  hunts, and feasts), his dress, and his arms.
     Noblemen are the leaders and warriors of society. They
  do not work for their own maintenance, but acquire food and
  goods from others. Even if they are often at each other’s throats,
  nobles exhibit a certain kind of solidarity and cooperation based
  on their commonality of interests. So insistent are noblemen
  on maintaining class differences that a knight loses his status
  for engaging in non-knightly behavior, such as physical labor or
  moneylending. A nobleman’s hawk and sword are “sacred” pos-
  sessions which cannot be confiscated or forfeited by law. Above
  all, the noble is a soldier, and in death he is buried with his armor
  and sword.
     A noble possesses vast, often diffuse domains, comprising
  thousands of hectares scattered in patches across different re-
  gions. The noble maintains himself by exploiting these domains,
  by hunting in the forest and using free peasants or bonded la-
  borers to farm the arable land. Established in a fortified house,
  a nobleman rules freely over the people who serve him and over
  his landed possessions, which he seeks to expand by conquest
  or marriage. His aim is to increase the wealth that makes for
  material strength, friendships, and political allegiance; these in
  turn open the way to political advancement. Many a noble har-
  bors the dream of ruling the lands in which he lives, either as the
  king’s count or, should the royalty grow weak, as the king’s rival.
     Not all people are equal within the noble class. Two distinct
  divisions exist, commonly called the higher and lower nobili-
  ty. The lower nobility are the knights. The higher nobility are
  called lords. Lords have vassals who are knights or other lords.
  The higher nobility includes all the hereditary landholders.
  Lords are also knights, of course, but are usually referred to by
  their higher rank. These ranks of noblemen, ranged from lowest
  to highest, are: banneret, count, duke, king.
     No lord rules alone. They surround themselves with their
  leading men and never act without taking counsel from these
  loyal followers. Counts appoint stewards or vicars, or even have
  the people choose them, who supervise their fief within the
  county. A lord’s household or retinue refers to all the personnel
  serving a lord, especially his knights and warriors. A viscount
  rules a city in the lord’s stead.
     To assure the loyalty and friendship of the men in his entou-
  rage, a lord is expected to spend his money generously. Money
  is necessary to maintain one’s station. At the same time, it is de-
  spised as filthy and base, because what distinguishes nobles from
  commoners is not their wealth but their culture, their courtly
  manners, and their honor. Knights owe their superior status to
  their noble mission of protector of the weak. At their knighting,
  they swear to hold as their enemy all those who violate the peace.
     The knights’ primary responsibility is to serve as the mili-
  tary force for their lord. They have many privileges and freedoms

      often in many different regions. Some of them hold their land di-
      rectly from the king (a baron, who may be a great count or duke, or
      a knight with a single manor), some from a local abbot, count or
      other noblemen (vavasour, or vassal’s vassal). The nobility includes
      the professional household warriors of the vassals as well. One of
      the prerogatives of nobles is the right to command armed men.
      Rich commoners may never have private troops at their service.
        Special rules dictate how to address noblemen: the king is
      “very glorious king,” a royal officer like the seneschal is a “mag-
      nificence,” other court officials are simply “noble sirs,” a count is
      an “illustrious lord,” a duke is a “glorious lord,” and a bishop or an
      abbot is a “venerable father.”

The noble is a horse-riding comrade at arms, and compan-
  ion in peace, of a lord, and has acquired grants of land or taken
  them for himself. His family descends from a noteworthy fore-
  bear, whose name is passed down from one generation to the
  next. A nobleman is marked as well by his way of life (in war,
  hunts, and feasts), his dress, and his arms.
     Noblemen are the leaders and warriors of society. They
  do not work for their own maintenance, but acquire food and
  goods from others. Even if they are often at each other’s throats,
  nobles exhibit a certain kind of solidarity and cooperation based
  on their commonality of interests. So insistent are noblemen
  on maintaining class differences that a knight loses his status
  for engaging in non-knightly behavior, such as physical labor or
  moneylending. A nobleman’s hawk and sword are “sacred” pos-
  sessions which cannot be confiscated or forfeited by law. Above
  all, the noble is a soldier, and in death he is buried with his armor
  and sword.
     A noble possesses vast, often diffuse domains, comprising
  thousands of hectares scattered in patches across different re-
  gions. The noble maintains himself by exploiting these domains,
  by hunting in the forest and using free peasants or bonded la-
  borers to farm the arable land. Established in a fortified house,
  a nobleman rules freely over the people who serve him and over
  his landed possessions, which he seeks to expand by conquest
  or marriage. His aim is to increase the wealth that makes for
  material strength, friendships, and political allegiance; these in
  turn open the way to political advancement. Many a noble har-
  bors the dream of ruling the lands in which he lives, either as the
  king’s count or, should the royalty grow weak, as the king’s rival.
     Not all people are equal within the noble class. Two distinct
  divisions exist, commonly called the higher and lower nobili-
  ty. The lower nobility are the knights. The higher nobility are
  called lords. Lords have vassals who are knights or other lords.
  The higher nobility includes all the hereditary landholders.
  Lords are also knights, of course, but are usually referred to by
  their higher rank. These ranks of noblemen, ranged from lowest
  to highest, are: banneret, count, duke, king.
     No lord rules alone. They surround themselves with their
  leading men and never act without taking counsel from these
  loyal followers. Counts appoint stewards or vicars, or even have
  the people choose them, who supervise their fief within the
  county. A lord’s household or retinue refers to all the personnel
  serving a lord, especially his knights and warriors. A viscount
  rules a city in the lord’s stead.
     To assure the loyalty and friendship of the men in his entou-
  rage, a lord is expected to spend his money generously. Money
  is necessary to maintain one’s station. At the same time, it is de-
  spised as filthy and base, because what distinguishes nobles from
  commoners is not their wealth but their culture, their courtly
  manners, and their honor. Knights owe their superior status to
  their noble mission of protector of the weak. At their knighting,
  they swear to hold as their enemy all those who violate the peace.
     The knights’ primary responsibility is to serve as the mili-
  tary force for their lord. They have many privileges and freedoms

title: The Clerical Class
leftColumn:
which are not available to the lower classes, gained in exchange
      for the pledge that they will die for their lord if necessary.
        Feuds among noble families are common. Lords are, above
      all, family patriarchs, dreaming of nothing beyond the interest
      of their families, the growth of their power, and the increase
      of their wealth. As a result, lords never participate in tourneys
      themselves. They no longer seek glory, as their injury or death
      would weaken their entire family and open the door to rival
      clans or internal strife.
      The Clerical Class

        The clergy includes all members of the Church, a powerful
      institution that owns considerable estates and has many rights
      of its own. Churchmen are exempt from most ordinary laws,
      and claim loyalty to God, a higher authority than the king — a
      claim which is sometimes a source of conflict between clergy and
      royalty.
        The clergy, supposed to be chaste, can hardly be expected
      to reproduce itself and so draws members from both the nobility
      and the commoners. It is not unusual for younger sons of the no-
      bility to join the clergy rather than be landless knights, seeking
      what opportunity the Church can give them. For bright and am-
      bitious commoners, the Church provides the best opportunity
      for advancement.
        Churchmen may be secular clergy or monastics. The secular
      clergy includes bishops and the village priests who administer the
      sacraments to commoners, and who oversee the spiritual develop-
      ment of their parish. Monastics are men or women who have taken
      the religious path of isolation and joined special communities that
      practice devotion apart from the ways of ordinary mankind.
      The Common   Class
        Everyone who is not noble or clergy is a commoner. They
      are the basis for society, and make up 95% of the population.
      They may not carry weapons other than knives or bows for
      hunting except in times of war.
        The status of a man depends on the size of his holding.
      The smaller his land, the more likely he is treated as a serf. The
      Formulary of Tours gives a generic oath of vassalage for free
      men subjecting themselves to a local magnate:
       “To the magnificent lord [name], I [name]: as it is ev-
       ident to all that I have no means to feed or clothe my-
       self, I have appealed to your piety and you have willing-
       ly agreed that I should deliver or recommend myself to
       your protection. This I do under the following conditions:
       You must help and support me with food and clothing,
       according to the degree that I serve you and merit from
       you. And for as long as I live, I must provide you service
       and honor according to my free rank, and at no point in
       my lifetime shall I have the power to release myself from
       your power and protection. Rather, I must remain un-
       der your power and protection all the days of my life. Ac-
       cordingly, it has been agreed that should one of us wish to
       withdraw from these stipulations, he shall pay so many
rightColumn:
solidi to another of equal station to take his place, and the
    agreement shall remain in force. It has also been agreed
    concerning this undertaking that two charters identical
    in wording shall be drafted and confirmed by the parties.
    This they have done.”
     Commoners are the ordinary people who provide the food
  and goods which allow noblemen and clergy to pursue their spe-
  cialized functions. Most commoners are farmers, whether poor
  serfs without any freedom or rich landholders who maintain the
  right to change lords at will. The artisans who populate cities and
  make their wares, and the merchants who act as middlemen for
  trade and cross Frankland with their goods, are all commoners.
     Peasants, whether freemen or serfs, sometimes flee from
  their lands in search of more clement masters. A corrupt and
  treacherous steward may enrich himself by releasing all men able
  to pay him a bribe, and then compensate for the loss of work
  force by exploiting the remaining families to the utmost.
     A commoner’s child automatically takes on the condition
  of his or her lowest born parents: if either one of a child’s parents
  is a slave, he or she is a slave, too.
     Inversely, commoners can sometimes enter the ranks of
  knighthood. Anyone who can acquire weapons and employment
  in the ranks of mercenaries might rise from soldier or sergeant to
  squire or knight through recognition by his leader. Commoners
  who perform outstandingly, even off the battlefield, can be raised
  to the status of squire or even knight by their grateful lords.
  Sometimes lords desperate for money sell knighthood to rich
  men. More often, though, their daughters marry commoners, who
  share their wealth in return for their own children being noble.

    Four Main Divisions of the Common Class

      Freemen are the most common type of peasant. They
   own the land they live on, but are obliged to work the lord’s
   lands as well in exchange for his protection. They owe the king
   military service.
      Settlers are free peasants who ask for a lord’s protection.
   They clear lands for their new lord. Over time, free men might
   acquire shared, or even full, ownership of land recovered from
   the wastes. A settler is free to marry and his sons inherit his
   possessions when he dies. He is under the obligation to work
   his land and to pay the lord’s taxes (in kind or coin) and mili-
   tary service. If the lord sells the land, he automatically sells the
   settled peasants living on it.
      Serfs are unfree peasants who must work exclusively for
   their lord. A serf cannot acquire wealth, but the lord has no
   say over his private life. Semi-serfs work on their lord’s land as
   well as on a bit of land they own themselves.
      Slaves are pagans sold at slave markets, or they may be
   prisoners of war (mostly Saxons or Slavs, from whom the word
   “slave” derives). Slaves are the property of their lord, who may
   dispose of them as he wishes, though he does not have the
   right to kill them. A master may free a slave, but generally does
   so only on certain conditions (baptism, first of all).

title: Land Ownership and Fiefs
leftColumn:
Land   Ownership    and  Fiefs

       That those who hold a benefice of us should strive in all
       things to improve it, and that our missi should take note
       of this.
           — Capitulary, anno 802

      A
          vassal has the duty to improve the land, corresponding
          to the Christian mission to improve the earth. But not
          all lands are held as a fief — different types of owner-
      ship conditions and benefices exist. To determine the exact sta-
      tus of a domain, some questions have to be answered. Who is the
      owner? Who is the overlord? Does the nobleman owning it owe
      his lord military service? Does the knight owe the lord presents?
      Who has jurisdiction?
        In the beginning of Charlemagne’s rule, most manors are
      given as gifts for life, not eternal grants, meaning they return to
      the lord when the knight dies. When a knight does homage to
      his lord and receives his manor, a charter defines what he owes
      his lord in return: usually military service and counsel.
        Several possible situations of land ownership and fiefs are
      presented below.
rightColumn:
Allodial Fief
     An allodial fief (or “bookland”) is a freely-held domain
  without overlord. The knight holding such a fief owes no fealty
  to the local count, but must still serve under his banner when the
  king calls his bannum. He owes no other military services, but he
  must allow the count entrance to his domains.
     Manors of this type are relatively rare in northern Frankland
  (Alemannia, Austrasia, Bavaria, Neustria, and Thuringia) but
  rather common in the south (Aquitaine, Burgundy, Gascony,
  Provence and Septimania).
  Demesne   Manor

     A desmesne manor is a personal manor of a lord, from which
  he collects his personal income. It is managed by a steward, not
  a knight. Therefore, the manor generates income but no knight
  muster (only the usual levy of free men), since no knight is pres-
  ent on the domain.

title: Enfeoffed Manor
leftColumn:
Enfeoffed Manor

        When a lord gives or grants a manor to a knight, this
      knight owes him fealty and military service, in addition to the
      king’s bannum. Enfeoffed manors are the most common ones for
      Player-knights to hold.
      Fisc

        A fisc is a rich manor owned by the king himself. Charlemagne
      possesses roughly a thousand of these, especially in Neustria and
      Austrasia. A fisc is usually given (not granted) in wardship to a
      royal steward (not necessarily a knight), who is appointed directly
      by the king or one of his high officers, like the palace count. Such a
      steward must manage the domain to make it prosper and send the
      king a set sum of goods and coin annually.
        The majority of the royal fiscs are administered by the local
      counts or abbots (who sometimes treat these fiscs as their own
      demesne manors), but if this is not the case no service in coin or
      kind is due to the local count (In the Ardennes, all fiscs depend
      on the duke’s authority).
        In later times, Charlemagne sometimes gives or grants fiscs
      to particularly valorous and loyal knights, turning them into
      enfeoffed manors. On very rare occasions, the king is known to
      grant a fisc as a free allod.
      Immunities
        An immunity is an enfeoffed ecclesiastical manor, usually
      held by an abbot, which is not dependent on the local count. A
      vassal knight holding the immunity owes the abbot advice and
      military service, but he must join the local count at the king’s
      bannum.
      Precarial Tenures

        To reward knights for loyal services, the king or a lord may
      donate a domain in precarial tenure. The beneficiary has the usu-
      fruct (the right to use the land, without actually owning it) for a
      certain duration: typically twelve years, or for life. The rightful
      owner is paid an annual rent. These so-called “lifetime tenures”
      are a type of allodial land which returns to the lord upon the vas-
      sal’s death. Sometimes the king even “borrows” such a domain
      from a monastery or abbey, before giving it as a precarial tenure
      to some loyal knight.
      Counts   and  Dukes

      Charlemagne instructs a new count:

       “It is the prerogative of his royal Clemency to select among
       his people those men who are known to be vigilant and
       loyal, and not to confer the dignity of justice lightly, but
       first to examine the fidelity and the valor of a candidate.
         Now, having ascertained your trustworthiness and
       efficiency, I bestow the dignity of the county of [Land]
       upon you, which was previously held by [Count Name],

When a lord gives or grants a manor to a knight, this
      knight owes him fealty and military service, in addition to the
      king’s bannum. Enfeoffed manors are the most common ones for
      Player-knights to hold.
      Fisc

A fisc is a rich manor owned by the king himself. Charlemagne
      possesses roughly a thousand of these, especially in Neustria and
      Austrasia. A fisc is usually given (not granted) in wardship to a
      royal steward (not necessarily a knight), who is appointed directly
      by the king or one of his high officers, like the palace count. Such a
      steward must manage the domain to make it prosper and send the
      king a set sum of goods and coin annually.
        The majority of the royal fiscs are administered by the local
      counts or abbots (who sometimes treat these fiscs as their own
      demesne manors), but if this is not the case no service in coin or
      kind is due to the local count (In the Ardennes, all fiscs depend
      on the duke’s authority).
        In later times, Charlemagne sometimes gives or grants fiscs
      to particularly valorous and loyal knights, turning them into
      enfeoffed manors. On very rare occasions, the king is known to
      grant a fisc as a free allod.
      Immunities
        An immunity is an enfeoffed ecclesiastical manor, usually
      held by an abbot, which is not dependent on the local count. A
      vassal knight holding the immunity owes the abbot advice and
      military service, but he must join the local count at the king’s
      bannum.
      Precarial Tenures

To reward knights for loyal services, the king or a lord may
      donate a domain in precarial tenure. The beneficiary has the usu-
      fruct (the right to use the land, without actually owning it) for a
      certain duration: typically twelve years, or for life. The rightful
      owner is paid an annual rent. These so-called “lifetime tenures”
      are a type of allodial land which returns to the lord upon the vas-
      sal’s death. Sometimes the king even “borrows” such a domain
      from a monastery or abbey, before giving it as a precarial tenure
      to some loyal knight.

king chooses all counts himself, but loyal, honest and capable
      men are hard to find; the king can dismiss a count in case of mis-
      conduct, but this is rare.
        The administrative system of counties is exported into
      newly conquered territories, where royal vassals hold immense
      domains in order to ensure effective royal presence and author-
      ity. The new counts are often chosen from the pool of court
      knights called scarae. Frankish counts can be found anywhere in
      the realm. In conquered territory, the king sometimes appoints
      counts from the local population. Later he even appoints con-
      verted Saxon noblemen as counts in Saxony. These must first de-
      liver hostages, who are sent to Frankland to be raised like Franks.
      Hereditary Titles
        In theory, the count merely administers the king’s lands, as
      well as his own, in a certain region. The problem is often that
      a count doesn’t care for the royal lands (which don’t give him
      much income), and mainly takes care of his own. Or he com-
      bines both domains and rules them as completely his own.
      Thus a count’s royal domain and his ancestral lands tend to
      be gradually merged into one hereditary fief. At the beginning
      of Charlemagne’s reign the title of count is not yet hereditary.
      The sons of loyal counts do not automatically become counts
      in their father’s county. Sometimes the county is given to other
      noblemen, or a son is given a different county than his father, de-
      pending on which counties are available. Over time, it becomes
      normal that a son inherits his father’s title and the royal lands
      become the count’s hereditary lands.
      Dukes
        A duke is a count, but he is also the military leader of a
      duchy, which usually consists of several counties. As the highest
      commander in the king’s army, he commands his counts in bat-
      tle. Royal troops are often assembled into large ducal battalions
      in order to produce group coherence. Counts owe their duke fe-
      alty, but not military service.
      Justice

       Learn justice, learn the celestial laws decreed
       by the Father enthroned in highest heaven.
       Let justice be observed by God, the prophets, the laws
       and princes too; may it be the reigning power in our
        hearts.
       If justice rules us, then we shall rule the people as we
        should,
       the mind ruled by God rules everything well.
           — Theodulf

      The Law

      A
          capitulary is a decree containing laws and administra-
          tive directions promulgated by the king, divided into
          articles called capitula (“headings”) which express his
rightColumn:
will as a ruler. Some capitularies deal with a particular land or
  a specific area of concern, others are more general in scope and
  mixed in content.
     New laws are usually communicated to all counts by the
  voice of royal messengers or missi dominici. Only bishops some-
  times receive a written copy for their archives.
  Public Justice

     There are three judicial channels whereby a party may ob-
  tain justice: private or family justice and ensuing minor feuds;
  public justice at a count’s court; and public royal justice. The two
  latter public courts have two possibilities to determine guilt and
  punishment: by accusation or by inquiry.
     Only in serious cases where the peace of the land is at stake
  do public officers intervene. In that case, justice is rendered in
  public by the king’s officials (count, bishop, or abbot). While
  Charlemagne has the power to demand public justice for seri-
  ous feuds and minor crimes, this is more properly the task of the
  counts. The palace court only deals with cases of high treason or
  other crimes against the king.
     Low Justice can be dispensed by any noble of the land, in-
  cluding knights. They can judge any case which is less critical
  than murder, rape, treason or other capital crimes (those crimes
  that may be punished by the death penalty). Knights can deliver
  justice to commoners, including imprisonment and the cutting
  off of hands, ears, and other body parts of commoners. They
  cannot judge on capital crimes or deliver a sentence of death, or
  judge other nobles or members of the clergy.
     High Justice is reserved for higher nobles. They make rul-
  ings on capital crimes. This includes treason, rape, murder, and
  theft of the lord’s goods.
  All in all, justice comes in several forms and at several levels:
     Private justice (family feud)
     Public justice
       Low justice (village, scabini)
       High justice (count’s court)
              By accusation (count)
              By inquiry (missi dominici)
       Royal justice (king’s court, Count of the Palace)
  Feuds

    If a man bearing arms is engaged in a feud, let there be
    an inquiry into which of the two parties is hostile to their
    being reconciled, and let them be compelled to reconcili-
    ation, even if they are unwilling; and if they refuse to be
    reconciled, let them be brought to our presence. And if one
    kills the other after reconciliation, he is to pay compen-
    sation for him and lose the hand which perjured and in
    addition pay the emperor’s bannum.
       — Capitulary, anno 806

title: Judicial Courts
leftColumn:
In many cases Frankish justice is a private matter, not a pub-
      lic one. People settle their quarrels and disputes according to
      their own traditional method: the feud. Knightly honor justifies
      vengeance by private war, which aims to restore justice by violent
      means. There are rules to a feud; those who commit dishonor-
      able acts or use excessive violence may be abandoned by their
      family or friends. Honorable conduct is expected of all knights,
      and many conflicts are settled in a more peaceful manner. In a
      feud, periods of violence are alternated by pleas in a court of
      justice and negotiations between warring families. Still, arson,
      murder, and mutilation are frequent in a blood feud.
        Charlemagne obliges the wronged party to accept reparations
      from the guilty party. Feuds can be ended by reconciliation before
      a neutral witness (a count or a bishop, for example), a symbolic kiss
      between the opposing family heads, and payment of a fine.
      Judicial Courts
        A count dispenses justice at an assembly called the mallus,
      where he is assisted by his vicars and legal assessors (scabini),
      whose job it is to learn the law. These scabini (or centenars, “hun-
      dredmen”) are commoners elected as full-time local judges, usu-
      ally twelve per county, and are paid by the count.
       Counts and centenars shall see to it that justice is done in
       full; and they shall have younger men in their service in
       whom they can securely trust, who will faithfully observe
       law and justice, and by no means oppress the poor; who
       will not, under any pretext, induced by reward or flat-
       tery, dare to conceal thieves, robbers, or murderers, adul-
       terers, magicians and wizards or witches, or any godless
       men; but will rather give them up that they may be bet-
       tered and chastised by the law: so that, God permitting,
       all these evils may be removed from the Christian people.
       Judges shall judge justly, according to the written law

In many cases Frankish justice is a private matter, not a pub-
      lic one. People settle their quarrels and disputes according to
      their own traditional method: the feud. Knightly honor justifies
      vengeance by private war, which aims to restore justice by violent
      means. There are rules to a feud; those who commit dishonor-
      able acts or use excessive violence may be abandoned by their
      family or friends. Honorable conduct is expected of all knights,
      and many conflicts are settled in a more peaceful manner. In a
      feud, periods of violence are alternated by pleas in a court of
      justice and negotiations between warring families. Still, arson,
      murder, and mutilation are frequent in a blood feud.
        Charlemagne obliges the wronged party to accept reparations
      from the guilty party. Feuds can be ended by reconciliation before
      a neutral witness (a count or a bishop, for example), a symbolic kiss
      between the opposing family heads, and payment of a fine.
      Judicial Courts
        A count dispenses justice at an assembly called the mallus,
      where he is assisted by his vicars and legal assessors (scabini),
      whose job it is to learn the law. These scabini (or centenars, “hun-
      dredmen”) are commoners elected as full-time local judges, usu-
      ally twelve per county, and are paid by the count.
       Counts and centenars shall see to it that justice is done in
       full; and they shall have younger men in their service in
       whom they can securely trust, who will faithfully observe
       law and justice, and by no means oppress the poor; who
       will not, under any pretext, induced by reward or flat-
       tery, dare to conceal thieves, robbers, or murderers, adul-
       terers, magicians and wizards or witches, or any godless
       men; but will rather give them up that they may be bet-
       tered and chastised by the law: so that, God permitting,
       all these evils may be removed from the Christian people.
       Judges shall judge justly, according to the written law
       and not according to their own judgment.
           — Capitulary, anno 802

      Trial by Combat
       When anyone declines to maintain his lasting fidelity to
       the king through guile, money or trickery, or if a wicked
       person seeks to bring some attack against the king or his
       children or his rule, contrary to the oath that he swore,
       then, if a brother Frank appears and denounces him, it
       is fitting and proper for them both to fight it out in the
       presence of the king and his council.
           — Ermold the Black, III
        In any case of justice, a knight may choose trial by combat
      instead of the normal court justice. In this trial everyone knows
      that God favors the right party, and that His might aids the
      right. A lord may, and a woman must, choose a champion to
      fight in their stead.
        The fight may be until the first combatant is knocked down
      or wounded, for conquest (the knight who yields loses), or to the
      death. The ruling made by God cannot be reversed or appealed.
        Frequently, the knights participating in a trial by combat
      must give the king hostages. These hostages are guarantors for
      the combatants, risking their lives on the outcome.
      At court, Charlemagne accuses Huon of a crime:
       “Give me hostages,” commands Charlemagne the fierce,
       “or it will cost you dearly!”
         “Lord,” says Huon, “I gladly obey you. Here is my
       brother Gerard, but I cannot propose you any other hos-
       tages, since in this magnificent palace I can see no other
       relatives of mine whom I could ask to vow for me.”
         “But you can see me,” declares the abbot, “and for the
       love of you I shall be the king’s hostage. Should you be beat-
       en in a judicial duel — if God allows such an injustice to
       happen — than Charlemagne be dishonored if he hangs
       me not before midnight, and eighty monks with me!”
           — Huon of Bordeaux, XI

      Trial by Ordeal
        Important cases are resolved by an ordeal. The most popu-
      lar ordeals are the Proof of the Cross, in which the accused must
      stand with his arms in the shape of a cross for a certain duration,
      sometimes holding weights as well; the Ordeal of Boiling Water
      — placing one’s arms into a vat of boiling water; or the Ordeal of
      Hot Iron — holding a red-hot iron. The truth of the allegations
      is determined by the time it takes for the injuries to heal. Ordeals
      are even used to pacify conflicts between disputing abbots.

Punishment

    The man who commits perjury is to lose his hand and
    cannot redeem this.
       — Capitulary, anno 779
     People (knights included) can be punished for disobeying
  their lord’s laws or the custom of the land. Most punishments are
  monetary “compensations” to the victims or the surviving rela-
  tives. The judge decides the reparation fine the wrongdoer has
  to pay. Two-thirds of the fine are handed over to the wronged
  family, the other third to the king or his representative. In case
  of murder or the liberation of a hostage, every person is worth
  a certain amount of money called wergild. Compensation is in-
  tended to limit the pursuit of bloody, long-lasting family feuds.
     A more severe penalty is banishment or the obligation to go
  on a pilgrimage; the knight must depart all of his lord’s holdings
  for the length of the banishment, which is typically a year and a
  day for the first offense. The banished knight is considered an
  enemy of the lord, and can even be killed without his kin justly
  claiming revenge. During his absence the lord controls all the
  lands and obtains all income and benefits therefrom.
     More serious offenses can be punished by outlawry, which
  is permanent banishment, and is usually accompanied by forfei-
  ture of all lands and titles to the lord.
     Degradation is the ultimate punishment; the knight is
  stripped of his title and right to his rank. The ceremony is a pub-
  lic humiliation and is permanent; another lord cannot re-bestow
  knighthood.
     Popular corporal punishments include beatings with a stick,
  branding with a hot iron, or amputation. The punishments for
  thieves, for example, are “first an eye, then the nose, and at last the
  head” (if they are caught stealing a third time).
     Capital punishment can only be handed down by a count
  (for commoners) or the king (for noblemen).
  Prison
     Imprisonment is not a punishment as such, but merely a
  means to prevent the prisoner from escaping. Nobles may send a
  vassal to prison in their stead, where he stays until his lord pays
  the ransom.
     Knights are often captured and held in various states of ar-
  rest. They may be held shamefully in dark dungeons, dirty and
  unfed. Or they may give their parole — their word of honor not
  to escape — and be maintained according to their station, shar-
  ing their captor’s table.
     Charlemagne often requires military or political prisoners
  (and sometimes their families) as hostages from important and
  loyal retainers like counts, bishops, or abbots.
     Surprisingly, even enemies of the worst kind do not kill
  their prisoners. Hated murderers languish away in a dungeon
  rather than being killed. Indeed, most knights and lords do

     Popular corporal punishments include beatings with a stick,
  branding with a hot iron, or amputation. The punishments for
  thieves, for example, are “first an eye, then the nose, and at last the
  head” (if they are caught stealing a third time).
     Capital punishment can only be handed down by a count
  (for commoners) or the king (for noblemen).
  Prison
     Imprisonment is not a punishment as such, but merely a
  means to prevent the prisoner from escaping. Nobles may send a
  vassal to prison in their stead, where he stays until his lord pays
  the ransom.
     Knights are often captured and held in various states of ar-
  rest. They may be held shamefully in dark dungeons, dirty and
  unfed. Or they may give their parole — their word of honor not
  to escape — and be maintained according to their station, shar-
  ing their captor’s table.
     Charlemagne often requires military or political prisoners
  (and sometimes their families) as hostages from important and
  loyal retainers like counts, bishops, or abbots.
     Surprisingly, even enemies of the worst kind do not kill
  their prisoners. Hated murderers languish away in a dungeon
  rather than being killed. Indeed, most knights and lords do

not have the right of life and death over their prisoners. This
      is determined by the division of Justice into High and Low, as
      mentioned above. Most lords have the rights only to Low Justice,
      which allows them to enforce most laws except those of capital
      crimes. Any crime which warrants death of the culprit are High
      Justice, enforceable against a noble only by the king. To execute
      a criminal would be unusual, illegal, and draw his lord’s attention
      and wrath significantly enough that the knight might lose his
      station for disobedience to his office. Remember, most knights
      are still law-abiding in their own realm and sworn to uphold
      their king’s justice. Instead of killing his foes, the knight simply
      throws the offender into the dungeon, which is well within the
      rights of his office.
      Ecclesiastical Law
        The Church holds lands, both abbeys and bishoprics.
      Abbots and bishops act in every way as vassals of whomever they
      hold the land from.
        The bishops have their own independent courts of justice
      to deal with the crimes of clergy members. Some monasteries
      have their own courts by right of the king. Church Justice, or
      Canon Law, is applicable only to members of the clergy, and it
      is handed down only by higher members of the clergy. Monks,
      friars and priests are generally tried under Canon Law.
        Furthermore, it applies (though not exclusively) to matters
      of Church property, and bishops and abbots claim the right to
      try anyone who harms their properties under this rule. They
      claim the right to try any laymen who have violated church laws,
      such as robbing the clergy, plundering abbeys, and so on.
      Missi Dominici

        Instituted by Charlemagne in 780, missi dominici are spe-
      cial envoys of the king. They operate in pairs, often a layman (a
      count) and a man of the Church (an abbot or bishop), accom-
      panied by a clerk. The ecclesiastical missus is often the leader,
      since he is most capable of studying written documents. Literate
      abbots and bishops frequently serve as diplomats or missi.
        Missi do not receive pay for their missions, so they serve
      only a short term — one season or a year.
      Prerogatives
        During each mission, missi usually visit several counties.
      While exercising their function for the king, they have the right
      to requisition lodging and provisions for their men and horses,
      but they should not accept bribes. In practice, friendship, loyalty
      and family business often lead to a conflict of interest between
      their official obligations and their personal goals.
        When they visit a district during an inspection tour, missi
      have the power to punish noblemen and even to degrade a lord in
      case of severe disloyalty or criminal behavior (corruption, abuse
      of power, despoilment, treason). They speak in the name of the
      king, and as such have to be obeyed unconditionally. Their let-
      ters are sealed in a special way and always take priority over other
      letters carried by couriers.
rightColumn:
Missions
     The main task of missi dominici is to supervise the counts and
  administer “justice for all.” Their role is to correct the abuses and ex-
  cesses of local lords and officers in order to maintain the peace. They
  check the income of the harvest and the part of the lord’s gift to the
  king. They must examine the general management of a county, de-
  tect corruption or power abuse, and hear complaints of commoners.
    The most serene and most Christian emperor Charles, did
    choose from among his nobles the most prudent and the wis-
    est men, archbishops as well as other bishops, and venerable
    abbots, and pious laymen and did send them over his whole
    kingdom; and did grant through them, by means of all the
    following provisions, that men should live according to law
    and right. He did order them, moreover, that, where any-
    thing is contained in the law that is otherwise than accord-
    ing to right and justice, they should inquire into this most
    diligently, and make it known to him: and he, God grant-
    ing, hopes to better it. And let no one, through his cleverness
    or astuteness — as many are accustomed to do — dare to
    oppose the written law, or the sentence passed upon him, or
    to prevail against the churches of God or the poor, or wid-
    ows, or minors, or any Christian man. (…) Let the missi
    themselves make a diligent investigation whenever any man
    claims that an injustice has been done to him by any one,
    just as they desire to deserve the grace of omnipotent God
    and to keep their fidelity promised to Him, so that entirely
    in all cases everywhere, in accordance with the will and fear
    of God, they shall administer the law fully and justly in the
    case of the holy churches of God and of the poor, of wards
    and widows and of the whole people. And if there shall be
    anything of such a nature that they, together with the pro-
    vincial counts, are not able of themselves to correct it and to
    do justice concerning it, they shall, without any ambiguity,
    refer this, together with their reports, to the judgment of the
    emperor; and the straight path of justice shall not be imped-
    ed by any one on account of flattery or gifts from any one, or
    on account of any relationship, or from fear of the powerful.
       — Capitulary on the missi, anno 802
     The missi dominici are sent to regions to recite the new ca-
  pitularies to the counts, abbots and bishops. Recite, because it
  is impossible to make enough copies for all the magnates! They
  also have to supervise the conduct and work of the clergy, and to
  check Bibles and other holy books on their contents.
  Royal Vassals
     In Phase 4, missi become permanent representatives of the
  king at the courts of the high magnates, who have become more and
  more independent. Thus, a new type of missus is created, who is like
  “a count without land,” serving at court only, and whose income de-
  pends on stipends awarded by the king himself. Such a “royal vassal”
  may even be a court serf engaged for specific missions or competen-
  cies (missus dominicus, spy, ambassador, clerk, etc.). For serfs, be-
  coming a missus is a good way of making a career, although they are
  sometimes more tempted to accept bribes than rich lords.

title: The Palace
leftColumn:
The  Palace

     T
         he royal court is called the Palace. The king has no fixed
         residence until Aachen (793). Before that he resides in
         one of the many small palaces spread across the kingdom.
      So a palace is not the Palace, but simply one of the many roy-
      al manors, or fiscs. Charlemagne personally owns about 1,000
      domains, with 200 royal palaces. Before 793, Charlemagne’s fa-
      vorite residences are Frankfurt, Mainz, Worms, Thionville and
      Herstal.
        Court is where the king is. Up to 806, the king spends most
      of his life perambulating the country from one palace or royal
      abbey to another in the company of his family. The itinerant
      court announces its arrival some time in advance. A palace is des-
      ignated to receive the king and his court for weeks, or sometimes
      months, at a time.
        A sign of the relative peacefulness of the times is that these
      palaces are generally not heavily fortified.
        In the many royal palaces there are a blacksmith, a gold-
      smith, a shoemaker, a turner, a carpenter, a weapon smith, fish-
      ermen, a soap maker, foilers and net-makers, and a beer brewer.
      Some palaces stable over 200 horses.
      Royal Income
        The kings draws his income from his personal possessions,
      spread throughout Neustria and Austrasia and later in Saxony,
      plus the hundreds of royal villas used as stopovers. All these pos-
      sessions are administered by royal stewards, who regularly give
      written accounts of their dealings and reserves.
        The king collects taxes, tolls and annual “gifts” from his
      landed barons (counts and abbots). These taxes to the king are
      due at the annual May Field. The king also receives some income
      from vacancies (lands which are temporarily without a lord).
      Foreign kings pay important tributes (usually in horses and sil-
      ver). Finally, all treasure captured in war is his.
      Royal Spending

        The king spends most of his money on his court (very ex-
      pensive), the missi dominici, diplomacy, gifts to reward loyal
      vassals and servants (especially those who participated in suc-
      cessful military campaigns), and the upkeep of his domains.
      He does not spend much money on his army, since its ranks are
      filled with freemen who owe service and who must pay for their
      own equipment.
      Government
        The royal court is the place where the king gathers his most
      trusted advisers, mostly counts and bishops. Furthermore, the
      court is inhabited by the king’s relatives, powerful vassals on a
      visit, the clergy needed for administration, and the palace guards
      (the scarae and the paladins).
rightColumn:
Almost all officers of the court administration are clergy-
  men. The most important ones are the Seneschal (provisions),
  Chamberlain (treasury), Stable Master or Marshal (travel, hors-
  es), Count of the Palace or Constable (military matters, com-
  mands the scarae), Chancellor (edicts, royal charters and laws),
  Gate Warden, and the Arch-chaplain (royal letters, clerks, ar-
  chives and religious matters). The word “chaplain” derives its
  name from the court relic of Saint Martin’s cloak (capella).
     To keep in touch with his councilors, the king has set up a
  courier service between the court, his palaces, great abbeys and
  other places of power. Royal pigeons carry messages on small silk-
  en cloths. Other letters are generally confided to pilgrims or mer-
  chants, but important ones are given only to trustworthy couriers.
  Often, letters are stolen or simply got lost. As Einhard says: “A
  faithful man is surer than a letter, for all the world knows that a letter
  which escapes its carrier will divulge its contents, while a faithful man
  will resist torture rather than betray what has been entrusted to him.”
     To mark official documents, the king has two seals: one for
  laws, one for judgments. Either can be in cast in lead, or gold on
  important occasions.
     Later, the sub-kingdoms of Aquitaine and Lombardy each have
  their own palace, chapel, chancery, treasury and minting facilities.
  General  Assemblies
     There are two annual assemblies of all the major vassals and
  councilors: one in May, while the army assembles for the sum-
  mer campaign; the other at Christmas, to plan the next year’s
  campaign with the dukes and to discuss financial and adminis-
  trative planning and vital political matters with all major coun-
  cilors and officers. Other items on the agenda can be important
  issues like food prices, monetary values, or diplomatic relations
  (i.e., the continuation of war by political means).
     These assemblies are occasions for all lords to present their
  king a gift in silver or goods.
    You ought to present your gift to us at the yearly assem-
    bly, or send them to us in mid-May wherever we shall
    then be. If the direction of your march should perchance
    so shape itself as to enable you to present them to us
    during your journey, we greatly desire it. See to it that
    you show no negligence in these regards, as you wish to
    keep our favor.
       — Capitulary, anno 806
  The  Royal Family

     During the first years of Charlemagne’s reign his mother,
  Bertrada, plays an important role at court, where she remains
  until her death in 783.
     The official role of the queen is to supervise the court’s
  administration, a very important function similar to that of
  Mayor of the Palace in the times of the Merovingian kings. She
  is in charge of the treasury. In the king’s absence, the queen is
  the highest authority at court, and they maintain close contact
  through the exchange of letters.

         he royal court is called the Palace. The king has no fixed
         residence until Aachen (793). Before that he resides in
         one of the many small palaces spread across the kingdom.
      So a palace is not the Palace, but simply one of the many roy-
      al manors, or fiscs. Charlemagne personally owns about 1,000
      domains, with 200 royal palaces. Before 793, Charlemagne’s fa-
      vorite residences are Frankfurt, Mainz, Worms, Thionville and
      Herstal.
        Court is where the king is. Up to 806, the king spends most
      of his life perambulating the country from one palace or royal
      abbey to another in the company of his family. The itinerant
      court announces its arrival some time in advance. A palace is des-
      ignated to receive the king and his court for weeks, or sometimes
      months, at a time.
        A sign of the relative peacefulness of the times is that these
      palaces are generally not heavily fortified.
        In the many royal palaces there are a blacksmith, a gold-
      smith, a shoemaker, a turner, a carpenter, a weapon smith, fish-
      ermen, a soap maker, foilers and net-makers, and a beer brewer.
      Some palaces stable over 200 horses.
      Royal Income
        The kings draws his income from his personal possessions,
      spread throughout Neustria and Austrasia and later in Saxony,
      plus the hundreds of royal villas used as stopovers. All these pos-
      sessions are administered by royal stewards, who regularly give
      written accounts of their dealings and reserves.
        The king collects taxes, tolls and annual “gifts” from his
      landed barons (counts and abbots). These taxes to the king are
      due at the annual May Field. The king also receives some income
      from vacancies (lands which are temporarily without a lord).
      Foreign kings pay important tributes (usually in horses and sil-
      ver). Finally, all treasure captured in war is his.
      Royal Spending

The king spends most of his money on his court (very ex-
      pensive), the missi dominici, diplomacy, gifts to reward loyal
      vassals and servants (especially those who participated in suc-
      cessful military campaigns), and the upkeep of his domains.
      He does not spend much money on his army, since its ranks are
      filled with freemen who owe service and who must pay for their
      own equipment.
      Government
        The royal court is the place where the king gathers his most
      trusted advisers, mostly counts and bishops. Furthermore, the
      court is inhabited by the king’s relatives, powerful vassals on a
      visit, the clergy needed for administration, and the palace guards
      (the scarae and the paladins).

Almost all officers of the court administration are clergy-
  men. The most important ones are the Seneschal (provisions),
  Chamberlain (treasury), Stable Master or Marshal (travel, hors-
  es), Count of the Palace or Constable (military matters, com-
  mands the scarae), Chancellor (edicts, royal charters and laws),
  Gate Warden, and the Arch-chaplain (royal letters, clerks, ar-
  chives and religious matters). The word “chaplain” derives its
  name from the court relic of Saint Martin’s cloak (capella).
     To keep in touch with his councilors, the king has set up a
  courier service between the court, his palaces, great abbeys and
  other places of power. Royal pigeons carry messages on small silk-
  en cloths. Other letters are generally confided to pilgrims or mer-
  chants, but important ones are given only to trustworthy couriers.
  Often, letters are stolen or simply got lost. As Einhard says: “A
  faithful man is surer than a letter, for all the world knows that a letter
  which escapes its carrier will divulge its contents, while a faithful man
  will resist torture rather than betray what has been entrusted to him.”
     To mark official documents, the king has two seals: one for
  laws, one for judgments. Either can be in cast in lead, or gold on
  important occasions.
     Later, the sub-kingdoms of Aquitaine and Lombardy each have
  their own palace, chapel, chancery, treasury and minting facilities.
  General  Assemblies
     There are two annual assemblies of all the major vassals and
  councilors: one in May, while the army assembles for the sum-
  mer campaign; the other at Christmas, to plan the next year’s
  campaign with the dukes and to discuss financial and adminis-
  trative planning and vital political matters with all major coun-
  cilors and officers. Other items on the agenda can be important
  issues like food prices, monetary values, or diplomatic relations
  (i.e., the continuation of war by political means).
     These assemblies are occasions for all lords to present their
  king a gift in silver or goods.
    You ought to present your gift to us at the yearly assem-
    bly, or send them to us in mid-May wherever we shall
    then be. If the direction of your march should perchance
    so shape itself as to enable you to present them to us
    during your journey, we greatly desire it. See to it that
    you show no negligence in these regards, as you wish to
    keep our favor.
       — Capitulary, anno 806
  The  Royal Family

During the first years of Charlemagne’s reign his mother,
  Bertrada, plays an important role at court, where she remains
  until her death in 783.
     The official role of the queen is to supervise the court’s
  administration, a very important function similar to that of
  Mayor of the Palace in the times of the Merovingian kings. She
  is in charge of the treasury. In the king’s absence, the queen is
  the highest authority at court, and they maintain close contact
  through the exchange of letters.

title: Court Scholars
leftColumn:
The children of the royal family are guarded by palace
      guards whenever the court moves from one palace to another.
      Bastards are cherished as much as legitimate children. All royal
      children receive not only a solid education, but they follow the
      king in war, assist at assemblies, and meet counts and bishops
      all around the empire. In this way they learn the arts of manage-
      ment, war, and diplomacy.
        Charlemagne refuses to marry his daughters to Frankish
      noblemen, keeping them at court instead. He also takes in his
      granddaughters. These young women live with their lovers and
      have children without being officially married. Princesses take
      part in all important acts of royal representation, at festivals,
      banquets, and on the hunt. They exercise considerable political
      influence and collectively fulfill the role of a queen.
      Court Scholars
       For although correct conduct may be better than knowl-
       edge, nevertheless knowledge precedes conduct.
           — Alcuin, letter

      Need For Brains
        Bearing in mind the radiance and splendor of the courts he
      saw in Pavia, Rome and Byzantium, Charlemagne is determined
      to found a circle of educated men who can act as his council-
      ors, administrators, ambassadors and interpreters. He therefore
      has an urgent need for people with useful language skills, as the
      Saracens and the Persians speak Arabic, the Romans and the
      Lombards speak Latin, the Slavs speak Slavic, the Byzantines
      speak Greek and the Huns speak Turkish. Only the Visigoths,
      Britons, Saxons and Danes speak Germanic dialects similar to
      the language of the Franks.
        Most Frankish scholars speak Latin, but apart from some
      monks in southern Italy, very few scholars speak Greek. Hebrew
      and Arabic are completely foreign to Christians.
      The Palace Academy
        In concordance with the idea of “spiritual paladins,” the
      Palatine Academy is founded in 780, formed by twelve intel-
      lectuals from all around the empire and led by Alcuin. Their
      main tasks consist of revising and correcting the Bible and other
      books, and educating court members.
        The Academy rapidly becomes a genuine center of learn-
      ing, focusing on Latin, theology and poetry. The curriculum,
      mapped out by Alcuin, consists of the classical trivium (Latin
      grammar, rhetoric, dialectic) and quadrivium (geometry, arith-
      metic, astronomy, music). Books are essential. They are brought
      to the palace from all around the empire to be copied, or given
      as gifts.
       Charlemagne was most eager in his search for wise men
       and in his determination to provide them with living
       conditions in which they could pursue knowledge in all
       reasonable comfort.
           — Einhard
rightColumn:
Apart from Charlemagne himself, the Academy’s most fa-
  mous members are the most learned Alcuin, Theodulf, Paul of
  Aquileia, Paul the Deacon, Dungal the Irishman, and Einhard.
     Poets from all over the empire compete for Charlemagne’s
  attention and his patronage, each hoping to be invited to the
  Palatine Academy one day. Such intellectuals are often not per-
  manent residents, but scholars who come to court for a certain
  period of time, during which they share their knowledge.
  The Palace School
     An important task of the Academy scholars is to maintain
  a Palace School for the instruction of the future administrative
  elite of the kingdom. Alcuin’s itinerant Palace School is open to
  both the sons of nobles and humble boys of talent. The king and
  his officers single out the most proficient and promote them to
  vacant offices. The Palace School evolves into a sort of universi-
  ty; graduating bishops, abbots and palace officers.
     Normally, teachers instruct their pupils in the Palatine
  Chapel, but Charlemagne likes to move around and benefit
  from their wisdom at any place he sees fit. The Palace School
  therefore follows the king around anywhere, including to hunt-
  ing lodges or the baths of the thermae. Charlemagne’s sons and
  daughters study at the Palace School, and the other members of
  the royal family often attend lessons as well.
     Poetry and other literary games are a favorite pastime, such
  as these metaphorical riddles:
   n
     What is air? — The guardian of life.
   n
     What is the moon? — The eye of the night.
   n
     What is the sea? — The road of the daring.
     In this manner, literacy among the young nobles (both men
  and women) who study at the Palace School becomes quite com-
  mon. The Carolingian nobility are the last laity to be educated
  for many generations.
     Rapidly, the School becomes more and more internation-
  al and cosmopolitan. People come from all over the world and
  bring presents like relics, books, silks, perfumes, tents, precious
  swords, or strange beasts. Charlemagne happily uses the splen-
  dor of foreign ambassadors and their gifts to impress hostages
  and other foreign envoys.
  Palatine Troops
  Scarae
     Charlemagne’s elite palace knights are called the scarae (sin-
  gular: scara). These are formed into small units of fast, heavy
  cavalry under the direct command of the king, his sons or the
  paladins in time of war. Scarae wear red cloaks or capes and bear
  the royal insignia. Most paladins are recruited from their ranks.
     The scarae are the army’s backbone. They are well-trained,
  well-equipped, immediately available and highly-mobile mount-
  ed troops, using coordinated lance charges. Their tasks include
  the defense of convoys and messengers, the construction of fron-
  tier defenses, and the protection of troops who are plundering
