title: Knighthood
leftColumn:
enemy territory. Apart from being a hardened task-force of loy-
      al troops, the scarae also provide the leadership for less-reliable
      warriors.
        The scarae themselves hold no land. The constable is re-
      sponsible for their upkeep, and they may provision themselves
      at the many royal palaces when they are sent out on a military
      mission. This enables them to be very mobile. They usually con-
      tinue their career as counts in conquered or confiscated lands.
      Paladins
       One day King Charlemagne was sitting in his great hall
       amidst his vassals, and he told them: “By the grace of
       God, and if you agree to it, I would like to choose twelve
       worthy men to lead the palace guards in battle to con-
       front the pagans with courage.” They all replied favorably
       and asked him to accomplish his wish.
         So the king declared: “I will name as paladins first my
       kinsman Roland, then Oliver, thirdly Turpin; the fourth
       man shall be Gerier, the fifth Garin, the sixth be Ber-
       enger, the seventh Otto and the eighth Samson; ninth I
       name Engelier, tenth is Ivo, eleventh Ivory and twelfth be
       Walter. I place them at the head of my army to fight the
       pagans, in memory of the order God gave his twelve apos-
       tles to spread His word all around the world; and like-
       wise shall each one of you bring aid and strength when
       danger is highest, as if you were all blood-brothers.” All
       accepted this mission gladly.
           — Karlamagnus Saga, I.59
        Charlemagne creates the order of paladins at the very be-
      ginning of his reign (see The Adventure of the Humble Squires
      in Chapter 19). The twelve paladins, or peers, are the king’s per-
      sonal bodyguard and friends, his most trusted councilors, excep-
      tionally valorous and skilled warriors, the most renowned and
      exemplary young knights of his realm and the honored paragons
      of chivalry.
        For a knight to be elected, a paladin must present him to
      the king and the other peers. They collectively decide if the can-
      didate is worthy of receiving the high honor of paladinhood.
        To symbolize their function as heroic knights on the path
      to sainthood, paladins dress in scarlet and gold. Paladins have
      the sacred task of converting pagan adversaries.
        Paladins hold many royal prerogatives. Broadly speaking,
      they have the powers later given to the missi dominici and the
      military command given to dukes. Another privilege is that they
      can only be judged by their peers.
      Charlemagne wishes to condemn Huon, a paladin, without
      a proper trial. Duke Naymo is furious and addresses himself
      to the remaining peers:
       “Peers, stand up and leave this court with me, for the em-
       peror has lost his wits; since Our Lord was born, never
       have I heard spoken such monstrous injustice as the one
       our emperor commits towards Huon, the young and noble
       paladin. Nobody should stay at this imperial court, for
rightColumn:
who knows if the same shameful fate awaits us all. Had
    you acted like Huon, you would have found yourselves
    disinherited like him; and as the emperor treats him in
    such a way, not respecting the lawful procedures, do you
    really think he will do us justice tomorrow?”
      All paladins immediately leave the palace, accompa-
    nied by Duke Naymon. Charlemagne sits alone on his
    throne; he has only servants and squires left. Seeing this,
    the emperor feels an immense sadness.
       — Huon of Bordeaux, XVIII
  Knighthood

    A knight without a horse and a lance is just a warrior.
  Knightly Class

  I
      n the beginning, all men were equal in a perfect world of
      harmony and peace. But Adam and Eve condemned all
      humanity to live in the world of trouble and death. Envy
  and covetousness came into being, and when men became vi-
  olent, then might triumphed over right. Cruel people became
  leaders and forced themselves upon the weak and helpless.
     Knighthood was instituted to restrain the unjust and to de-
  fend the weak. The most courageous, most loyal, strongest man
  in every thousand was chosen to be a knight (mille). He was giv-
  en weapons, armor, a noble horse and a squire to serve him. He
  was placed over the common people to protect them from tyr-
  anny and wild beasts. Commoners, in turn, were to till the earth
  and support the knight. Since virtue and valor are inherited, it
  has been the duty of each knight to train his son to follow in
  his noble steps, and so the institution has continued. The great
  Biblical heroes were knights: Judas Maccabeus and King David,
  for instance. Ancient pagans were knights as well: Alexander
  and Julius Caesar are among their number.
  The  Rise of Knighthood
     “Who knighted you?” is a very common and important ques-
  tion. The man who gave you spurs and a sword is like a father to
  you, even if he doesn’t happen to be your lord — which is usually
  the case. Knighthood becomes the unquestioned standard un-
  der Charlemagne, perfected in the concept of chivalry. But what
  were things like for the warrior class before Charlemagne?
     Before Charles Martel’s time, very little distinguished the
  cavalry from foot soldiers, as their fighting methods did not
  fundamentally differ. Charles Martel introduced the use of the
  stirrup and the early versions of the high-framed saddle. Using
  this technological advance, he taught the Franks the use of the
  cavalry charge.
     During Pepin’s reign the word “knight” described successful
  warriors owning land and a horse, and who were often distant
  relatives of the king. “Knight” became the name of a distinct
  group of fighters, strengthened in their unity by the fame of

        The scarae themselves hold no land. The constable is re-

      Paladins
       One day King Charlemagne was sitting in his great hall
       amidst his vassals, and he told them: “By the grace of
       God, and if you agree to it, I would like to choose twelve
       worthy men to lead the palace guards in battle to con-
       front the pagans with courage.” They all replied favorably
       and asked him to accomplish his wish.
         So the king declared: “I will name as paladins first my
       kinsman Roland, then Oliver, thirdly Turpin; the fourth
       man shall be Gerier, the fifth Garin, the sixth be Ber-
       enger, the seventh Otto and the eighth Samson; ninth I
       name Engelier, tenth is Ivo, eleventh Ivory and twelfth be
       Walter. I place them at the head of my army to fight the
       pagans, in memory of the order God gave his twelve apos-
       tles to spread His word all around the world; and like-
       wise shall each one of you bring aid and strength when
       danger is highest, as if you were all blood-brothers.” All
       accepted this mission gladly.
           — Karlamagnus Saga, I.59
        Charlemagne creates the order of paladins at the very be-
      ginning of his reign (see The Adventure of the Humble Squires
      in Chapter 19). The twelve paladins, or peers, are the king’s per-
      sonal bodyguard and friends, his most trusted councilors, excep-
      tionally valorous and skilled warriors, the most renowned and
      exemplary young knights of his realm and the honored paragons
      of chivalry.
        For a knight to be elected, a paladin must present him to
      the king and the other peers. They collectively decide if the can-
      didate is worthy of receiving the high honor of paladinhood.
        To symbolize their function as heroic knights on the path
      to sainthood, paladins dress in scarlet and gold. Paladins have
      the sacred task of converting pagan adversaries.
        Paladins hold many royal prerogatives. Broadly speaking,
      they have the powers later given to the missi dominici and the
      military command given to dukes. Another privilege is that they
      can only be judged by their peers.

  Knighthood

A knight without a horse and a lance is just a warrior.
  Knightly Class

I
      n the beginning, all men were equal in a perfect world of
      harmony and peace. But Adam and Eve condemned all
      humanity to live in the world of trouble and death. Envy
  and covetousness came into being, and when men became vi-
  olent, then might triumphed over right. Cruel people became
  leaders and forced themselves upon the weak and helpless.
     Knighthood was instituted to restrain the unjust and to de-
  fend the weak. The most courageous, most loyal, strongest man
  in every thousand was chosen to be a knight (mille). He was giv-
  en weapons, armor, a noble horse and a squire to serve him. He
  was placed over the common people to protect them from tyr-
  anny and wild beasts. Commoners, in turn, were to till the earth
  and support the knight. Since virtue and valor are inherited, it
  has been the duty of each knight to train his son to follow in
  his noble steps, and so the institution has continued. The great
  Biblical heroes were knights: Judas Maccabeus and King David,
  for instance. Ancient pagans were knights as well: Alexander
  and Julius Caesar are among their number.
  The  Rise of Knighthood
     “Who knighted you?” is a very common and important ques-
  tion. The man who gave you spurs and a sword is like a father to
  you, even if he doesn’t happen to be your lord — which is usually
  the case. Knighthood becomes the unquestioned standard un-
  der Charlemagne, perfected in the concept of chivalry. But what
  were things like for the warrior class before Charlemagne?
     Before Charles Martel’s time, very little distinguished the
  cavalry from foot soldiers, as their fighting methods did not
  fundamentally differ. Charles Martel introduced the use of the
  stirrup and the early versions of the high-framed saddle. Using
  this technological advance, he taught the Franks the use of the
  cavalry charge.
     During Pepin’s reign the word “knight” described successful
  warriors owning land and a horse, and who were often distant
  relatives of the king. “Knight” became the name of a distinct
  group of fighters, strengthened in their unity by the fame of

leftColumn:
their ancestors. For these knights, their illiteracy was a source of
      pride: they valued only the blood and the body, not the mind.
        Without something to distinguish knights from other war-
      riors (apart from their equipment) no real knighthood existed.
      With Charlemagne, however, the lance charge gives knights
      this something special. Before that time, the lance was used as
      a javelin, thrown over-hand. The lance charge is most efficient
      in disciplined formations (conroi) rallied around the leader’s
      banner. This way of fighting reinforces group consciousness and
      fraternity between mounted knights, and gives them a sense of
      superiority over the ‘common warriors’.
        The development of lance charges leads to the upgrading
      of the existing ring mail armor: first comes chain mail (Phase
      1) followed by the reinforced chain (Phase 2), the partial plate
      harness (Phase 3) and finally full plate armor (Phase 4). A good
      war horse is necessary to the knightly fighting style. Failure to
      present oneself fully equipped at the army muster can lead to the
      loss of both knighthood and lands!
        So, knights become special not only because of their equip-
      ment, but by their way of fighting. They separated themselves as
      a group, needing special training and funds to equip themselves
      with horses and armor. Knights prefer to surrender to another
      knight rather than to a foot soldier, the latter being less hon-
      orable. Knights gradually develop a code of conduct proper to
      their class: the code of chivalry, based on the pillars of loyalty,
      honor, valor, generosity, courtesy, and glory.
        It isn’t until Charlemagne comes to power that dubbing
      a new knight becomes more than a simple non-religious fami-
      ly ceremony, during which a soldier is given armor, weapons, a
      horse and spurs by his lord. Knighting becomes a symbol of an
      elite, a sort of a military decoration during one’s career, an hon-
      orific title. To become part of the group of warriors serving a
      lord, a warrior has to pass initiatory rites or trials of courage and
      strength to forge a sense of fraternity.
      Hereditary Titles
        Knighthood becomes hereditary in Phase 1. Before that
      time knighthood isn’t yet a social class, and the warrior class does
      not coincide with landed nobility. Up until Charlemagne’s time
      all nobles were knights, but not all knights were nobles — far
      from it.
        As titles and lands are not yet hereditary, young Frankish
      knights need to win lands in foreign territory. Those who are
      in the fortunate position to inherit status and property are not
      allowed to do so while their father is still able to “exercise juris-
      diction, march with the army, judge people, leap on his horse and
      carry his arms effectively.”
      Becoming  a Knight
        Generally, sons of the nobility spend their first years under
      the care of their mothers. But they are also looked after by wet
      nurses and later by teachers. From about six years of age, they
      learn to ride, to use weapons and to hunt.

A formalized sequence for learning the skills of knighthood
  is an established part of the feudal tradition. Except under very
  special conditions, every aspirant to knighthood must follow
  these steps:
     Pages are young boys and girls between the ages of 10 and
  14, who are learning the ways of courtly life by observing their
  elders and doing those tasks assigned to them. After serving as
  pages, most girls become maids-in-waiting and wives. Boys be-
  come squires, often in the service of a maternal uncle. The un-
  cle-nephew bond is much stronger than the father-son relation-
  ship, so sons were attached to their mothers’ rather than to their
  father’s families.
     Boys become squires at age 15. Squires are servants of their
  knights. They study the ways of knighthood while they serve.
  Those who are confident in themselves, who show promise, and
  have the right connections may become knights. Most remain
  squires.
     Older squires are sometimes their lord’s minstrels. These
  warrior-minstrels fight on the battlefield, like young Graelant in
  the Chanson d’Aspremont, or William Shortnose’s squire in
  the Chanson de Guillaume.
     Squires may practice, but may not fight, with swords. Upon
  reaching adulthood, a young nobleman receives his sword from
  his father and is dubbed a knight. Knights vow “to protect peace,
  churches, God, orphans and widows, and to fight crimes against
  the poor, the Church and women.” Most aspirants must wait until
  age 18 to be knighted after serving three years as squires. Men
  knighted younger are exceptional, but not unknown.
     Young knights often leave their homes (voluntarily or not)
  to become knights errant. There usually is not enough land to
  inherit (if any), so those who won’t inherit must go adventuring
  in the hope of gaining Glory, a wife, and land elsewhere.
  Coat  of Arms
     Each knight has his individual and unique coat of arms.
  This is a design carried on his shield and surcoat, and is used to
  mark anything of the owner’s as a personal possession. Only the
  man, his wife, and his herald (who wears a special type of coat
  called a tabard) can wear a knight’s personal arms. His eldest son
  wears the arms, but with a special mark called a difference, which
  is taken off only after he inherits the title and rights of his dead
  father. Other sons generally make some modification to their fa-
  ther’s coat, and so families often have similar coats of arms. The
  art and science of understanding coats of arms is called Heraldry,
  which becomes extremely detailed and complex over the course
  of the campaign.
  Chivalry
     With the development of chivalry, warfare becomes less
  barbaric — civilian populations are no longer systematically put
  to the sword or sold into slavery after a successful raid or a siege.
  In ritualizing warfare, knighthood distils an elite amongst the
  warrior class. The intent to civilize knights — to turn the elite
  warriors into a moral elite as well — gives rise to the ideal of

title: Court Life
leftColumn:
chivalry (Phase 1) which tries to change “might makes right”
      into a warrior ethos based on service and respect.
        Paladin differentiates between knighthood and chivalry.
        Knighthood is the simple act of being a knight: a mounted,
      armored fighting man loyally serving his lord and maintaining
      his status. Honor is required, because Honor is a personal virtue
      that maintains loyalty and proves class status.
        Chivalry, however, is a higher standard. It requires be-
      havior that is above and beyond that of simple knighthood.
      It is the behavior of noblesse oblige, or the “obligations of no-
      bles.” This means that the knight must act in a manner that
      does not exploit their superior class status, but behave in a
      reasonable manner towards all people of their land, including
      commoners and women; and towards all people of their own
      class, even if foreign.
        Chivalry is not expected, or even honored, at the start of
      the Paladin campaign, but from Phase 2 on it becomes the
      norm, especially for landless knights.
      Combat  for Love or Conquest

        Knights may decide to do combat “for love” or “for con-
      quest.” Both knights must agree to the terms or else the combat
      is for conquest.
        “For Love” means that the knights fight for the love of
      fighting, not for personal gain. When there is a friendly joust,
      the winner receives the Glory for winning, but nothing else.
      Paladins are always expected to joust and fight one another for
      love.
        “For Conquest” is more serious. This combat is hostile,
      roughly equivalent to an act of war. This does not mean that it
      will end in death, but it might. The loser in the struggle is not
      always held for ransom, but can be. Alternatively, and more pop-
      ularly, the winner seizes the loser’s horse, weapons, and armor as
      his reward, and lets the man go. Some vile knights fight for con-
      quest but accept no ransoms, preferring to keep their captives in
      shameful imprisonment.
      Chivalric Sieges
        To reduce the traditional wanton slaughter of the gar-
      rison and the population after the capture of a town, King
      Charlemagne issues the following rules for chivalric sieges:
       n
        A besieging army may isolate a castle by siege, seeking
        victory through starvation of and deprivation to the
        resident.
       n
        A besieging army may assault a castle or city, and at-
        tack it with full force, but may not kill non-combat-
        ants; nor may they burn down or otherwise destroy
        buildings, crop fields, orchards, vineyards or other
        sources of income.
       n
        Besieger or besieged may offer individual combat to
        resolve the seige; combatants agree to obey the rules
        of chivalry in this combat.
rightColumn:
n
     The besieged agrees to surrender if he is not relieved
     within 90 days after the siege is fully engaged. “Fully
     engaged” is determined by the besieged, who may
     still be able to get supplies and men into the castle.
   n
     A surrendered city agrees to pay a “plunder tax” to the
     victor equal to a fifth of the total value of the city at
     the moment of its surrender (envoys from the royal
     treasury determine its value).
  Court   Life
  C
      ourt” refers to three things: a ceremony, the members of
      a ruling body, and the location where they meet. Holding
      court is an activity during which nobles perform their
  public duties and includes legal and property judgments, rul-
  ings on criminal charges, public announcements, receiving fealty
  from vassals, and knightings.
  Membership
     It is the duty of all vassals to offer advice in their lord’s
  court, so they are often there. They must come whenever sum-
  moned, and are welcome to come whenever they want or need
  to. Appointed household officers, such as a seneschal or marshal,
  are always at court. The important persons of a court are called
  courtiers.
  Location
     The location where court is held may be an outside court-
  yard. Often that is the only place large enough to hold the as-

segments.text:
chivalry (Phase 1) which tries to change “might makes right”
      into a warrior ethos based on service and respect.
        Paladin differentiates between knighthood and chivalry.
        Knighthood is the simple act of being a knight: a mounted,
      armored fighting man loyally serving his lord and maintaining
      his status. Honor is required, because Honor is a personal virtue
      that maintains loyalty and proves class status.
        Chivalry, however, is a higher standard. It requires be-
      havior that is above and beyond that of simple knighthood.
      It is the behavior of noblesse oblige, or the “obligations of no-
      bles.” This means that the knight must act in a manner that
      does not exploit their superior class status, but behave in a
      reasonable manner towards all people of their land, including
      commoners and women; and towards all people of their own
      class, even if foreign.
        Chivalry is not expected, or even honored, at the start of
      the Paladin campaign, but from Phase 2 on it becomes the
      norm, especially for landless knights.
      Combat  for Love or Conquest

Knights may decide to do combat “for love” or “for con-
      quest.” Both knights must agree to the terms or else the combat
      is for conquest.
        “For Love” means that the knights fight for the love of
      fighting, not for personal gain. When there is a friendly joust,
      the winner receives the Glory for winning, but nothing else.
      Paladins are always expected to joust and fight one another for
      love.
        “For Conquest” is more serious. This combat is hostile,
      roughly equivalent to an act of war. This does not mean that it
      will end in death, but it might. The loser in the struggle is not
      always held for ransom, but can be. Alternatively, and more pop-
      ularly, the winner seizes the loser’s horse, weapons, and armor as
      his reward, and lets the man go. Some vile knights fight for con-
      quest but accept no ransoms, preferring to keep their captives in
      shameful imprisonment.
      Chivalric Sieges
        To reduce the traditional wanton slaughter of the gar-
      rison and the population after the capture of a town, King
      Charlemagne issues the following rules for chivalric sieges:
       n
        A besieging army may isolate a castle by siege, seeking
        victory through starvation of and deprivation to the
        resident.
       n
        A besieging army may assault a castle or city, and at-
        tack it with full force, but may not kill non-combat-
        ants; nor may they burn down or otherwise destroy
        buildings, crop fields, orchards, vineyards or other
        sources of income.
       n
        Besieger or besieged may offer individual combat to
        resolve the seige; combatants agree to obey the rules
        of chivalry in this combat.

n
     The besieged agrees to surrender if he is not relieved
     within 90 days after the siege is fully engaged. “Fully
     engaged” is determined by the besieged, who may
     still be able to get supplies and men into the castle.
   n
     A surrendered city agrees to pay a “plunder tax” to the
     victor equal to a fifth of the total value of the city at
     the moment of its surrender (envoys from the royal
     treasury determine its value).
  Court   Life
  C
      ourt” refers to three things: a ceremony, the members of
      a ruling body, and the location where they meet. Holding
      court is an activity during which nobles perform their
  public duties and includes legal and property judgments, rul-
  ings on criminal charges, public announcements, receiving fealty
  from vassals, and knightings.
  Membership
     It is the duty of all vassals to offer advice in their lord’s
  court, so they are often there. They must come whenever sum-
  moned, and are welcome to come whenever they want or need
  to. Appointed household officers, such as a seneschal or marshal,
  are always at court. The important persons of a court are called
  courtiers.
  Location
     The location where court is held may be an outside court-
  yard. Often that is the only place large enough to hold the as-
  sembly. Court may also be held in the bailey of the castle. Some
  ancient customs insist that the local court be held outside on a
  hill, near an ancient landmark, or by some sacred grove. In large
  palaces the court might be held inside a building, in which case
  the room is called a courtroom.
     In any setting, the presiding lord has a high seat or throne
  from which he listens to petitioners and pronounces his
  judgments.
  Court  Protocol

One of the most frequently occurring events in Paladin is
  to visit the court of a lord, either your own or a stranger. Upon
  arrival at any court, a knight or other nobleman is obliged to go
  to the lord and present himself. He is then treated according to
  his station. To be at court unannounced or to depart without
  permission are both grave insults to the host lord. To do either
  is a violation of the laws of hospitality as well, and costs Honor.
  In general, a knight visiting a strange court goes to the lord, then
  expects to:
   n
     Be interviewed
   n
     Be feasted
   n
     Receive appropriate accommodations
   n
     Depart when finished

title: Hunting
leftColumn:
The Interview
        Visitors should always go before their host and announce
      themselves, their lineage, and their business. In this way, every-
      one knows and recognizes the visitor and their correct station
      at court. The lord learns just what kind of person has come into
      his home.
      The Feast

        Everyone eats together at night. The great hall is converted
      into a dining room. Noble guests are always invited to stay and
      are given a place to eat appropriate to their station. If they are of
      great Glory they sit at the high table, where ladies and knights
      are seated alternately. Lowly errant knights are relegated to eat
      with the household knights.
        At a feast, the participants engage in courtly activities, like
      playing knightly games (chess or backgammon), challenging
      other knights to (sometimes mock) combat, reading poetry, tell-
      ing stories, boasting, singing, dancing, seducing, gossiping, or
      talking to the clergy about the True Faith.
      Accommodations
        Accommodations are simple. Visiting knights are usually
      invited to spend the night in the main hall with the household
      knights of the lord. Alternatively they may sleep in the stables,
      occasionally on the ramparts, or in the outer court. Most of the
      rest of the castle is occupied by the lord and his family, officers,
      household knights, and servants.
        Ranking noblemen are given more private accommoda-
      tions. Groups of knights might be given a tower room.
      Departure
        Protocol demands that the lord approve a knight’s depar-
      ture. Under normal conditions this is granted without problems.
      Refusal, however, can be used to political purposes.

      A Typical Court  Session

        Any court action requires the presence of witnesses and ad-
      visers for the lord. Vassals provide the lord these services. The
      advisers include knights, the lord’s wife, possibly other lords,
      priests, or whoever the lord finds useful or necessary.
        When entering court, noblemen enter in reverse order of
      precedence: the least important enters first and the more im-
      portant later. Visitors, plaintiffs, and others with court duties
      wait outside at the door until summoned.
        During the session pages and squires, and occasionally
      knights, clear a path for entry of their lord. Guards take positions
      to protect the throne. As a fanfare is blown heralds announce,
      “All rise for (name and title),” as the lord enters and takes his seat.
        Court is opened with a solemn announcement, the lord sits,
      and everyone begins business. The lord and advisers are at one
      end, guards and courtiers along the walls, and others in the rear
      or outside. The center of the room is open for speakers.
rightColumn:
Matters of the court are addressed in order of precedence.
  The matters dealing with the highest-ranking petitioner are act-
  ed upon first, with the lowly waiting patiently for their turn later.
     The lord acknowledges gifts, receives envoys, and greets im-
  portant visitors. Petitions are presented, boons are sought, feuds
  are judged, and criminal actions are punished.
     After business ends the lord rises, a fanfare is blown, and the
  lord departs with his officers and men-at-arms.
  Hunting

  H
      unting is a form of combat training with horses and weap-
      ons. Both lay and ecclesiastical aristocrats share a passion
      for the hunt. Counts, bishops and abbots maintain sizable
  dog packs. In some places the king has set aside forests for him-
  self alone, and to take game in them without permission is an
  offense of High Treason, punishable by death. The king charges
  foresters with a survey of the royal hunting reserves, particularly
  in the Vosges, the Ardennes and the forested Massif of the Oise
  and the Aisne. He employs numerous hunters and falconers.
  Prey
     Commoners are allowed to hunt only from foot, and usu-
  ally with snares, dead-falls, or bows; to take squirrel, hare, and
  birds, or vermin — like badgers, which are a danger to chicken
  coops, but not to humans.
     Deer are usually reserved for noblemen to hunt. Nobles
  hunt from horseback, with packs of hounds to lead the pur-
  suit and a train of commoners to assist and to carry the meat.
  Hunting is not just for entertainment; the food gathered is nec-
  essary for survival. Lions and bears are killed for the public good,
  as well as for the glory of chivalry. If monsters are discovered, it is
  always the duty of knights to destroy them.
  The  Hunt

     A hunt can be an important social occasion. Any kind of
  finery may be worn. Practical men wear good leather hunting
  clothes, similar to light (1 point) armor. Boar spears and swords
  are the main weapons taken, but it is not dishonorable for a
  knight to use a bow when hunting deer.
     The process of the hunt begins slowly, and is suitable for
  ladies. At dawn the hounds and dog boys go out to find the first
  traces of game. Knights and ladies have a light breakfast, a stirrup
  cup for luck, and when the horn sounds the departure they set
  off to pre-selected sites. These are centrally located and, hopeful-
  ly, suitable for a picnic. Out in the woods and fields, the hunts-
  men sound certain calls on their hunting horns when they find
  suitable game. The knights set off when they hear the distant
  horns and the cries of hounds, which signal beasts to pursue. The
  women can’t usually follow the rapid coursing of the chase after
  this stage and remain behind, ready to succor whatever knight
  returns.

title: Fin’amor Formalization
leftColumn:
The hunters follow the cries of hounds until they see the
      animal, then blast their horns to signal the others that the crea-
      ture is in sight. Manners insist that the highest-ranking guest be
      allowed to slay the beast, though he can graciously decline in fa-
      vor of others if desired. Skinning and cleaning the animal, then
      cutting it into parts (called “breaking”) is a task every knight
      knows. Once properly butchered, peasants carry the meat back
      to the central ground.
        The chase is at high speed through difficult terrain, and
      large parties disintegrate as luck and skill favor individuals. It
      is not unusual for people to get lost during the chase, even in
      familiar territory with lots of noise from horns and hounds all
      around. However, these make finding the way back relatively
      simple; probably to join the picnickers at the field until another
      sighted quarry calls the knight away. The skinned and dressed
      animals are collected here, and at the end of the day the party
      gathers up everything and returns to the castle.
      Fin’amor

      I
         f God is love, then for some knights and ladies fin’amor,
         or Courtly Love, is the path to salvation! Defined by its
         practitioners as the ultimate love which unites both body
      and soul, it finds social acceptance in its goal, which is to inspire
      knights to acts of heroism. It encourages virtues such as patience,
      elegance, sincerity, modesty, chastity, trust and courage. By those
      not practicing it, it is seen as a game for court lords and ladies.
        Fin’amor is an invention of ladies and poets to recognize
      and reward the gentler sex. It is deemed morally superior to or-
      dinary love. The knightly passion for ladies transcends mundane
      values. It is not based on social status and family politics, but on
      the elevating force of sheer passion. This type of love can only
      grow outside marriage, between lovers. Marriage has little to do
      with love, while fin’amor allows lovers to celebrate these sup-
      pressed emotions.
       “Is a maiden to die, then, because she permitted her true
       love to discharge his passion in her loving arms? A curse
       on the man who imposed such a law, and a curse on the
       man who can suffer it! She who is without a heart de-
       serves to die, not she who confers life upon her faithful
       lover!”
           — Orlando Furioso, IV.63
        In this sense, fin’amor can be seen as an attack against the
      institution of marriage, in which feelings of love have no place.
      Fin’amor presents a new and radical way of life, where Love be-
      comes a person’s only true master, creating an ideal in which
      the social order of marital, religious or military loyalty become
      inferior to Love. The perfect lover has no other “lord” than his
      beloved lady! In this sense, love is like an illness: it perverts the
      chivalrous ideal, for a knight in love may even forsake his loyalty
      to lord and family.
        Men must adore women. Adoration, in word, thought,
      and action is an overwhelming preoccupation. When problems
      occur, and only failure and frustration ensue, a man must be
rightColumn:
nourished by his agony until love becomes the all-encompassing

The hunters follow the cries of hounds until they see the
      animal, then blast their horns to signal the others that the crea-
      ture is in sight. Manners insist that the highest-ranking guest be
      allowed to slay the beast, though he can graciously decline in fa-
      vor of others if desired. Skinning and cleaning the animal, then
      cutting it into parts (called “breaking”) is a task every knight
      knows. Once properly butchered, peasants carry the meat back
      to the central ground.
        The chase is at high speed through difficult terrain, and
      large parties disintegrate as luck and skill favor individuals. It
      is not unusual for people to get lost during the chase, even in
      familiar territory with lots of noise from horns and hounds all
      around. However, these make finding the way back relatively
      simple; probably to join the picnickers at the field until another
      sighted quarry calls the knight away. The skinned and dressed
      animals are collected here, and at the end of the day the party
      gathers up everything and returns to the castle.
      Fin’amor

I
         f God is love, then for some knights and ladies fin’amor,
         or Courtly Love, is the path to salvation! Defined by its
         practitioners as the ultimate love which unites both body
      and soul, it finds social acceptance in its goal, which is to inspire
      knights to acts of heroism. It encourages virtues such as patience,
      elegance, sincerity, modesty, chastity, trust and courage. By those
      not practicing it, it is seen as a game for court lords and ladies.
        Fin’amor is an invention of ladies and poets to recognize
      and reward the gentler sex. It is deemed morally superior to or-
      dinary love. The knightly passion for ladies transcends mundane
      values. It is not based on social status and family politics, but on
      the elevating force of sheer passion. This type of love can only
      grow outside marriage, between lovers. Marriage has little to do
      with love, while fin’amor allows lovers to celebrate these sup-
      pressed emotions.
       “Is a maiden to die, then, because she permitted her true
       love to discharge his passion in her loving arms? A curse
       on the man who imposed such a law, and a curse on the
       man who can suffer it! She who is without a heart de-
       serves to die, not she who confers life upon her faithful
       lover!”
           — Orlando Furioso, IV.63
        In this sense, fin’amor can be seen as an attack against the
      institution of marriage, in which feelings of love have no place.
      Fin’amor presents a new and radical way of life, where Love be-
      comes a person’s only true master, creating an ideal in which
      the social order of marital, religious or military loyalty become
      inferior to Love. The perfect lover has no other “lord” than his
      beloved lady! In this sense, love is like an illness: it perverts the
      chivalrous ideal, for a knight in love may even forsake his loyalty
      to lord and family.
        Men must adore women. Adoration, in word, thought,
      and action is an overwhelming preoccupation. When problems
      occur, and only failure and frustration ensue, a man must be

audience. Women may come to court to inquire of the rules, to
      complain of their lover (who remains anonymous), and to re-
      ceive the judgment of the court whether an action (“A theoret-
      ical activity, of course…” ) is romantically correct or not. If the
      Court of Love condemns an affair, or an activity in the affair, the
      court may even rule that the love be ended!
        Troubadours are an important part of the romantic scene.
      They write and sing passionate songs that praise the lady’s
      beauty, grace, generosity, and chastity. The poems are often dis-
      guised, using the names of ancient lovers so as not to name the
      lady directly; the poet pretends to be entertaining everyone, but
      secretly sends his love and messages to someone in the court.
      Romantic Affairs
        The basic procedure for an affair is for the man to court
      the lady, who marks his success by granting favors. The granting
      of favors is always up to the lady. The man has no rights other
      than whatever she deigns to grant him. Usually the woman de-
      mands awesome proof from the lover that he is sincere. Knights
      perform great deeds, compose poetry, and wait patiently in si-
      lence for the moment that their lover grants a smile, a glance, or a
      gentle word. To a true lover, frustration only intensifies passion.
      Troubles are welcome as tests to prove ardor. The romantic love
      affair moves through these stages:
       n
        Passionate declaration of love (in private).
       n
        Virtuous rejection by the lady.
       n
        Wooing, with proofs and oaths of fidelity to the lady.
       n
        Deeds of valor and heroism to prove courage and
        strength.
       n
        A test of chastity, called the “essai,” where the lovers
        lie in bed naked without touching each other.
       n
        Acceptance of the lover by the woman, followed by
        consummation of their secret affair.
        With luck, this is as far as the affair goes. But lovers need
      to worry about:
       n
        Subterfuge and troubles, keeping their affair secret
        and alive.
       n
        A tragic ending when the affair is discovered, made
        more poignant by the depth of the tragedy.
      Chastity
        Fin’amor is often chaste and formalized. Some lovers con-
      sider the chaste affair to be the highest form of amor, gaining
      the benefits without the dangers. Unmarried women must al-
      ways be chaste. Virginity is the highest virtue for young wom-
      en. Lack of it brings shame and guilt in abundance, often re-
      sulting in the woman being forced into a convent as atonement
      and punishment.
        Married women are expected to be chaste in their exercise
      of fin’amor. To maintain their bloodline, nobles virtually impris-
      on their wives in marriage, for only then can they be sure that

their heir is actually their son. Laws state that a man may kill
  his wife and her lover if they are discovered in flagrante delicto.
  Such murder is frowned upon, but is often excused because it is
  a “crime of passion.”
     Many women work hard to maintain their chastity and use
  every device to make their lover work for each touch, glance, and
  kiss. Her obstacles are not cause for sorrow, but opportunities
  for the knight to express his devotion and prove that he is made
  powerful by the love and can overcome anything for it.
     So, despite the oppression of society, chastity is often a rel-
  ative commodity in many affairs. Courtly manners sometimes
  allow a gentle knight to kiss the hand or cheek of a lady if he has
  performed some marvelous deed for her. Meetings even between
  chaste lovers are supposed to be secret, so who can tell what goes
  on after a discreet public kiss?
     A critical aspect of fin’amor is that it is forbidden. The most
  intense of all romances have a married woman cheating on her
  husband. The purity of their bliss sets both lovers free from the
  gross material concerns of the world and places them into the
  rarefied realm of emotional commitment. The fact that adultery
  is forbidden makes its success all the sweeter. Particularly sus-
  picious or jealous husbands lock up their wives or engage spies.
  Lovers sometimes dig tunnels to the chamber of their lover! The
  suitor may take considerable risks, but the lady must be protect-
  ed from harm at all times. Discretion is primal for the preserva-
  tion of her reputation and security.
  Tournaments
  A
       tournament is a friendly competition that provides op-
       portunity for knights to exercise their martial skills in
       a non-lethal situation. It is also a market, a fair, and a
  general gathering for merry-making. A tournament provides the
  opportunity to win glory, mingle with other knights and ladies
  from around the country, and gain experience in war and courtly
  skills.
     A tournament is a formal affair that, over the years, develops
  a set of rules and procedures governing the events. Tournaments
  undergo some changes from the start of the game as the courtly
  style becomes more elegant. The older styles are still practiced in
  distant lands throughout the campaign.
     Another factor determines the style of tournament: wheth-
  er or not dulled weapons are used. Weapons so-dulled are called
  rebated. The rebated sword and lance with coronal are called
  “arms of courtesy,” (à plaisance). Regular, sharp, weapons are
  called the “arms of war” (à outrance). Knights should always
  check the style and the weaponry of a tournament before they
  enter!

        Heralds are official announcers for the events. The Marshals
      of the List include two knights and two squires whose duty is to
      act as judges, arbiters, and overseers of the event.
      Events

        Knights normally expect to participate in three events at a
      tournament: the joust, the melee, and the challenges.
      Animal Fights (Phase 1)

        These are meant as an entertainment for the commoners, in
      which animals fight each other (bulls versus bears is popular) or,
      occasionally, men fight against beasts.
      The Bohort (Phase 1)
        This is a rough-and-tumble fight of non-knights seeking to
      prove their prowess to overlords, perhaps so that an individual
      might be chosen as a squire.
      Challenges (Phase 1)

        Next come the Challenges, where one contestant can chal-
      lenge other contestants to various forms of combat for various
      reasons: proving skill or strength, resolving disputes in a civilized
      manner, to increase one’s standing in the eyes of his peers, or sim-
      ply for love of the fight.
        A knight may issue a challenge of whatever sort he wish-
      es. They generally state who is invited to the contest, and what
      weapons or other conditions. Some example challenges might
      be: “to any Lombard, a fight with maces; ” “to anyone, sword fight-
      ing on foot; ” “to anyone, a fight to knockdown with two-handed
      weapons; ” “to any Gascon knight, a joust to first blood; ” “to any
      paladin, a joust and sword.” Any qualified individual may accept
      these open challenges. Glory is accumulated in the normal way.
        A knight may also challenge a particular knight, by name,
      to a combat. This is an individual contest, and although Glory is
      gained for it, there are often other motives in this sort of match.
      To refuse such a duel without some reasonable excuse (such as
      wounds) brings a Cowardly check, and maybe rumors and the
      loss of Honor.
      The Joust (Phase 2)
        The Joust is a chance to show off individual skill and luck.
      It is the popular knightly sport of knocking each other off hors-
      es with sticks. The joust is a single-elimination tournament that
      results in a single winner. Jousts are almost always à plaisance, as
      the chance for injury or death is simply too great if war lances are
      used. As a result, Glory is gained as through normal competitive
      combat, but at the peaceful rate of 1/10 normal for each round
      in which your knight succeeds (usually 1–2 points). In addition,
      the winner gets a bonus amount which value varies with the size
      of the tournament.
        An elimination occurs when a knight knocks his opponent
      off his horse. Each knight who wins continues in the contest and

  necessary until he is eliminated, or he has eliminated all the oth-
  er knights. If the latter occurs, he wins the joust.
     In the event that one or both jousters break their lances
  without unhorsing their opponent, new lances are available. Up
  to three lances may be used. If all three lances are broken with no
  winner, the matter is settled with swords on foot. The winner is
  the first man to knock the other to the ground.
     Jousting is a martial art and although not intended to hurt,
  damage can occur. It uses the jouster’s Lance skill, but with
  blunted, hollow weapons rather than pointed and barbed spears.
  Special rules apply to jousting, see Chapter 7: Combat.
  The Melee (Phase 2)
     The Grand Melee is a mock battle between the host’s team
  and the visiting team. All combatants fight in a great battle, until
  one side is declared the winner. All participants must join either
  the host’s or visitor’s side. Glory is given to all participants as in a
  normal battle, but at 1/10 the rate. Result modifiers and victory
  modifiers are granted as in battle (see Calculate Glory in Chapter
  8). Finally, judges select the single outstanding fighter, chosen
  from either side, who is named Champion of the Melee. He is
  the winner of the tournament, and wins the grand prize.
     The game procedure for the melee is exactly like the one for
  a battle. The battle is fought in an area of several square miles,
  marked off as the combat field which often overruns fields and
  villages. A safe area, called refuge, is marked for each team. A
  time limit is set, usually half a day.
     All combatants are expected to use blunt weapons or to
  withhold their blows. Use of either method lessens the killing
  and maiming power of blows. As in battle, a knight may be as-
  sisted by his squires, sergeants or even masses of footmen. The
  object is to capture enemy knights and to bring them to the ref-
  uge, whereupon they must forfeit their horse and armor. This is
  very expensive for the losers and very lucrative for the winners.
     There are a few special rules for the Melee:
   n
     No striking foes from behind.
   n
     No striking opponents who are unhelmeted.
   n
     No striking horses — injury to a man’s steed warrants
     immediate dismissal from the tourney.
     Combatants remain in the fight until they voluntarily with-
  draw or are sent out by marshals, who act as judges to eliminate
  contestants. Simply being unhorsed does not eliminate a knight
  — sometimes his squire can bring a steed, he might capture one
  from a mounted foe, or he can receive one from a friend.
     Marshals’ rulings are final and no one may re-enter the
  melee afterward. Marshals separate combatants whose passions
  overcome their chivalry. Such bad behavior, or other bloodshed,
  usually results in the expulsion of the offender from the melee,
  and possibly from the entire tournament.

  continuous fighting. Squires ride about with new horses and
  lances for their knights, to administer first aid, and to lead

title: The Feudal Estate
leftColumn:
prisoners off the field. Knots of reserve knights wait patiently
      for their opportunity, sipping wine and critically observing the
      fight. Marshals ride about in heraldic garb shouting announce-
      ments and judgments. Leaders hold conferences to decide where
      reserves should be sent. A charge erupts here, a counter charge
      there. When a valiant fighter is unhorsed a raging melee boils
      all around him as friends seek to re-horse him before he is dis-
      charged by the marshals.
      Other Activities (Phase 2)
        Interspersed among these battles are lavish feasts, amorous
      quests, courtly socializing, and other opportunities to engage in
      Paladin roleplaying.
        Upon arrival at the tournament site a knight must present
      himself to the host, the same as at any time he enters a lord’s do-
      main. Then he must present himself to the Marshal of the List,
      to sign up for the events. There he must decide which team to
      join for the melee — the host’s, or the visiting team. Once pre-
      sented, he may enter the rest of the social activity. Before the
      competition begins, the participants are inspected to make sure
      that they qualify. Other activities are aimed at obtaining a lady’s
      support for the event.
        The Helm Show is an occasion when all tournament partic-
      ipants show up for inspection without their helmets. This gives
      the viewers a chance to review them and, if any are guilty of re-
      proach, name them.
        The Making of Windows serves a similar function. Banners of
      the participants are hung from battlements and windows so that
      the viewers can check to see who is participating. This is import-
      ant, since knights may be refused entrance into a tournament if
      they have less than 10 Honor. This is the time when ladies give
      their favors (a conspicuously-worn token) to a lover or a knight.
      Knights seek a lady’s favor to inspire them and guide them safely
      through a tournament’s perils. The usual favor-token is a scarf or
      sleeve, though a glove, necklace, or ring can be given. The favor is
      often either tied to the knight’s arm or to the tip of a lance.
      Daily  life

      The Forest
      F
         rankland is covered with “a mantle of trees.” Oaks, beech-
         es, maples, and birches are most common. Other than
         some cultivated clearings and a few slopes planted with
      vines, the forest dominates the vegetable kingdom, its boundar-
      ies giving way to heaths, swamps and bogs. Occupied clearings
      are linked by roads. The population is clustered in towns and
      around abbeys and palaces. In between lie deserted and danger-
      ously wild stretches.
        For peasants the light forest is a necessary source of income:
      nuts, wood, game, coal, honey, and resin for torches are found
      there. Shepherds, coal burners, lumberers, bee keepers, and
      poachers make their living from gifts of the woods. The light
      forests are also the hunting grounds for nobles.
rightColumn:
The deeper forest is like a desert, a vast no-man’s-land into
  which almost no one ventures. Only those who want to flee
  from society take refuge there: hermits, lovers, knights errant,
  brigands and outlaws. Hermits pursue their vocation of solitude,
  mortification and meditation, and for the same reason many
  monasteries are founded in the middle of a forest.
     The forest is a haunted place of savage beasts and swampy
  wastes. Some rare clearings aside, the deep woods are a place of
  many dangers: overgrown and hidden ponds, quicksand, marsh-
  es, thorny bushes. Chief among the terrors of the forest are the
  wild beasts who live there: stags, boars, bears, buffaloes, aurochs
  and, most of all, wolves. Other mysteries of the deep forest in-
  clude woodland sprites, trolls, sacred groves, enchanted springs,
  werewolves, giant boars, dragons, sorcerers and witches, green
  ladies, faeries and demons.
     Wolves are fought by any means: poisoning, trapping
  and hunting. Every community has a wolf hunter who collects
  the pelts of slaughtered wolves. Their skins are quite valuable.
  Sometimes knights, priests and peasants participate in collective
  hunts to eradicate wolf packs.
  The  Feudal Estate
     Most of the land is frightful wilderness with, in the words
  of Abbot Sturmius, “wild beasts of which there are great many;
  and birds flying and huge trees.” Estates are often far apart and
  separated by thick forests and swamps, with only the occasional
  small village.
     Frankish society is profoundly rural. Towns and cities are
  rare. As a result, population density is rather low. Most of the
  population works the land and only five percent lives in cities.
  The economy has sunk to a rural level and the city inhabitants
  are often peasants more than merchants or artisans.
     The lands are globally underpopulated, and certain areas
  are nearly barren of inhabitants. Villages are often quite isolat-
  ed from the outside world. In the Mediterranean areas, village
  houses are often built of stone, whereas in the north wood and
  clay are used.
  The Estate
     The large domain on which live the counts and other
  land-owning nobles is called a villa or a manor. Such a rural es-
  tate is the basis of wealth. It is a self-sustaining landholding of
  a size and income sufficient to support a knight. It is his home,
  the house where his family lives. Each estate represents a closed
  economy, and is therefore particularly vulnerable. In the absence
  of good roads and means of transport, natural disasters inevita-
  bly cause famines.
     The person who runs the economic life at the domain is
  called a steward. He is often recruited from the local freemen and
  has to know agriculture, husbandry and viticulture, and he should
  be able to write accounts and understand the law. Such men are
  hard to find. Often the priest is the only literate person in the
  village, so he often acts as a steward. Wealthy lords recruit skilled

      competition begins, the participants are inspected to make sure
      that they qualify. Other activities are aimed at obtaining a lady’s
      support for the event.
        The Helm Show is an occasion when all tournament partic-
      ipants show up for inspection without their helmets. This gives
      the viewers a chance to review them and, if any are guilty of re-
      proach, name them.
        The Making of Windows serves a similar function. Banners of
      the participants are hung from battlements and windows so that
      the viewers can check to see who is participating. This is import-
      ant, since knights may be refused entrance into a tournament if
      they have less than 10 Honor. This is the time when ladies give
      their favors (a conspicuously-worn token) to a lover or a knight.
      Knights seek a lady’s favor to inspire them and guide them safely
      through a tournament’s perils. The usual favor-token is a scarf or
      sleeve, though a glove, necklace, or ring can be given. The favor is
      often either tied to the knight’s arm or to the tip of a lance.
      Daily  life

The Forest
      F
         rankland is covered with “a mantle of trees.” Oaks, beech-
         es, maples, and birches are most common. Other than
         some cultivated clearings and a few slopes planted with
      vines, the forest dominates the vegetable kingdom, its boundar-
      ies giving way to heaths, swamps and bogs. Occupied clearings
      are linked by roads. The population is clustered in towns and
      around abbeys and palaces. In between lie deserted and danger-
      ously wild stretches.
        For peasants the light forest is a necessary source of income:
      nuts, wood, game, coal, honey, and resin for torches are found
      there. Shepherds, coal burners, lumberers, bee keepers, and
      poachers make their living from gifts of the woods. The light
      forests are also the hunting grounds for nobles.

The deeper forest is like a desert, a vast no-man’s-land into
  which almost no one ventures. Only those who want to flee
  from society take refuge there: hermits, lovers, knights errant,
  brigands and outlaws. Hermits pursue their vocation of solitude,
  mortification and meditation, and for the same reason many
  monasteries are founded in the middle of a forest.
     The forest is a haunted place of savage beasts and swampy
  wastes. Some rare clearings aside, the deep woods are a place of
  many dangers: overgrown and hidden ponds, quicksand, marsh-
  es, thorny bushes. Chief among the terrors of the forest are the
  wild beasts who live there: stags, boars, bears, buffaloes, aurochs
  and, most of all, wolves. Other mysteries of the deep forest in-
  clude woodland sprites, trolls, sacred groves, enchanted springs,
  werewolves, giant boars, dragons, sorcerers and witches, green
  ladies, faeries and demons.
     Wolves are fought by any means: poisoning, trapping
  and hunting. Every community has a wolf hunter who collects
  the pelts of slaughtered wolves. Their skins are quite valuable.
  Sometimes knights, priests and peasants participate in collective
  hunts to eradicate wolf packs.
  The  Feudal Estate
     Most of the land is frightful wilderness with, in the words
  of Abbot Sturmius, “wild beasts of which there are great many;
  and birds flying and huge trees.” Estates are often far apart and
  separated by thick forests and swamps, with only the occasional
  small village.
     Frankish society is profoundly rural. Towns and cities are
  rare. As a result, population density is rather low. Most of the
  population works the land and only five percent lives in cities.
  The economy has sunk to a rural level and the city inhabitants
  are often peasants more than merchants or artisans.
     The lands are globally underpopulated, and certain areas
  are nearly barren of inhabitants. Villages are often quite isolat-
  ed from the outside world. In the Mediterranean areas, village
  houses are often built of stone, whereas in the north wood and
  clay are used.
  The Estate
     The large domain on which live the counts and other
  land-owning nobles is called a villa or a manor. Such a rural es-
  tate is the basis of wealth. It is a self-sustaining landholding of
  a size and income sufficient to support a knight. It is his home,
  the house where his family lives. Each estate represents a closed
  economy, and is therefore particularly vulnerable. In the absence
  of good roads and means of transport, natural disasters inevita-
  bly cause famines.
     The person who runs the economic life at the domain is
  called a steward. He is often recruited from the local freemen and
  has to know agriculture, husbandry and viticulture, and he should
  be able to write accounts and understand the law. Such men are
  hard to find. Often the priest is the only literate person in the
  village, so he often acts as a steward. Wealthy lords recruit skilled

title: The Town
leftColumn:
stewards at the royal court. The increasing intellectual level of
      land administrators has a positive effect on many local economies.
        Apart from the steward, the bailiff and a few soldiers, the
      only artisans and other non-farmers on the domain are typically
      a cook, a baker, a beekeeper, a blacksmith, a ferryman, a falconer,
      a forester, a jeweler, a master of hounds, a miller, a priest, a stable
      master, a vintner, and possibly a wise woman.
      The Hall
        The heart of a domain is the stone manor. This is a fine
      farmhouse for the knight and his family. It is surrounded by a
      palisade and protected by a handful of soldiers. Its unique char-
      acteristic is its great hall where the knight holds court for his
      holdings. Sometimes, in fact, a manor is called a “hall,” implying
      everything that lies around it as well. Apart from the banqueting
      hall, it contains sleeping quarters, cellars, stables, a storehouse
      and a little chapel.
        The knight’s squire and a couple of the manor’s chief ser-
      vants live in the hall too. Other servants (the pig boy, gardener,
      stable hands, and so on) live in the buildings they work in; a sta-
      ble for the horses, a barn for the other livestock, chicken coop,
      pigsty, and storage sheds. The hall and its building are, basically,
      the nicest farm in the area.
      Demesne Lands
        These are lands that are owned by the knight. The peasants
      from the holding send men and plows to work the land. They are
      planted mostly in wheat for people and oats for horses. The peas-
      ants also pay a portion of their own harvest, generally of barley.
        Most landholders have their land in strips scattered among
      the many fields, which increases community cooperation and
      cohesion.
      The Town

        The town is the local market where the local craftsmen (black-
      smith, carpenter, cooper, etc.) can be found, and itinerant peddlers
      meet once a week to sell their wares. A town usually has a mill, a
      communal bakery, a press for wine or oil and a couple of nice hous-
      es for the richer farmers. Most buildings are peasant shacks, storage
      sheds, barley granaries and cattle byres. The population is around
      120 people, including those people who live in the Hall.
      The Church

        A small, poor church is at the center of the town. It is the larg-
      est building around, and made of stone. The priest, himself nearly
      as illiterate as the farmers, is in charge of the local congregation.
      The church is called the baptistery because baptisms, as well as
      marriages and funerals, are performed and recorded there.
      Villages
        Villages, each about a mile apart, are part of the manor.
      They each have about 60 residents who are all peasants, and who
      may engage in small crafts aside from their occupation as labor-
      ers of the land. They all go to the town for major church events,
      festivals, and to work their share for the lord. The village usually

has a small wooden church, and most other buildings are huts,
  sheds, byres and granaries.
  Land Use
     Each village is surrounded by plowed fields, meadows
  used for hay, pastures for grazing, vegetable gardens, orchards,
  vineyards, bee hives, enclosed or public fields, fishing ponds,
  and some small forests for wood gathering and charcoal burn-
  ing. Vineyards are an enterprise for the wealthy, which requires
  much hand work and care.
     Plow lands are usually crowded into the quarter-mile
  around a village or town. Much more distant than that and the
  work day is too short for the oxen to be herded daily from the vil-
  lage. Most fields grow the barley that makes the bread and ale of
  daily life. Oats are a secondary crop, while wheat is a luxury crop.
  Some foodstuffs are altogether unknown to the Franks, like
  turkey, rice, corn, citrus fruits, apricots, tomatoes, artichokes,
  brown beans and potatoes. At the beginning of Charlemagne’s
  reign, half the fields are plowed each year. The other half is left
  fallow, and used to graze livestock. By the end of his reign, the
  Franks are practicing the more effective three-field farming.
     Between the plowed lands of each village lie lands which are
  not cultivated at all, but instead supply wood, occasional wild
  fruit, and serve as the place where pigs eat. Hunting is not al-
  lowed to the peasants but, unless it is a royal forest, the knight
  can hunt on his own lands.
  Mills
     Mills grind the grain for the daily bread of the peasants.
  These are either wind mills, or water mills on floating pontoons
  attached to bridges at places where there is a narrow, fast-flowing
  water course.
     The manor lord owns the biggest mill, the ban mill, and all
  townsmen must grind their grain there. The lord collects a per-
  centage for this service, and collects a tax on all other local mills.
  Animals

     The knight needs at least five working horses at all times (1
  charger, 1 rouncy for himself, and rouncies for his squire, wife,
  and a servant). Unfortunately, most knights do not have the re-
  sources to raise chargers and the herd is usually restricted to rais-
  ing rouncies, sumpters, and cobs, and sometimes a good courser
  or palfrey (see Chapter 18: Opponents and Creatures).
     The horse herd for the manor has about 10 horses (1 stal-
  lion, 4 mares, 2 yearlings, 2 colts, 1 gelding being trained).
     Cattle provide meat, leather, and work force (plow oxen are
  castrated bulls). The manor has a herd of around 20 cattle (1 bull,
  1 yearling bull, 6 oxen, 5 milk cows, 2 unseasoned oxen, 5 calves).
     Sheep provide food and wool. A herd of about 21 serves the
  manor (1 ram, 14 sheep, 6 lambs).
     Pigs provide the most meat per pound of hoof of any do-
  mestic animal. The herd is around 31 animals (1 boar, 6 sows, 24
  piglets) and is loosed into the wasteland each year to fatten on
  wild acorns. They are rounded up in the fall.

title: Peasant Life
leftColumn:
Peasant  Life

        The year of a peasant goes roughly like this: In March the
      vines are pruned. In April the animals are put out to pasture and
      the soil is prepared. In May forage is collected and the vines are
      tied to props. June is the plow month. July is for hay growing
      and August for hay harvest. In September and October grapes
      are collected and pressed, and grain is gathered. In November,
      the wine is put into barrels and grain threshed. In December the
      pigs are slaughtered. January and February are for small repairs
      to houses, stables and fences.
        A peasant’s most precious possession is their heavy plow.
      Since metal farming utensils are rare, only rich farmers have an
      iron plow; others make do with simple wooden plows.
        Peasants are vulnerable and live a life of fear, facing natural
      disasters, illness, war and many sins, all blocking their path to
      a happy existence both on earth and in the hereafter. Winter,
      especially, is a terrible season for the poor folk.
        Food is an obsession for many — Carolingian men and
      women are haunted by the fear of hunger. Famine regularly
      strikes the population, causing the deaths of adults and chil-
      dren alike. Shortages can be caused by floods that delay the
      sowing, winters that last too long, late frosts that destroy the
      first crops, torrid summers that dry up the vegetation, or inva-
      sions of grasshoppers. The hungry are sometimes tormented
      by hallucinations: “In 793, people saw false wheat in the fields
      or covering swamps. It could be seen and touched, but not eaten.”
      There are even sporadic outbursts of cannibalism. “Some wel-
      comed the hungry into their houses, killed them and put them
      in a salt tub.”
        Epidemics of animal diseases are catastrophes on a par with
      human epidemics. Helpful monks copy books about the veteri-
      nary arts, while the common people recite magical incantations
      to save sick or lame beasts.
      Travel
     T
         ravel is a risky, time-consuming business. Outside of a few
         cultivated clearings and a few slopes planted with vines,
         almost the entire land is covered with trees. The forest
      boundaries give way to heaths, swamps and bogs. The popula-
      tion is clustered in towns and around abbeys and palaces. To go
      from one place to another requires days and nights spent travers-
      ing apparently deserted and dangerously wild stretches.
      Maps
        Geographic knowledge dates from antiquity; maps are
      nearly nonexistent. The Pope has an annotated wall-map in the
      Lateran Palace. There is a similar one in the scriptorium of Saint
      Riquier, and Bishop Theodulf has a map in his episcopal palace
      in Orleans. These maps generally represent the world as three
      continents: Asia, Africa and Europe, with Jerusalem in the cen-
      ter of the world and Paradise to the east.
rightColumn:
However, most people are illiterate and unable to read a
  map anyway. The most common type of map is an itinerarium, a
  list of stops along a road, indicated by a coat of arms of the castle
  or other stop along the way. Symbols indicate whether the stop is
  a manor, castle, monastery, city, or other landmark.
     The usual manner of getting around in a strange place is to
  have a general idea of direction, and ask for more specific infor-
  mation every time you meet someone along the way. Since most
  people you meet are locals, they have a pretty good idea of the
  local landmarks, which in the case of peasants is probably a five-
  mile radius around their homes, while knights know their own
  lands. People have only vague, and often incorrect, information
  of areas outside their homelands.
     Directions are not usually given in miles, but rather in
  vague travel times, like “a long time,” or “until noon,” or “a little
  while.” Landmarks are better described, and may be specific, like
  “the ford,” but can be confusing too: “the big tree,” or “where the
  rocks fall down” or “the ruin.” Information about dangerous ar-
  eas will be particularly sketchy, and often plain wrong. Vast areas
  of forest are unknown to anyone. Even moderately settled areas
  may be lost should brigands or a natural disaster cut off the roads
  and trails to the settlement.
  Roads  and  Other By-Ways
     Carts and mule trains are most commonly used for land
  travel, and barges for river travel. Mounts have simple wicker fit-
  tings rather than iron horseshoes; they are cheaper and less likely
  to slip on snow and ice. On busy crossroads and in some towns
  hackneymen offer branded horses for hire.
     Despite decay, the Roman road network is still in place.
  And where the ancient roads are lacking, as in Germany, the king
  creates coach roads over which his armies can pass. One of the
  prime factors of Charlemagne’s military success is the speed of
  his armies. Therefore, Charlemagne works to maintain bridges
  and ancient Roman roadways; as much to expedite the move-
  ment of armies as to facilitate commerce.
    It was the custom in those days that whenever some work
    had to be accomplished on the emperor’s orders, wheth-
    er bridges, ships, or fords, or else the cleaning, surfacing,
    or improvement of muddy roads, the counts could fulfill
    these tasks through their vicars and officials insofar as
    they were minor works. With respect to major works, and
    especially new constructions, no duke or count, and none
    of the bishops or abbots, might be excused in any way.
       — Notker
     Still, after a rainy period, mud swamps the roads. The paths
  through the forests are poorly marked and one may easily lose them.
     The Pyrenees can be crossed in the east at the Pass of La
  Perche, and in the west at Roncevaux. The Alps may be crossed
  at the Great Saint Bernard Pass in the north and at Mount Cenis
  in the west. Mountain passes are often difficult, snowy or mud-
  dy roads, best crossed with the help of local guides and porters.
  They are almost impossible to cross during winter.
