segments.text:
The year of a peasant goes roughly like this: In March the
      vines are pruned. In April the animals are put out to pasture and
      the soil is prepared. In May forage is collected and the vines are
      tied to props. June is the plow month. July is for hay growing
      and August for hay harvest. In September and October grapes
      are collected and pressed, and grain is gathered. In November,
      the wine is put into barrels and grain threshed. In December the
      pigs are slaughtered. January and February are for small repairs
      to houses, stables and fences.
        A peasant’s most precious possession is their heavy plow.
      Since metal farming utensils are rare, only rich farmers have an
      iron plow; others make do with simple wooden plows.
        Peasants are vulnerable and live a life of fear, facing natural
      disasters, illness, war and many sins, all blocking their path to
      a happy existence both on earth and in the hereafter. Winter,
      especially, is a terrible season for the poor folk.
        Food is an obsession for many — Carolingian men and
      women are haunted by the fear of hunger. Famine regularly
      strikes the population, causing the deaths of adults and chil-
      dren alike. Shortages can be caused by floods that delay the
      sowing, winters that last too long, late frosts that destroy the
      first crops, torrid summers that dry up the vegetation, or inva-
      sions of grasshoppers. The hungry are sometimes tormented
      by hallucinations: “In 793, people saw false wheat in the fields
      or covering swamps. It could be seen and touched, but not eaten.”
      There are even sporadic outbursts of cannibalism. “Some wel-
      comed the hungry into their houses, killed them and put them
      in a salt tub.”
        Epidemics of animal diseases are catastrophes on a par with
      human epidemics. Helpful monks copy books about the veteri-
      nary arts, while the common people recite magical incantations
      to save sick or lame beasts.
      Travel
     T
         ravel is a risky, time-consuming business. Outside of a few
         cultivated clearings and a few slopes planted with vines,
         almost the entire land is covered with trees. The forest
      boundaries give way to heaths, swamps and bogs. The popula-
      tion is clustered in towns and around abbeys and palaces. To go
      from one place to another requires days and nights spent travers-
      ing apparently deserted and dangerously wild stretches.
      Maps
        Geographic knowledge dates from antiquity; maps are
      nearly nonexistent. The Pope has an annotated wall-map in the
      Lateran Palace. There is a similar one in the scriptorium of Saint
      Riquier, and Bishop Theodulf has a map in his episcopal palace
      in Orleans. These maps generally represent the world as three
      continents: Asia, Africa and Europe, with Jerusalem in the cen-
      ter of the world and Paradise to the east.

However, most people are illiterate and unable to read a
  map anyway. The most common type of map is an itinerarium, a
  list of stops along a road, indicated by a coat of arms of the castle
  or other stop along the way. Symbols indicate whether the stop is
  a manor, castle, monastery, city, or other landmark.
     The usual manner of getting around in a strange place is to
  have a general idea of direction, and ask for more specific infor-
  mation every time you meet someone along the way. Since most
  people you meet are locals, they have a pretty good idea of the
  local landmarks, which in the case of peasants is probably a five-
  mile radius around their homes, while knights know their own
  lands. People have only vague, and often incorrect, information
  of areas outside their homelands.
     Directions are not usually given in miles, but rather in
  vague travel times, like “a long time,” or “until noon,” or “a little
  while.” Landmarks are better described, and may be specific, like
  “the ford,” but can be confusing too: “the big tree,” or “where the
  rocks fall down” or “the ruin.” Information about dangerous ar-
  eas will be particularly sketchy, and often plain wrong. Vast areas
  of forest are unknown to anyone. Even moderately settled areas
  may be lost should brigands or a natural disaster cut off the roads
  and trails to the settlement.
  Roads  and  Other By-Ways
     Carts and mule trains are most commonly used for land
  travel, and barges for river travel. Mounts have simple wicker fit-
  tings rather than iron horseshoes; they are cheaper and less likely
  to slip on snow and ice. On busy crossroads and in some towns
  hackneymen offer branded horses for hire.
     Despite decay, the Roman road network is still in place.
  And where the ancient roads are lacking, as in Germany, the king
  creates coach roads over which his armies can pass. One of the
  prime factors of Charlemagne’s military success is the speed of
  his armies. Therefore, Charlemagne works to maintain bridges
  and ancient Roman roadways; as much to expedite the move-
  ment of armies as to facilitate commerce.
    It was the custom in those days that whenever some work
    had to be accomplished on the emperor’s orders, wheth-
    er bridges, ships, or fords, or else the cleaning, surfacing,
    or improvement of muddy roads, the counts could fulfill
    these tasks through their vicars and officials insofar as
    they were minor works. With respect to major works, and
    especially new constructions, no duke or count, and none
    of the bishops or abbots, might be excused in any way.
       — Notker
     Still, after a rainy period, mud swamps the roads. The paths
  through the forests are poorly marked and one may easily lose them.
     The Pyrenees can be crossed in the east at the Pass of La
  Perche, and in the west at Roncevaux. The Alps may be crossed
  at the Great Saint Bernard Pass in the north and at Mount Cenis
  in the west. Mountain passes are often difficult, snowy or mud-
  dy roads, best crossed with the help of local guides and porters.
  They are almost impossible to cross during winter.

title: Travel Accommodations
leftColumn:
Crossing rivers is difficult, as safe bridges are rare. The
      Rhine, for example, can only be crossed by a wooden bridge
      at Mayence. On great rivers a ferry service is usually assured.
      Military convoys are equipped with amphibious carts covered in
      tightly-sewn leather, waterproofed with wax, pitch and tow. By
      far the easiest way to cross a river is to find a ford, but these are
      often supervised and taxed. Finding a ford in the wilderness is
      often done by following fleeing deer.
        Although slower than travel by land, waterways are very
      popular because they are safer. The army uses the navigable rivers
      to rapidly advance on the enemy. In 793 Charlemagne under-
      takes a great project to dig a canal connecting the Rhine with the
      Danube (the Fossa Carolina), but it is never completed.
      Dangers
        Traveling is not just a matter of going from one place to
      another. Besides the problems of knowing where to go are the
      problems of traveling safely and finding accommodations. This
      increases travel time. Traveling is rare during the winter season.
      With the fall of night, everybody burrows in.
        Travel is usually safe within the close demesne of a lord.
      Only knights, or clergy accompanied by soldiers or knights, can
      travel in relative safety. Other travelers are merchants, clerics
      who broke their vows, thieves and outlaws, pilgrims, self-made
      saints and heretic preachers, purveyors of false relics, peasants
      looking for better lands and kinder masters, slaves in flight, refu-
      gees from invasions, beggars, prostitutes, jugglers and minstrels,
      and slave-traders.
        For individuals, traveling is both expensive and dangerous.
      As soon as a man leaves his home he becomes a stranger, subject
      to many perils. Adventure starts at one’s front door. Bandits often
      hide within forests to waylay the unwary; travelers must always
      be on the lookout. Brigandage along secondary roads is rampant,
      especially in the forests and in the mountains. Hungering bands
      of outlaws hide in the forests and position themselves at the en-
      trances of defiles to rob travelers of the few precious objects they
      might be carrying. Although refugees are protected by the king,
      on their arrival in a new region they are sometimes captured and
      sold as slaves.
       Concerning brigands we command that the following be
       observed: for a first offense the brigand is not to die but is
       to lose an eye; for a second his nose is to be cut off; but for
       a third, if he has not mended his ways, he is to die.
           — Capitulary, anno 779
        Brigands follow the army across the country in the hopes
      of pillaging the baggage. Some brigands even work for a local
      nobleman; in return for a share in their loot, the lord lets them
      operate freely in a certain area. These bands of outlaws are some-
      times called upon to resist invaders.
      Time and Distance
        Stopping to eat and rest is a necessary part of travel. Persons
      not used to traveling, especially women or children, require
rightColumn:
more frequent stops. Large retinues can rarely cover more than
  15 or 20 miles a day, as they are often encumbered by carts, lit-
  ters, and those on foot. Depending on the road and the number
  of obstacles, like rivers, forests, and swamps, very small units of
  riders on fast and enduring horses may be able to travel up to 80
  miles in a single day along a well-maintained Roman road, stop-
  ping only to change horses at royal palaces along the way.
  Travel Accommodations

     Knights may normally stay at any castle, manor, or other
  settlement along the way. Hospitality is an honored tradition,
  and standard custom is to help any traveler according to their
  status. Most people travel very little, and are likely to be starved
  for information and gossip about the outside world. Strangers
  who are known not to be enemies are welcome, and if they are
  entertaining then they are the more welcome. No payment is ex-
  pected from visitors.
     The normal procedure is for a party to ride to the gate and
  knock, blow a horn, ring a bell, or simply shout until the porter
  comes to hear their identities. The porter is so called because his
  job is to tend the porta, or door. Being a porter is a prestigious
  job at any location, as he determines who enters immediately
  and who has to wait. The porter asks who is there and what they
  want. He may decide to allow entry right away, especially if the
  visitor is known, but more likely will go to his lord and relay the
  information before making a decision. The travelers wait pa-
  tiently outside, perhaps in the rain or the dark.
     Not everyone is welcomed. If it is an enemy who has inad-
  vertently come to the door, the porter simply stalls for a while,
  perhaps exchanging bitter or insulting words while knights and
  soldiers arm and prepare to rush out and capture the foe.
     Once guests enter a castle or manor they are shown to the
  long hall or the lord’s bedroom, where the lord welcomes and
  interviews them, and instructs servants to show the guests to
  their accommodations. Occasionally they are shown to a place
  to wash up before seeing the lord.
     Accommodations for visiting knights are normally in the
  great hall, where the household knights and ladies sleep, unseg-
  regated and without much privacy. Honored guests may be giv-
  en a chamber or tower room for themselves, but most likely have
  to share it with the rest of their party. These rooms are normally
  the residence of someone else, who has given it up for the guests.
  Only a truly great place has enough space to give individual
  guests their own private quarters.
     A worthy visitor has pages or women assigned to help him
  disarm and wash. Washing may be from a public basin or, luxury
  of luxuries, a hot bath. Women commonly help men bathe, with-
  out any sexual implication (but plenty of opportunity).
     If no castle is available, travelers sleep in hostelries near
  main roads and outside towns, administered by the local bish-
  op or a nearby monastery. Separate rooms are often available for
  different social ranks, keeping the nobility away from the com-
  moners. High-ranking individuals may actually be offered the
  quarters of the abbot.

title: Traded Goods
leftColumn:
Where no noble accommodations exist, knights may seek
      to stay at peasant dwellings. The traveler goes from building to
      building asking for hospitality until someone tentatively agrees.
      The commoner complains that he is poor with nothing to spare,
      and the traveler offers to compensate somehow. They bicker over
      the price until agreement is reached. Nothing is guaranteed except
      what is agreed upon by both parties. Remember that commoners
      are usually reluctant to allow powerful strangers into their houses,
      and may recommend someone in town who is less suspicious. Out
      of these individuals’ hospitality grow public inns.
        Inns are not known until the end of Phase 1. They are fre-
      quented mostly by pilgrims and merchants. Cities may have an
      inn or two, but they are rare elsewhere. Inns are generally of very
      poor quality, and are unlikely to have private accommodations, a
      menu to choose from, or food other than common peasant fare.
      The building is likely to house everyone in a single large room
      with a single fireplace.
        Finally, if no accommodations can be found, knights do
      what soldiers have always done: camp out on the cold, hard
      ground.
      Cities
        Many Roman towns and cities survived the fall of the
      Roman Empire and have started to grow again, especially the
      trading depots along the main rivers. Cities are normally walled
      and garrisoned, and most have a castle within their walls.
        A city, with its surrounding lands, is usually a bishopric.
      Urban life is centered around the bishop and his cathedral. Many
      taverns, for example, are owned by the bishop or a nearby abbey.
        Most citizens are members of the clergy, artisans, or local
      merchants. Each profession unites in guilds which control prod-
      ucts and protect their rights. Very specialized professions, like
      masons, glass workers and goldsmiths, produce luxury goods
      which are not for sale, but solely for the benefit of the bishop
      or abbot. The wergild of a specialized artisan is twice that of a
      normal free man.
        A typical city block consists of a cluster of wooden houses
      with thatched roofs separated by narrow alleys. These buildings
      are only two stories high, at best. Shops on the bottom floor give
      out directly to the streets, while at the back are vegetable gardens.
        A city is an administrative and political center, but plays
      only a very small economical role in the kingdom. While towns
      hold a weekly market, often on Friday or Saturday, all cities have
      a permanent market within the protecting walls of a castle or a
      monastery. Luxury goods aren’t normally produced for sale, but
      only as ordered by a rich magnate.

         merchants work in the service of wealthy counts, abbots

Important international markets last for several days
  around an annual feast day. The famous horse fair of Saint Denis
  is in the first week of October. Another such great fair is held at
  Pavia in spring.
     Travel and commercial activity is taxed, including the vehi-
  cles transporting merchandise. Harbor taxes are 10% of the car-
  go value. Some merchants working for monasteries are exempt
  from such taxes. Abbots have their own fleets and generally in-
  stall commercial land holdings on the banks of rivers and lakes.
     The main sea ports of Frankland are Marseille, Arles and
  Narbonne in the south; Nantes and Bordeaux in the west; and
  Dorestad, Boulogne, Quentovic in the north. Often, small en-
  claves of many different nationalities live in a port city, some
  of which have established permanent trading posts. There are
  many river ports along the rivers Rhone, Rhine and Meuse. Due
  to the insecurity of overland travel, river transport is the most
  common way of transporting bulk goods (wood, salt, grain, etc.)
  over long distances.
  Traded  Goods
     The principal trade goods are wheat, oats, wine, salt, mill
  stones, wood, wax and oils, slaves, and iron (a rare and precious
  metal).Salt is essential for meat and fish preservation. It comes
  from coastal salterns.
     Spices, silk (for robes) and ivory are imported from the
  East, via Italy or Spain. Frisian and Frankish merchants buy
  grain, amber, copper, fur, leather, dried fish, and carnelian in
  the Baltic and in Circassia, while the northern people buy linen,
  wool, wine, bronze and glass.
     Most trans-Mediterranean trade is in the hands of Jewish
  merchants. They buy eunuchs, slaves, cloth, bear skins, furs and
  swords in Frankland to be sold in Babylon or Byzantium. On
  their return to Italy (Pavia, Pisa, and Venice), they bring silks,
  perfumes and spices (musk, camphor, aloeswood, cinnamon). In
  some southern ports like Marseille, Arles and Narbonne, Saracen
  merchants can be found.
     In Dorestad and Nijmegen, Frisian merchants do business
  with the British Isles, where they obtain such goods as lead, tin,
  wool and cloth.
     Iron is primarily used for military purposes. Frankish swords
  are renowned and a few famous weapon smiths are considered
  magicians. It is strictly forbidden to sell Frankish metal weapons
  or armor to foreigners: “Concerning coats of mail: that no one is
  presumed to sell these outside our realm.” — Capitulary, anno
  779.
  Money
     The Franks produce quite a lot of silver from mines in the
  mountainous regions from the Ardennes to the Central Massif.
     Only the king has the right to mint coins. Minting centers
  include Dorestad, Mayence, Verdun, Paris, Limoges, Lyon and
  Marseille. Byzantine gold coins are used by wealthy merchants only.

Where no noble accommodations exist, knights may seek
      to stay at peasant dwellings. The traveler goes from building to
      building asking for hospitality until someone tentatively agrees.
      The commoner complains that he is poor with nothing to spare,
      and the traveler offers to compensate somehow. They bicker over
      the price until agreement is reached. Nothing is guaranteed except
      what is agreed upon by both parties. Remember that commoners
      are usually reluctant to allow powerful strangers into their houses,
      and may recommend someone in town who is less suspicious. Out
      of these individuals’ hospitality grow public inns.
        Inns are not known until the end of Phase 1. They are fre-
      quented mostly by pilgrims and merchants. Cities may have an
      inn or two, but they are rare elsewhere. Inns are generally of very
      poor quality, and are unlikely to have private accommodations, a
      menu to choose from, or food other than common peasant fare.
      The building is likely to house everyone in a single large room
      with a single fireplace.
        Finally, if no accommodations can be found, knights do
      what soldiers have always done: camp out on the cold, hard
      ground.
      Cities
        Many Roman towns and cities survived the fall of the
      Roman Empire and have started to grow again, especially the
      trading depots along the main rivers. Cities are normally walled
      and garrisoned, and most have a castle within their walls.
        A city, with its surrounding lands, is usually a bishopric.
      Urban life is centered around the bishop and his cathedral. Many
      taverns, for example, are owned by the bishop or a nearby abbey.
        Most citizens are members of the clergy, artisans, or local
      merchants. Each profession unites in guilds which control prod-
      ucts and protect their rights. Very specialized professions, like
      masons, glass workers and goldsmiths, produce luxury goods
      which are not for sale, but solely for the benefit of the bishop
      or abbot. The wergild of a specialized artisan is twice that of a
      normal free man.
        A typical city block consists of a cluster of wooden houses
      with thatched roofs separated by narrow alleys. These buildings
      are only two stories high, at best. Shops on the bottom floor give
      out directly to the streets, while at the back are vegetable gardens.

title: Slavery
leftColumn:
Banks are unknown. Jews and abbeys fulfill the rôle of mon-
      ey-lenders. Normally, it is forbidden to claim interest on loans.
      Slavery

        Slave trading takes place at the market of Verdun. The slave
      trade is the most important element in the Eastward trade. In
      Spain, the two main centers for slavery are Cordoba and Toledo.
      It is forbidden for Franks to sell Christian slaves to pagans or
      Jews. This is why some rich slave traders are opposed to the
      Christianization of the Slavs, who constitute a vast reserve of
      slaves. Jews are sometimes accused of stealing young boys to be
      castrated and sold as eunuchs to Spain or Byzantium.
      The  Way    of Life

      Technology

      L
         ight is obtained by burning fat and beeswax, whale and fish
         oil, olive, walnut or poppy oil, or torches of resinous bark.
           Glass vases are very rare and precious, as are glass win-
      dows. Slightly more common are windows made of thin pieces
      of horn.
        Time is measured with the aid of sundials, hourglasses,
      measured candles, or the time it takes to say certain prayers.
        Medicinal or surgical skills are poor, although some monas-
      teries have books on illnesses, herbs, medicines and chirurgery.
      Customs

        Taverns — drinking establishments — are intrinsic to both
      rural and urban life. Even the priest is no stranger to the village
      tavern. They can be found everywhere: in market places, places
      of pilgrimage, on royal domains, episcopal and abbatial estates.
        Drinking contests are common. Bilingual conversation
      manuals (Germanic-Latin) used by wealthy travelers begin with
      the phrase “Give me a drink.” And by drink, nobles mean wine,
      not beer.
        In many villages, there are “oath guilds” for mutual help and
      assistance. In some places they turn into downright conspiracies
      against the lord. Other guilds are prayer guilds and drinking as-
      sociations. Charlemagne tries to ban all these guilds and sworn
      associations, because the bonds of loyalty among their members
      might be given preference in a conflict with the king. It is quite
      common, though, that members of the same village or town live
      as a very tight community in times of harvest, prayer or feasts.
        It is not uncommon to bury someone on the same day he dies.
      Hospitality
        A man’s house is considered sacrosanct. This is true wheth-
      er he lives in a hovel or a mighty castle. Tradition insists that a
      person need not invite anyone into the safety of his hearth, but if
      he does, then both people must obey certain rules of respect and
      safety. Once inside, peace must reign between them, even if they

discover they are deadly enemies. They can go outside and fight,
  or one of them can leave and then return with hostile intentions,
  but while inside both men must be peaceful and the visitor must
  even aid the owner of the house to defend it if they are attacked.
  In general, the host may never act against his visitor, but must
  treat him as an honored guest. The visitor must in turn be civil
  and not insult his host.
  Symbolism

     To drop an important object relevant to a task is considered
  a bad omen for the outcome thereof.
     Physical deformity is viewed as an outward sign of sin.
  Lepers are despised by many and an unhealthy prince cannot
  become king.
     An olive branch is a sign of peace.
  Family

  T
      he world is a dangerous place. There is plenty to mistrust
      in others, even if they are not strangers speaking a differ-
      ent tongue and worshipping alien gods. Strangers are, a
  priori, hostile and threatening. They are the ideal victim when
  villagers look for someone to blame for a plague, a drought or
  a cattle disease. Strangers are often suspected of poisoning wells
  or pastures.
     The family is sacred. An individual without a family is
  weird and suspect, and even if a kinsman acts despicably he is still
  to be trusted. The family can be counted upon in an emergency.
  The loyalty and affection of a person for his family is considered
  to be inherent to nature. It is unthinkable that someone would
  turn against his family. A kinslayer is unheard of, inhuman, al-
  most demonic.
     Sometimes a knight has to choose between loyalty to his
  kin and loyalty to his lord. There may be no way to resolve prob-
  lems without offending someone important. Such dilemmas are
  what the greatest stories are made of, and offer the best chances
  to roleplay.
     Some of the commonly used terms for nobles are:
   n
     House (or clan): All people who can trace their an-
     cestry to a common ancestor, sharing the same blood.
   n
     Kindred: All people who are relatives, including
     those which are outside a man’s lineage (i.e. his wife’s
     family).
   n
     Lineage: A nobleman’s direct ancestors and
     descendants.
   n
     Family: The nuclear family, consisting of a husband
     and wife, and their dependents.
     Infancy lasts till the age of 6, youth till 12, and men are con-
  sidered adult at 18. A noble receives his sword when knighted,
  usually 18. Girls are marriageable at 14.

title: Patriarchy
leftColumn:
People avoid naming children after a living relative, but
      great Frankish families have a tendency to give alliterative names
      to their children.
        “Brothers germaine” are brothers born of the same mother
      and father, the term “milk brother” is used for a man with whom
      someone shared a wet nurse.
      Patriarchy

        Men and male things are seen to be more important than
      women and female things. Property belongs to the father, or pa-
      triarch, so the system is called patriarchal. Everything of impor-
      tance revolves around the family head. The position of women
      in this system is secondary. They are degraded by the church and
      diminished by the legal system. Women are promised as pledges
      of friendship between would-be allies. Their only power comes
      from overseeing the household and land.
      Secular Marriage

        Marriage is an institution which is intended to secure inher-
      itance rights for all members involved. It is not a private affair, or
      only between a couple, but a serious family business — and take
      the word “business” very literally. Family alliances are often con-
      cluded by marriage, aiming to put an end to a history of rivalry
      (or even open warfare in case of a genuine feud) between two
      families, initiating and sealing a truce. A married woman’s role is
      to maintain the alliance by her irreproachable conduct, her sex-
      ual fidelity, and the assurance of the blood-bond by procreation
      (the woman’s primary duty).
        On the other hand, if a family won’t agree to a particular
      alliance, the woman is sometimes abducted to be married, re-
      gardless. Only at the end of Phase 1 does the Church insist on
      the mutual consent for a marriage, which is often concluded in
      private family circles to keep out nosy strangers and the clergy.
       “Sirs,” answers Boniface, “I voluntarily consent
       in giving you the hand of Ermengard,
       but on the condition that she agrees as well,
       For it is folly to marry a woman against her will.”

      with her husband when she marries, thereby joining herself and
      her children to his family. A critical function of marriage is to
      produce an heir to inherit control of the properties of both fa-

      not moral, institution. Children born to a legally married couple
      are legitimate, or within the law, and can inherit things without
      problem or question. Children born outside of wedlock are ille-
      gitimate, commonly called bastards, and discussed below.

title: Divorce
leftColumn:
see each other for the first time on their wedding day. The oc-
      casional happy marriage inspires bards to write poetry, spiteful
      overlords to become jealous and cruel, and lovers to take heart.
      Most, however, are not so full of love.
        The desire for the lord to maintain his bloodline demands
      fidelity from his wife, and fearful punishment can be invoked
      upon her for having a lover. Churchmen, themselves servants
      of a jealous Father God, constantly thunder about chastity
      from their pulpits. Most women follow the social norm and
      remain faithful to their loveless marriage, just to keep things
      simple and safe.
        Such fidelity is not expected, or at least not as expect-
      ed, from men. The infamous double standard is in its heyday.
      Women can be murdered for having a lover, but men are ad-
      mired for their capacity to engender children upon numerous
      women.
      Temporary  Unions
        Frankish commoners have premarital relations, and many
      even never officially marry at all. Their sexual morality is not
      much influenced by religious teaching. Monogamy is not a
      Frankish tradition; when a woman sleeps with a man, she be-
      comes his wife.
        Custom recognizes unions of limited duration, conclud-
      ed without transfer of a dower, simply marked with a morning
      gift which a man is expected to make to one who has shared
      his bed. This is unlike a marriage, which remains a legal bond,
      a public contract of transfer between the fiancé and the kin
      of the young girl, although a wedding is also concluded by a
      morning gift.
      Bastard Children

        A man’s partners outside wedlock are called lovers, con-
      cubines, courtesans, or paramours. For a nobleman they are
      frequently of a social class significantly lower than himself.
      Children of such issue are illegitimate or, basely said, bastards.
      The issue is not one of knowing one’s father or not. Often the
      children know quite well who their father is, but because they
      are born outside of marriage they have fewer rights than legiti-
      mate children.
        Bastards remain part of the family and are allowed to in-
      herit if no legitimate children survive. Even then, other kinsmen
      close to the deceased father can challenge their rights.
        Noblemen often provide for their concubines after they
      are dismissed. Sometimes the women are married to one of
      the noble’s retainers as a reward. Often the women receive
      valuable properties which are passed on to the bastard sons.
      Fathers keep half an eye on their illegitimate sons, and use
      their influence to help their sons advance in station beyond
      their mother’s class. This influence may be quite overt.
      Illegitimate sons often help their more legitimate brothers as
      loyal, reliable retainers.
rightColumn:
Divorce

     Divorce is the dissolution of the sacred bond of matrimony.
  The Church authorizes divorce only under certain conditions:
  the bad conduct of a wife (adultery), impotence of the husband,
  or consanguinity (marriage of close relatives).
     In general, marriages between any persons more closely re-
  lated than third cousins are prohibited. Proving consanguinity
  for nobles is an expensive and laborious matter, inquiries are
  necessary to establish how close they are related. Annulment
  for consanguinity means that the person whom you married is
  more closely related to you than you originally believed, or when
  a godfather marries his goddaughter.
     Sterility is no cause for divorce, although noblemen some-
  times repudiate their legitimate wives in favor of concubines
  who bear them healthy children.
  Inheritance
     Frankish family laws do not recognize the right of primo-
  geniture (wherein all goods go to the eldest son), so a father’s
  heritage (his lands, possessions, titles) is split evenly among all
  the sons (or uncles, cousins or nephews if need be). Daughters
  do not legally inherit, but in practice widows may exercise some
  power over their lands.
     The laws of inheritance may be bent, but cannot be broken
  without someone intervening. Parties who defend the laws are
  usually the next of kin who stand to inherit the property, and the
  lord, who has much to say in its governing.
     The sons inherit their father’s coat of arms, but with a small
  mark called a difference to set them apart as long as both father
  and sons are alive.

     If there are no sons, the eldest daughter can inherit the land, or
  the widow may keep it. There is a good chance, however, that some
  other male of close kinship receives it instead. Likely candidates are
  the dead lord’s brothers, bastard sons, or father if he still lives. In all
  cases the lord of the lands has some say about who gets disputed
  property. If a woman, whether daughter, widow, or mother, retains
  property rights, a lord always has final say on who she marries.
     Wills may specify the inheritance preference of a de-
  ceased property holder. If legal disputes arise, they must be
  settled through trial by combat, or be referred to the judgment
  of the next-highest lord the two have in common, perhaps
  Charlemagne himself.

title: Women Lovers
leftColumn:
Women

      I
         n accordance with the trifunctional model, a Carolingian
         woman can occupy one of three classes: she is either a noble
         woman, a nun, or a peasant. For noble women three roles
      are available: maid, wife, or widow. Marriage is fundamental; it
      determines a noble woman’s position and, often, her entire life.
        The image of women in Church discourse isn’t very flat-
      tering. They are depicted as “lustful like a serpent,” “sly as an eel,”
      garrulous, nosy, and sulky (just the kind of things many married
      men like to hear). Widowhood threatens women with rapid de-
      cline in social status and a plunge into poverty if they are un-
      able to force their husband’s heirs to respect their rights. Lone
      widows, poor women, servants and “useless” or marginal women
      are often suspected of prostitution or bad conduct, leading to
      punishment and further exclusion.
      Activities and Skills
        Even the most extraordinary Carolingian women still have sup-
      pressed roles when compared with adventuring knights. Aristocratic
      women spend their leisure time weaving and spinning, and they are
      usually also skilled in Chirurgery and Stewardship. Chirurgery is like-
      ly to save lives, and is not commonly practiced by men. Stewardship
      affects the income from landholdings. Women often have courtly
      skills useful for entertaining, such as Dancing or Singing.
      Heiresses

        A woman cannot inherit land if she has brothers, but she
      can exercise power on the lands she holds from her husband or
      her father. Thus, daughters of men with no sons may come into
      property in their own right. Although rich, they are without
      power under the law of the land, as if held in a state of perpetu-
      al childhood. An heiress is placed under the care of her father’s
      liege lord, and he has the right to choose her husband. This ef-
      fectively makes her a pawn in her lord’s hands.
        The liege lord generally takes control of all the property of
      an heiress, taking its income for himself until she is married, pro-
      viding for her welfare out of his own coffers. Since the income
      from the land is usually much more than the expense of keeping
      a rich maiden, lords like to have heiresses in their care, and are
      often in no hurry to have them wed.
        Because the hand of a rich heiress is the greatest prize that
      could be awarded to a loyal retainer for his service, many knights
      maintain their bachelorhood in the hopes of obtaining the hand
      of such an heiress.
        The law requires that if an heiress is widowed, her liege lord
      can choose her next husband. However, the law also holds that a
      woman cannot be forced by her lord to marry a third time. The
      twice-widowed heiress must obtain her lord’s permission to mar-
      ry, but she has no obligation except to herself. All other rights of
      possession can be exercised, unencumbered, by her. Knights can
      swear fealty to her, she determines how to spend the fief’s money
      and so on. Such an heiress is independent and quite powerful.
rightColumn:
Lovers

     The custom of fin’amor provides limitless opportunity for
  adventurous, though perhaps reckless, women to pursue per-
  sonal interests. Although the consequences of an affair may be
  personally disastrous, love is one of the areas where women have
  great freedom, albeit secretly.
     Romance is one way of effectively controlling men. A woman
  may be courted by several suitors, all of whom she is refusing, all
  of whom work hard to please her. If she is cruel and clever, she may
  test the dedication of her lovers by sending them against her per-
  sonal enemies, or otherwise engaging in troublesome tasks for her.
     Because women are effectively blocked from great personal
  achievement, they often find their outlet for power and respect
  by manipulating men. Some men do not mind this, and some
  actually prefer it to thinking for themselves.
     Women often entertain strangers and friends through the
  use of courtly skills. These skills are useful to a man who wishes
  to entertain and impress a woman, and may be used in competi-
  tions. Whenever a woman wishes to learn more about a man, she
  may use such courtly skills.
     However, simple playing of games is not the entire point,
  for there are things to be discovered in the banter and talk which
  passes across the boards between moves. Here behavior comes to
  the fore, and personality is revealed. A lady may decide to esca-
  late her passion in the affair only after learning the facts about
  her lover, careful to make sure he is the right kind of man.
  Nuns
     Religious women can hold great power, even in a man’s
  world. Their claim of loyalty to a higher power gives them au-
  thority denied to people with only mundane pursuits. Their
  proximity to spiritual powers often makes them feared as well
  as respected.
     Historically, religious communities serve many functions
  relevant to women. They provide:
   n
     A place for women to follow a religious vocation.
   n
     A place where orphaned girls can be raised until they
     are of marriageable age.
   n
     Refuge for widows who are trying to avoid another
     marriage or completing a period of mourning for
     their husbands.
   n
     Refuge for women deposed from their rightful lands
     until their lord returns, or until their lands are other-
     wise returned.
   n
     Education and training for women.
   n
     Sanctuary and care for travelers, outcasts, the sick,
     and the wounded.
   n
     A socially acceptable means of removing troublesome
     women from positions of power without violence.

title: Religion
leftColumn:
Religion

       The Church provides spiritual guidance for knights.
      Ideology

      C
         hristianity in the Middle Ages was very different from
         today. To capture the feelings and attitudes of medieval
         literature it is important for players to understand the
      basic, accepted attitudes held about religion by their characters,
      who are members of the ruling class. Christianity is the domi-
      nant religion in Frankland, and even the most ignorant worship-
      er knows its basic precepts.
        In the perception of the Franks, they are a Chosen People,
      loved by God. The Christian Church is the cement of their
      culture, and the progress of Christianity is identified with the
      growth of Charlemagne’s power. The king is the chieftain of a
      very large tribe which has the monopoly of God’s truth.
      Mythology
        Christianity is a monotheistic and trinitary religion. It be-
      lieves in a single God who exists in three complementary forms:
      the Father, the Son and the Holy Ghost. The fundamental sto-
      ries of Christianity are written down in a book called the Bible.
      The founding mythology of the Christians is as follows:
        God created the world and everything in it. The first peo-
      ple were called Adam and Eve. Because humans were made with
      free will, many descendants of Adam and Eve fell away from the
rightColumn:
worship of God and the world was corrupted. God then mani-
  fested himself as his Son to offer salvation to the world.
     During the reign of Emperor Augustus was born the son of
  God named Jesus Christ in the kingdom of Judea. Barely escap-
  ing death at his birth, Jesus was raised in obscurity as the son of
  a carpenter in a small town in Judea. He spent a short time as a
  wandering teacher, attended by his selected followers called the
  apostles. He allowed himself to be killed by being tortured and
  nailed to a cross. They day he died is called Good Friday. He
  was buried in the tomb of his uncle, Joseph of Arimathea, but
  after three days he miraculously rose from the dead, celebrated
  as Easter. He visited his closest disciples and instructed them in
  his new religion. Fifty days after the first Easter, the Holy Ghost
  descended upon the apostles and gave them the gift of speaking
  other languages, after which they went around the world teach-
  ing about the miracle. The converted people formed the start of
  the Christian religion.
     Christ’s self-sacrifice allowed humans to obtain eternal sal-
  vation and, after death, to join God in Heaven. Worshipers can
  find personal salvation through imitating the life of Jesus Christ
  and following his teachings.
     The Christian doctrine is briefly spelled out in the Credo
  (“I believe”), to which have been added numerous commentaries
  and explications of the Holy Scriptures. Together, they form the
  basis of Canon Law.

title: Morality
leftColumn:
Morality

        The aim of Christianity is to provide its worshipers with a
      path to Heaven; a paradise of eternal life after death. Christians
      obtain salvation by good conduct, participation in the rituals and
      sacraments of the Church, and absolution of their sins. On the
      other hand, sinners who do not follow the path to salvation will be
      sent to Hell, a place of eternal torment and damnation. Purgatory,
      which is a place in between Heaven and Hell, is for venal sinners,
      who must wait there until they are ready to go to Paradise.
        The Devil, who is the Lord of Hell, tries to seduce and
      corrupt people in order to win their souls. Proper and good
      conduct for a Christian is the love for others, as defined by the
      seven heavenly virtues: Charity, Chastity, Diligence, Humility,
      Kindness, Patience, and Temperance.
        Despite all efforts from the Church, everyday morality in
      Frankland is not based on this kind of ascetic Christianity, but
      on more ancient tribal precepts. The dominant warrior class un-
      derstands religion accordingly: Jesus is a lord and the Apostles
      are his vassals. Jesus is a great hero, a miracle-worker, a winner.
      The Franks do not worship the humble crucified man. Indeed,
      as Clovis said: “If I had been present in Jerusalem at the time, I
      would have surely rescued our Lord Jesus!”
        Jesus, like everybody else, owes obedience to his father: God.
      The Christian image of God himself is feudal: The Church is the
      army of God, wielding both the sword and the scepter — symbols
      of power and justice. The Frankish God is a punishing one, distant
      and severe, often represented as the lord of a divine castle, presiding
      like a powerful king over a celestial court of his vassals, the saints.
        Many knights show their spiritual interest the most when
      they swear oaths or profanities, while the most religious ones are
      true fanatics, slaying pagans as a sacrifice to God.
        For the common folk, the simplified religious obligations
      are baptism, abstention from work on Sundays and religious
      feasts (at least during mass), regular attendance at mass, and
      communion three times a year. Confession is not a regular duty,
      so most people only confess once a year at Pentecost, in public.
      These acts are essential to Faith, whereas the understanding of
      doctrine is secondary.
        The payment of a tithe (a tenth of all money) to the Church
      is a Christian obligation, and understandably the least popular one.
       Concerning tithes: that everyone is to give his tithe and
       that they are to be disbursed at the order of the pontiff.
           — Capitulary, anno 779
        Hospitality, as a form of alms-giving, is another Christian virtue.
       That strangers, pilgrims and the poor should have hostels
       established by monks and canons in various places, for
       the Lord Himself will say on the great day of reward: ‘I
       was a stranger and you took me in’ (Matt. 25.35), and
       the apostle, praising hospitality, said: ‘Through this some
       have pleased God, that they have given hospitality to an-
       gels’ (Hebr. 13.2).
           — Capitulary, anno 789
rightColumn:
The related ancestral custom of sanctuary is even written
  down in the law:
    If anyone shall have fled to a church for refuge, let no one
    presume to expel him from the church by violence, but
    he shall be left in peace until he shall be brought to the
    judicial assembly.
       — Capitulary, anno 775
  Celebration

     The holiest day of the liturgical year is Easter, the day that
  Jesus rose from the dead and proved he was the Son of God.
  Another important day is Pentecost, fifty days after Easter, when
  the Holy Ghost descended to the apostles. Christmas marks the
  birth of Christ in the city of Bethlehem. Many lesser holy days
  exist, but these are the most important.
     The most important recurring spiritual moment in the life of
  Christians is Sunday mass in a church. During this formal worship
  gathering, a priest reads passages of the Bible and sermons to his
  audience. Mass is the time when other sacraments are celebrated:
     Baptism: By pouring water over the new believer’s head, a
  priest marks his or her entry into the Christian community.
     Confirmation: A bishop confirms the baptized person as a
  Christian and a soldier of Christ. A priest can baptize, but only a
  bishop can administer confirmation.
     Penance: By confessing one’s sins to a priest and doing sin-
  cere penance, a Christian receives absolution of his sins and is
  reconciled with God.
     Communion: By participating in the communal celebra-
  tion of God during mass, Christians witness the miracle of bread
  and wine which transform into Christ’s body and blood.
     Holy Orders: This rite transforms a man into a priest.
     Extreme Unction: Given to the dying, a priest prepares the
  passage of the person’s soul to Heaven.
     Note that matrimony is not yet an official sacrament, al-
  though after Phase 1 no one dreams of celebrating a wedding
  without the presence of a priest to bless the couple. In the eyes
  of the Church, this gives the newlyweds the right to have inter-
  course without committing a carnal sin.
  Heresies

     In a time when Church dogma is not yet firmly established
  — when Church fathers are still standardizing the Bible, the
  sacraments, and holy days — many alternative versions and in-
  terpretations of Christianity find fertile ground in the illiterate
  minds of the poor and the misguided.
     Wandering pseudo-monks rely on charity and the hospitality
  of others. Many of these wandering charlatans, disguised as monks,
  priests or bishops, spread heretical doctrines, knowingly or not. One
  heretic preacher pretends to have received a letter from God, fallen
  directly from Heaven, in which he is ordered to reform the Church.
  Another, a certain Adalbert, preaches his heretic views in the north
  of Neustria, distributing his fingernails as amulets.

segments.text:
The aim of Christianity is to provide its worshipers with a
      path to Heaven; a paradise of eternal life after death. Christians
      obtain salvation by good conduct, participation in the rituals and
      sacraments of the Church, and absolution of their sins. On the
      other hand, sinners who do not follow the path to salvation will be
      sent to Hell, a place of eternal torment and damnation. Purgatory,
      which is a place in between Heaven and Hell, is for venal sinners,
      who must wait there until they are ready to go to Paradise.
        The Devil, who is the Lord of Hell, tries to seduce and
      corrupt people in order to win their souls. Proper and good
      conduct for a Christian is the love for others, as defined by the
      seven heavenly virtues: Charity, Chastity, Diligence, Humility,
      Kindness, Patience, and Temperance.
        Despite all efforts from the Church, everyday morality in
      Frankland is not based on this kind of ascetic Christianity, but
      on more ancient tribal precepts. The dominant warrior class un-
      derstands religion accordingly: Jesus is a lord and the Apostles
      are his vassals. Jesus is a great hero, a miracle-worker, a winner.
      The Franks do not worship the humble crucified man. Indeed,
      as Clovis said: “If I had been present in Jerusalem at the time, I
      would have surely rescued our Lord Jesus!”
        Jesus, like everybody else, owes obedience to his father: God.
      The Christian image of God himself is feudal: The Church is the
      army of God, wielding both the sword and the scepter — symbols
      of power and justice. The Frankish God is a punishing one, distant
      and severe, often represented as the lord of a divine castle, presiding
      like a powerful king over a celestial court of his vassals, the saints.
        Many knights show their spiritual interest the most when
      they swear oaths or profanities, while the most religious ones are
      true fanatics, slaying pagans as a sacrifice to God.
        For the common folk, the simplified religious obligations
      are baptism, abstention from work on Sundays and religious
      feasts (at least during mass), regular attendance at mass, and
      communion three times a year. Confession is not a regular duty,
      so most people only confess once a year at Pentecost, in public.
      These acts are essential to Faith, whereas the understanding of
      doctrine is secondary.
        The payment of a tithe (a tenth of all money) to the Church
      is a Christian obligation, and understandably the least popular one.
       Concerning tithes: that everyone is to give his tithe and
       that they are to be disbursed at the order of the pontiff.
           — Capitulary, anno 779
        Hospitality, as a form of alms-giving, is another Christian virtue.
       That strangers, pilgrims and the poor should have hostels
       established by monks and canons in various places, for
       the Lord Himself will say on the great day of reward: ‘I
       was a stranger and you took me in’ (Matt. 25.35), and
       the apostle, praising hospitality, said: ‘Through this some
       have pleased God, that they have given hospitality to an-
       gels’ (Hebr. 13.2).
           — Capitulary, anno 789

The related ancestral custom of sanctuary is even written
  down in the law:
    If anyone shall have fled to a church for refuge, let no one
    presume to expel him from the church by violence, but
    he shall be left in peace until he shall be brought to the
    judicial assembly.
       — Capitulary, anno 775
  Celebration

The holiest day of the liturgical year is Easter, the day that
  Jesus rose from the dead and proved he was the Son of God.
  Another important day is Pentecost, fifty days after Easter, when
  the Holy Ghost descended to the apostles. Christmas marks the
  birth of Christ in the city of Bethlehem. Many lesser holy days
  exist, but these are the most important.
     The most important recurring spiritual moment in the life of
  Christians is Sunday mass in a church. During this formal worship
  gathering, a priest reads passages of the Bible and sermons to his
  audience. Mass is the time when other sacraments are celebrated:
     Baptism: By pouring water over the new believer’s head, a
  priest marks his or her entry into the Christian community.
     Confirmation: A bishop confirms the baptized person as a
  Christian and a soldier of Christ. A priest can baptize, but only a
  bishop can administer confirmation.
     Penance: By confessing one’s sins to a priest and doing sin-
  cere penance, a Christian receives absolution of his sins and is
  reconciled with God.
     Communion: By participating in the communal celebra-
  tion of God during mass, Christians witness the miracle of bread
  and wine which transform into Christ’s body and blood.
     Holy Orders: This rite transforms a man into a priest.
     Extreme Unction: Given to the dying, a priest prepares the
  passage of the person’s soul to Heaven.
     Note that matrimony is not yet an official sacrament, al-
  though after Phase 1 no one dreams of celebrating a wedding
  without the presence of a priest to bless the couple. In the eyes
  of the Church, this gives the newlyweds the right to have inter-
  course without committing a carnal sin.
  Heresies

In a time when Church dogma is not yet firmly established
  — when Church fathers are still standardizing the Bible, the
  sacraments, and holy days — many alternative versions and in-
  terpretations of Christianity find fertile ground in the illiterate
  minds of the poor and the misguided.
     Wandering pseudo-monks rely on charity and the hospitality
  of others. Many of these wandering charlatans, disguised as monks,
  priests or bishops, spread heretical doctrines, knowingly or not. One
  heretic preacher pretends to have received a letter from God, fallen
  directly from Heaven, in which he is ordered to reform the Church.
  Another, a certain Adalbert, preaches his heretic views in the north
  of Neustria, distributing his fingernails as amulets.

title: Superstitions
leftColumn:
At the end of the century, the issue of the Filioque poses the
      question whether the Father, the Holy Ghost and the Son are
      on the same level. The Frankish Credo says that the Holy Ghost
      comes from the Father and the Son (“qui ex Patre Filioque pro-
      cedit” — “who from the Father and the Son proceeds”), but Greek
      credo, used in Italy and Byzantium, doesn’t (“τὸ ἐκ τοῦ Πατρὸς
      ἐκπορευόμενον” — “from the Father proceeding”).
        The Byzantine patriarch condemns the Filioque, but a
      Frankish counter-council approves it as the official Roman
      Credo. Charlemagne demands that the Filioque be sung in all
      churches without waiting for papal approval. When, a few years
      later, the news of the Filioque reaches the Christians of the Holy
      Land, the majority of eastern monks are shocked. The Pope tries
      to calm things down by admitting the truth of the Frankish dog-
      ma, but not allowing the Credo to be changed. Charlemagne
      ignores the Pope and orders his monks to sing the Credo the
      Frankish way.
        Around the same time, the heresy of Adoptionism spreads
      from the Pyrenees into Septimania. It claims that Jesus, the Son
      of God, was neither as eternal as God nor consubstantial with
      him, and that Jesus was clearly a lesser person than God himself,
      who had adopted Jesus as his mortal son. Adoptionism holds
      that Jesus was born as a normal man, and later was adopted as
      the son of God.
        This heresy is preached by Bishop Felix of Urgel and
      Archbishop Elipand of Toledo, but is officially condemned at
      a council and by Alcuin, who writes a treatise Against Felix’s
      Heresy. After a debate with Alcuin at Aachen, Felix recognizes
      his errors and retracts his former statements.
        The Iconoclast Controversy sweeps over the Byzantine
      Empire in the beginning of the 8th century and is only halted
      by a measure of compromise at the Second Council of Nicea in
      780. This decision unleashes a furious propaganda campaign
      against Byzantium, again to distinguish the catholic Franks from
      the “other Christians,” i.e. those outside Charlemagne’s realm.
        In Aquitaine, another heresy lingers on: the teachings of
      Bonose, who claims that Mary is the mother of many mortal
      children, one of whom is Christ.
      Swearing
        Knights regularly swear, usually in a subtle way acceptable
      to the tender ears of their courtly times. Cursing in the name
      of God is forbidden by the second commandment: Thou shalt
      not take the name of thy Lord God in vain. Swearing by saints is
      popular among knights, as if invoking the saint’s name will keep
      his attention turned towards the speaker.
      Punishments
        Doing penance is a way to pay off sins. Penances for grave
      faults must be done in public. Sometimes penitents can ask for a
      third person to do penance in their place, for it is written: “Bear
      the burden, one for the other.”
rightColumn:
A book called the Penitentiary lists which and how many
  penances a priest must give for what sins. They vary from the
  saying of a certain number of prayers to doing good works or
  going on a pilgrimage.
     Rome is the primary destination for pilgrims; only few pil-
  grims travel all the way to Jerusalem. Charlemagne is the patron
  of the Eternal City. He obtains the security and protection of
  Christian travelers from the Saracens, and helps the patriarch
  and the churches of Jerusalem materially. Some popular local pil-
  grimage centers include Le Puy, Saint Denis and Saint Michael’s
  Mount. Pilgrims often bring back souvenirs (named eulogies)
  from their visits; most commonly phials of water, clothes which
  have touched the sanctuaries, powders and oils.
     The ultimate punishment a bishop may pronounce against
  sinful parish members is excommunication. This religious con-
  demnation publicly excludes a sinner from the Christian com-
  munity. The sinner can no longer participate in the rituals and
  is shunned by others. Only a very important act of penance can
  resolve excommunication.
  Superstitions
     In many areas of the empire the veneer of Christianity is
  thin at best. Christianity, in the absence of teachers and the com-
  plete illiteracy of the people, is not able to offer any kind of day-
  to-day spiritual guidance. Animistic and magical practices have
  their adepts among the people and even among the clergy and
  rich nobles, who are often as illiterate and uneducated as their
  peasants, and are prey to the same superstitions. Therefore, pa-
  ganism still flourishes in isolated regions, where people are con-
  tent with the crudest kind of magic and superstitions.
     The fight against paganism and superstition is long, and
  the Church struggles to replace the pagan worship of nature
  with the Christian worship of saints. Just as the Church re-con-
  secrates stones, trees, and fountains to the saints, priests replace
  pagan incantations with prayers to the saints for rain, fertility of
  the fields and recovery of the sick.
     Popular pagan rituals include lighting fires near sacred trees,
  rocks or springs, or making a wish near a well or fountain while
  invoking pagan powers. The feasts called spurcales in February,
  the celebration of nature’s renewal in spring, and observances of
  the summer solstice in June, all provide occasions to commune
  with nature with drinking bouts and sexual irregularities. Other
  rituals include sacrifices to the dead, purification by fire at sol-
  stices, ritual fertility dances, leaving food near ponds or oaks to
  appease witches or elf maids, or making loud noise on the night
  of the lunar eclipse in order to chase the Black Horsemen into
  the forest.
     Groves, enclosures, stones and springs still have their cults.
  Sacrifices and magical incantations are still used to ensure a good
  harvest. Divinations, amulets, various potions and magical for-
  mulas are all very popular, just like Christian relics.

title: Church Organization
leftColumn:
“weather-wizards” (tempestarii) to protect them from natural di-
      sasters. These special sort of magicians are said to be able to con-
      jure up hail storms that destroy the harvests. Some claim to see
      them sailing in flying vessels from a cloud-land called Magonia.
        By far the most popular magical practices are those de-
      signed to protect and cure. Prisoners seeking to be free of their
      bondage, or peasants concerned about the health of their cattle,
      recite magical formulas. There are many spells to obtain rain,
      fertility, or health for the sick.
        Pagan superstition is particularly attached to cults of the
      dead. Animal sacrifices for the dead are widely practiced, usually
      accompanied with ritual dances — for in pagan tradition, both
      religious and judicial customs must be validated with a dance.
      Funerary wakes include dancing, singing and eating. In some
      places, a coin is put into the mouth of the corpse, in durable
      memory of the old custom of a small offering for Charon.
       No one shall make a vow at springs or trees or groves, or
       shall have made any offerings after the manner of the
       heathen and shall have partaken of a repast in honor of
       the demons. We command that dead bodies shall be car-
       ried to the church cemeteries and not to the mounds of the
       pagans. We order that diviners and soothsayers shall be
       given to the church and priests.

      are often abandoned at a church door, the first orphanage is
      founded in Milan in 787 by a priest named Datheus). Maleficia
      appear in many forms: love potions, protection and curing po-
      tions, amulets or phylacteries sold at markets.

      everybody scrutinizes the heavens in search of omens. Year by
      year, chroniclers note meteorological events which to them are
      disquieting signs.

       dreams or to practice augury’ (18.10) and again ‘There
       is to be no magician or enchanter or consultant with fa-
       miliar spirits’ (18.11). Therefore we order that men do
       not become sorcerers or enchanters or weather-prophets
       or makers of magical ligatures; and wherever they are
       found, they are to be set to rights or condemned. Further,
       as regards trees and stones and springs where foolish peo-

favorable. Scholars are attentive to the heavens, which they de-
  pict on maps. Charlemagne himself commissions a map of the
  constellations. Before any expedition, he asks his councilors
  (especially Alcuin or Dungal) to consult the heavens. Eclipses,
  comets or other natural phenomena are invariably seen as im-
  portant omens. Though magicians, enchanters, diviners, dream
  interpreters, and fortune tellers are all outlaws in the eyes of the
  Church, court astrologers are not. Even if it is officially forbid-
  den to interpret dreams, visions are welcomed by all, including
  Charlemagne, as divine warnings or commands.
     Abusing this belief, magicians, fortune tellers, diviners, and
  dream interpreters can be found at almost every town market.
  They sell magical amulets, philters, potions, poisons and phylac-
  teries for all sorts of uses.
     Women are thought to be particularly disposed towards
  sorcery (either as clients or practitioners), and are often defense-
  less when faced with the charge of witchcraft. Even such a highly
  placed woman as Gerberga, Duke Bernard’s sister, was “shut up in
  a barrel and thrown into the river Arar” and drowned as a witch.
  Church    Organization

  T
      he Church is the spiritual institution of the land. It bless-
      es the people and land, oversees crises, and guards the
      realm from magic. The church is feudal, having its own
  hierarchy of bishops and abbots, priests and monks, and the lay
  clergy. The ultimate clerical authority lies with the Bishop of
  Rome, the Pope, who is declared to be pre-eminent. Church cen-
  tralization grows over time, as does control of all churches. As
  the Church wields more temporal power, dogma and orthodoxy
  increases and the Roman Church becomes less and less tolerant
  of non-Roman Christians, whose doctrines and practices are de-
  clared heretical.
  The  Center of Civilization
     Charlemagne promotes the Church as the primary way
  commoners can raise themselves from their humble origins to
  a position where they can use their talents. Monks have pre-
  served the knowledge of the ancients, and the Church is the
  only institution that fosters education, both for itself and for
  others. It provides protection and peace in a violent, brutal age.
  Churchmen continually plead for mercy for their followers
  against the violence and hostility of the knights and lords. The
  Church provides for the poor, sick, and homeless.
     At the same time, some church members and lay men take
  advantage of the spiritual and temporal power of the Church.
  At places it turns into a materialistic and greedy organization,
  interested only in enriching itself and its clergy at the expense of
  all else, selling and buying spirituality like bread. Some clergy are
  deceitful, grasping men without belief in their own preaching,
  interested only in enriching themselves and in extending the in-
  fluence of the Church for their personal benefit.

title: Vassal of the Church
leftColumn:
Vassal of the Church

        As the Church holds many lands, a knight may be a vassal or
      household knight to an abbot or bishop. The fact that a lord of the
      land is a member of the Church changes none of the normal obliga-
      tions for the knight. In fact, the bishop or abbot generally acts in ev-
      ery way as if he is a count, for that is the function he is fulfilling. The
      only real effect of vassalage to the Church is that certain crimes are
      more likely to be judged by an ecclesiastical court than by a count.
      The Clergy

       Priests are to be revered, my son, because they have been
       chosen for God’s ministry and because, in holding sacred
       orders, they intercede for our sins.
           — Dhuoda, 3.11
        While it is the king’s task to defend the Christians from the
      pagans, it is the Pope’s task to pray for the king’s success — much
      like a royal arch-chaplain. Subsequently, it’s the function of the
      clergy (especially monks) to pray for the salvation of others. To
      fulfill their functions, clergy members should be literate and
      have access to a Bible.
       That abbots should live where the monks are, and whol-
       ly with the monks, according to the rule; and that they
       should diligently teach and observe the canons; and that
       abbesses shall do the same. That bishops, abbots and ab-
       besses, shall have bailiffs and sheriffs and judges skilled
       in the law, lovers of justice, peaceful and merciful: so that,
       through them, more profit and gain may accrue to the
       holy church of God. For on no account do we wish to have
       harmful or greedy provosts or bailiffs in a monastery; for,
       from them, the greatest blasphemies or evils may arise
       for us. (…) The poor, widows, orphans and pilgrims shall
       have consolation and protection from the clergy; so that
       we, through their good will, may merit, rather than pun-
       ishment, the rewards of eternal life. (…) That no clergy
       member shall presume to have hunting dogs or hawks,
       falcons or sparrow-hawks; but each one shall keep him-
       self wholly in his proper sphere, according to the canons,
       or according to the rule. Anyone who presumes to do this
       shall know that he loses his standing.
           — Capitulary, anno 802
      Abbot
        Many new monasteries and abbeys are founded during
      Charlemagne’s reign, in isolated forests or on mountainsides.
      By anno 800 there are about 650 abbeys in the empire. These
      large domains often are small towns in themselves. They attract
      laborers, possess slaves, and obtain royal charters of privilege and
      immunity. Great monasteries develop as to resemble veritable
      cities. A monastic town is usually surrounded by walls, and sol-
      diers, commanded by a knight, are hired to defend it.
        A great monastery usually has between 75 and 150 monks,
      plus servants, poor and sick in the infirmary, and travelers in
rightColumn:
the hostelry. Up to a thousand people may live inside the walls.
  Some abbots live with the monks, but the richer ones generally
  live separately, in a house with its own chapel, cellar, kitchen and
  sometimes even a bath.
     Some monasteries fall under the moral authority of a bishop,
  who controls all public places of worship, but other abbeys benefit
  from grants of “immunity.” This entitles an abbot to deal direct-
  ly with the king and remain “immune” from the interference of
  counts or bishops. Such an institution levies its own troops for the
  royal army, administers local justice, and collects fines and taxes,
  turning over a portion to the king. In order to prevent the clergy
  from losing sight of their proper spiritual function, landholding
  clergy are assisted in their worldly tasks by a lay advocate.
     Ecclesiastical domains are often run much more rationally
  than lay estates. Thanks to this, and many pious donations, some
  monasteries become huge, wealthy estates holding many man-
  ors. Abbeys pursue efforts on forest clearing, promising to the
  peasants that they will freely own the “assarted” (cleared) lands.
  As a result, the properties of a monastery are often spread over
  a wide area and stretch far into distant regions, so many abbots
  spend their days traveling from one domain to another.
     Monks are not forbidden to acquire wealth intended to fat-
  ten the capital of their church, embellish the liturgy or help the
  disinherited. Outside their landed property, churches dispose of
  moveable goods which constitute their “treasure,” produced by
  tithes and other offerings of the faithful.
     Abbeys often agree to accept and accommodate lay folk
  (both men and women) in exchange for gifts of lands or goods.
  Many rich nobles plan to spend their old age in monasteries.
  They leave their worldly goods to an abbey in order to have
  priests and monks pray for the family, and support them in
  their ambitions (conversely, counts sometimes confiscate church
  wealth to satisfy their military needs). Another good source
  of income are the taverns in the village around the monastery,
  as well as the markets. Some rapacious abbots even force their
  monks to go out begging, or forge official documents to support
  claims of royal donations or privileges.
     Like his ancestors, Charlemagne bestows extensive eccle-
  siastical property upon laymen — political friends and knights
  who helped him in his campaigns. He frequently appoints so-
  called lay abbots, a layman on whom he bestows an abbey as a
  reward or for services rendered. A lay abbot has the charge of
  the estate belonging to the abbey, and is entitled to part of the
  income. Sometimes Charlemagne gives church property, even
  entire abbeys, in feudal tenure. Moreover, many monasteries,
  though not founded by the king, place themselves under royal
  patronage in order to share his protection, and so become pos-
  sessions of the Crown. Under such influences, the abbeys may
  turn into scenes of worldliness and revelry.
     Monasteries in newly converted territories are often found-
  ed by Charlemagne himself, or are directly under his protection.
  The king distributes many church property as precarial holdings
  to loyal vassals. This means the Church remains owner of the
  lands, but the layman uses it more or less indefinitely, paying an

           — Capitulary, anno 802
      Abbot
        Many new monasteries and abbeys are founded during
      Charlemagne’s reign, in isolated forests or on mountainsides.
      By anno 800 there are about 650 abbeys in the empire. These
      large domains often are small towns in themselves. They attract
      laborers, possess slaves, and obtain royal charters of privilege and
      immunity. Great monasteries develop as to resemble veritable
      cities. A monastic town is usually surrounded by walls, and sol-
      diers, commanded by a knight, are hired to defend it.
        A great monastery usually has between 75 and 150 monks,
      plus servants, poor and sick in the infirmary, and travelers in

the hostelry. Up to a thousand people may live inside the walls.
  Some abbots live with the monks, but the richer ones generally
  live separately, in a house with its own chapel, cellar, kitchen and
  sometimes even a bath.
     Some monasteries fall under the moral authority of a bishop,
  who controls all public places of worship, but other abbeys benefit
  from grants of “immunity.” This entitles an abbot to deal direct-
  ly with the king and remain “immune” from the interference of
  counts or bishops. Such an institution levies its own troops for the
  royal army, administers local justice, and collects fines and taxes,
  turning over a portion to the king. In order to prevent the clergy
  from losing sight of their proper spiritual function, landholding
  clergy are assisted in their worldly tasks by a lay advocate.
     Ecclesiastical domains are often run much more rationally
  than lay estates. Thanks to this, and many pious donations, some
  monasteries become huge, wealthy estates holding many man-
  ors. Abbeys pursue efforts on forest clearing, promising to the
  peasants that they will freely own the “assarted” (cleared) lands.
  As a result, the properties of a monastery are often spread over
  a wide area and stretch far into distant regions, so many abbots
  spend their days traveling from one domain to another.
     Monks are not forbidden to acquire wealth intended to fat-
  ten the capital of their church, embellish the liturgy or help the
  disinherited. Outside their landed property, churches dispose of
  moveable goods which constitute their “treasure,” produced by
  tithes and other offerings of the faithful.
     Abbeys often agree to accept and accommodate lay folk
  (both men and women) in exchange for gifts of lands or goods.
  Many rich nobles plan to spend their old age in monasteries.
  They leave their worldly goods to an abbey in order to have
  priests and monks pray for the family, and support them in
  their ambitions (conversely, counts sometimes confiscate church
  wealth to satisfy their military needs). Another good source
  of income are the taverns in the village around the monastery,
  as well as the markets. Some rapacious abbots even force their
  monks to go out begging, or forge official documents to support
  claims of royal donations or privileges.
     Like his ancestors, Charlemagne bestows extensive eccle-
  siastical property upon laymen — political friends and knights
  who helped him in his campaigns. He frequently appoints so-
  called lay abbots, a layman on whom he bestows an abbey as a
  reward or for services rendered. A lay abbot has the charge of
  the estate belonging to the abbey, and is entitled to part of the
  income. Sometimes Charlemagne gives church property, even
  entire abbeys, in feudal tenure. Moreover, many monasteries,
  though not founded by the king, place themselves under royal
  patronage in order to share his protection, and so become pos-
  sessions of the Crown. Under such influences, the abbeys may
  turn into scenes of worldliness and revelry.
     Monasteries in newly converted territories are often found-
  ed by Charlemagne himself, or are directly under his protection.
  The king distributes many church property as precarial holdings
  to loyal vassals. This means the Church remains owner of the
  lands, but the layman uses it more or less indefinitely, paying an
