annual rent. Ecclesiastical vassals have the same obligations as lay
      vassals: the dispatch of a military contingent to the king’s host,
      aid and counsel, and regular presence at court. In addition to
      soldiers and silver, the abbeys give animals and wine as their par-
      ticipation in the war efforts.
        Most monasteries have numerous additional lay functions:
      a monastery is often a center for specialized artisans, who pro-
      duce their art for the Church. Some abbeys produce weapons
      and armor, and serve as arsenals, where armor, helmets, weap-
      ons and horse fodder is stocked. Monks living near a great forest
      often breed wild horses, which they round up once a year and
      then train into war horses for the local count and his knights.
      Abbeys often operate as regional money lenders. Royal abbeys
      sometimes serve as a sort of prison for high-born criminals, po-
      litical adversaries, prisoners of war or other hostages.
      Bishop
        Charlemagne reestablishes the system of archbishoprics, each
      of which is subservient to an archbishop. In the beginning, there is
      only one archbishop: Turpin. Only archbishops wear the pallium,
      a white sash with black crosses. By 814 there are 21 archbishops: in
      Rome, Paris, Milan, Cividale, Grado, Cologne, Mainz, Salzburg,
      Trier, Sens, Besançon, Lyon, Rouen, Reims, Arles, Vienne,
      Moûtiers-Tarentaise, Embrun, Bordeaux, Tours and Bourges.
        Archbishops and bishops are appointed by Charlemagne,
      not by the Pope. More than once Charlemagne deposes bishops
      or abbots who displease him. As soon as a bishopric is vacated,
      noblemen rush to beseech the king on behalf of family or friends.
      Many bishoprics remain vacant until the king gives them to loyal
      members of important families — or simply to the highest bidder.
        Like abbots, bishops are usually noblemen, but in some rare
      cases, a man of humble origins gets appointed bishop if the king
      considers him especially capable.
       “I, [name], bishop of [see], shall now and henceforth be
       a faithful follower of my lord Charlemagne, as a vassal
       rightly should be to his lord and as a bishop should be
       to his king; and I shall be obedient, as a vassal rightly
       should be obedient to his lord and as a bishop of Christ
       should, according to his knowledge and power, be obedi-
       ent to the will of God and Him who keeps the king safe.”
        Bishops are guides for the people and the lords. Interpreters
      of God’s will through a profound understanding of the Scriptures,
      they must read the signs God sends through natural events.
        Bishops must spend their time at their see and in their dio-
      ceses, and a bishop should never hold more than one see. Their
      religious tasks include pastoral care, education and overseeing
      the clergy (what they teach and how they celebrate the rites of
      the Church), and administering all of the churches and church
      property, the ecclesiastical institutions, and charitable works.
        Bishops are at the head of a school, organized around their
      cathedral, where talented children may receive a basic educa-
      tion in singing, reading, writing and calculating. Charlemagne
      encourages local priests to hold schools “in complete charity.”
      Episcopal schools are established to ensure basic education,

Ranks and Titles
      Abbess: This woman is in charge of a house of holy wom-
   en called a nunnery. Nunneries are usually associated with a
   nearby monastery whose abbot receives loyalty from the abbess.
      Abbot: An abbot is the head of a monastery. He may or
   may not be a priest. The abbot’s loyalty is not to the bishop,
   but to his local count or the king. Great abbots are among the
   most powerful men in the kingdom.
      Archbishop: Archbishops receive the loyalty of their
   bishops. They oversee the spiritual well-being of a very large
   territory, such as Austrasia or Burgundy.
      Bishop: Bishops are city administrators and guides for a
   number of priests in a large area, called a bishopric.
      Cardinal: A cardinal is a bishop who has been elected to
   an important position. He must live in Rome, and is charged
   with electing the new Pope whenever necessary, and may be
   appointed to be in charge of some important church business
   as a Papal legate.
      Cenobite: A monk who lives in a community, as distinct
   from a hermit or anchorite who lives alone.
      Chorbishop: An auxiliary bishop working under the
   command of an archbishop, without having the care of a town
   himself. Later replaced by archdeacon.
      Deacon: These are clerics serving at a cathedral monas-
   tery, whether as priests or monks, and have a say at the chapter
   of the bishop’s council.
      Friar: A member of a religious order that combines
   aspects of monasticism with active ministry in the world.
   Friars comprise the “mendicant orders,” emphasizing corpo-
   rate poverty.
      Hermit: Anyone who lives a secluded life devoted to
   prayer and contemplation can be called a hermit. Many stan-
   dards exist. Some are monks or priests. Many are lay folk.
   Knights often retire to become monks, and in some cases they
   take the title of hermit and live in the wilds part-time, return-
   ing later to their castles. Contrast this with the cenobite.
      Monk: A monk is a man who lives in a religious com-
   munity under vows of chastity, poverty, and obedience, en-
   gaging primarily in communal worship and self-perfection.
   Further tasks depend on the order and on the individual. Not
   all monks are priests.
      The most popular monastic order is the Benedictines.
   Known as the black monks, from the color of their habits, the
   Benedictine order established vows of poverty, chastity, and
   obedience, and stresses communal life and its spiritual benefits.
      Nun: A woman who retires to a life of religion. Nuns dif-
   fer from sisters in having taken a “solemn vow.”
      Pope: The Archbishop of Rome, the Heir of St. Peter,
   is titled the Pope (father). He is the highest authority of the
   Roman catholic religion. All archbishops owe him loyalty.
      Priest: The basic holy person of the Christian faith is a
   priest, who serves as a go-between for man to God. He over-
   sees all sacraments, services, and salvation in a small commu-
   nity or parish.
      Sister: A woman may join a religious order as a lay sister.
   Sisters differ from nuns in that they take only “simple vows.”

title: Chapter Thirteen: Frankish Society
leftColumn:
and they help with the education of the clergy. More and more
      priests come to know Latin and have accurate knowledge about
      the liturgy and Holy Scriptures. The school curriculum is ele-
      mentary and consists of the trivium and the quadrivium (see The
      Palace Academy, page 225.
        Often, bishop’s cities have houses of charity or infirmaries
      for the ill. These are in addition to hostels where nobles and their
      entourage are received or the hospices where the poor and the
      pilgrims can eat and sleep. In times of famine, the food stored by
      a city’s bishop must be distributed to the hungry citizens.
        A crypt is generally built under the sanctuaries of larger
      churches, both to safeguard relics and to permit the faithful to
      venerate them. Since banks do not yet exist, ecclesiastical trea-
      sure is often confided to a knight guardian. Thieves might pierce
      the church walls and unscrupulous pilgrims might take advan-
      tage of crowded days to take away precious objects. Note that it
      is forbidden to sell liturgical objects (this particular sin is called
      simony), especially to Jews.
        Bishops rely on grants of land For their income, but they are
      town administrators most of all. They serve at royal court or are
      sent on foreign or local missions (as a missus dominicus),and aid
      the count in the secular administration of their city.
        Bishops have their own courts of justice to judge cases
      where laymen are in opposition to members of the clergy. If he
      finds a nobleman to be oppressing his people, the bishop must
      warn him verbally and inform the king or his envoys.
        In the beginning of Charlemagne’s reign, most bishops can’t
      read, and some that can are said to be enchanters. Many bishops,
      abbots and priests think only of their own wealth. Whether em-
      ployed by king or count, they live in the same way as their fellow
      aristocrats: banqueting, hunting, political scheming, fighting
      blood feuds, and waging war.
        Not all clergy members live in this style. As a regretful bishop
      writes: “In winter, I do not get a single moment of leisure to devote
      myself to my favorite studies, for I am always en route to the palace.
      In spring, with my parchments under my arm, I go down to the coast
      to fight the invaders. By day, I put my sword to work, and by night I
      employ my books and my pen. Thus I seek fulfillment of my dreams.”
        Like other noblemen, bishops usually try to have a family
      member named as their successor, just like counts do for their
      land holdings. Bishops rarely have the time to pursue pastoral
      duties. But since Charlemagne needs the bishops as vassals, he
      doesn’t insist on their clerical duties. He admonishes them as far
      as women, drinking and hunting is concerned. At the same time,
      he demands military service from them. Later, bishops only ac-
      company the army to celebrate mass and guard the relics, not
      fight. They have to dress in clerical garments. In reality, they
      often continue to behave (and dress) more like military vassals.
      Monk
        Monks are clergymen who retire from the world. They no
      longer owe obedience to the bishop, but to an abbot. A man who
      enters a monastery leaves the world and his family behind, and is
      supposed to belong to a new family, that of the monks of his new
rightColumn:
home. Some men flee to monasteries to escape taxes, military
  service, or punishment.
     Monks swear oaths of stability, chastity, and obedience. A
  monk’s mission is to lead a truly pure and religious life, based on
  withdrawing from society. They live in a community to study
  and meditate; care for the sick; pray for the king, the people, and
  the dead; and fight the invisible enemies of the Franks. Singing
  liturgical songs is an important skill for a monk. Monks are not
  allowed to possess personal wealth.
     Most monasteries follow Saint Benedict’s rule, which is found-
  ed on spiritual and economic independence instead of charity.
  Benedictines must perform manual labor (gardening and farming)
  as well as intellectual occupations (praying and copying books).
     Spiritual and intellectual training does not include reading
  classical literature, which is distrusted even if education neces-
  sarily involves Latin and pre-Christian authors. To Alcuin, read-
  ing these pagan texts is an act of slothfulness. In monasteries for
  women (mostly in Ireland), the nuns are intellectually skilled.
     The reputation and pride of a monastery are founded on its
  relics, its library and scriptorium, and its teachers. Manuscripts
  are rare and precious, written on parchment made from sheep-
  or goatskins. Several works are often bound into one volume.
  Scribes copy manuscripts by hand, but do not produce entirely
  new texts themselves. The sale of copied books is a good source
  of income. It takes about two or three months for a monk to
  copy a manuscript of normal size. Borrowing and not returning
  books can lead to serious disputes between abbots.
     Unfortunately, many Bibles contain errors and show wide di-
  vergences. Alcuin and Theodulf come up with one standardized
  and flawless Bible edition, to be copied out and sent all around
  the empire. For clarity, Alcuin invents a standard way of writing
  letters: the Caroline minuscule, as he noticed that scribes cannot
  not always read each other’s writing. Punctuation is added in 800.
     Certain grand monasteries are rich enough to educate talented
  children for free. It would be sinful to ask money to open the way to
  the understanding of holy books. But only very rich monasteries are
  free for oblates, who are usually of noble origin. Often only mem-
  bers of the family of the founder can enter a monastery, which may
  remain a part of the landed property of that particular family.
     Monks interpret all sorts of signs (comets, weird births,
  miracles) in order to reveal God’s plans as it is laid down in the
  Bible. They do this by studying comparative history, looking for
  parallels and premonitions or prophecies.
     Monks are not yet bound to their cloister; they are free to
  travel from one monastery or abbey to another to exchange mes-
  sages and books, study, or buy grains for their gardens — garden-
  ers are always on the look-out for better seeds.
  Priest
     The job of a village priest is to help the bishop in his duties
  by administrating a small area called a parish. Priests live in their
  church, which should have a bell. To be efficient, a priest must know
  Latin and the liturgy and be able to deliver an understandable ser-
  mon to his flock (Reading & Writing, Religion, Eloquence).

and they help with the education of the clergy. More and more
      priests come to know Latin and have accurate knowledge about
      the liturgy and Holy Scriptures. The school curriculum is ele-
      mentary and consists of the trivium and the quadrivium (see The
      Palace Academy, page 225.
        Often, bishop’s cities have houses of charity or infirmaries
      for the ill. These are in addition to hostels where nobles and their
      entourage are received or the hospices where the poor and the
      pilgrims can eat and sleep. In times of famine, the food stored by
      a city’s bishop must be distributed to the hungry citizens.
        A crypt is generally built under the sanctuaries of larger
      churches, both to safeguard relics and to permit the faithful to
      venerate them. Since banks do not yet exist, ecclesiastical trea-
      sure is often confided to a knight guardian. Thieves might pierce
      the church walls and unscrupulous pilgrims might take advan-
      tage of crowded days to take away precious objects. Note that it
      is forbidden to sell liturgical objects (this particular sin is called
      simony), especially to Jews.
        Bishops rely on grants of land For their income, but they are
      town administrators most of all. They serve at royal court or are
      sent on foreign or local missions (as a missus dominicus),and aid
      the count in the secular administration of their city.
        Bishops have their own courts of justice to judge cases
      where laymen are in opposition to members of the clergy. If he
      finds a nobleman to be oppressing his people, the bishop must
      warn him verbally and inform the king or his envoys.
        In the beginning of Charlemagne’s reign, most bishops can’t
      read, and some that can are said to be enchanters. Many bishops,
      abbots and priests think only of their own wealth. Whether em-
      ployed by king or count, they live in the same way as their fellow
      aristocrats: banqueting, hunting, political scheming, fighting
      blood feuds, and waging war.
        Not all clergy members live in this style. As a regretful bishop
      writes: “In winter, I do not get a single moment of leisure to devote
      myself to my favorite studies, for I am always en route to the palace.
      In spring, with my parchments under my arm, I go down to the coast
      to fight the invaders. By day, I put my sword to work, and by night I
      employ my books and my pen. Thus I seek fulfillment of my dreams.”
        Like other noblemen, bishops usually try to have a family
      member named as their successor, just like counts do for their
      land holdings. Bishops rarely have the time to pursue pastoral
      duties. But since Charlemagne needs the bishops as vassals, he
      doesn’t insist on their clerical duties. He admonishes them as far
      as women, drinking and hunting is concerned. At the same time,
      he demands military service from them. Later, bishops only ac-
      company the army to celebrate mass and guard the relics, not
      fight. They have to dress in clerical garments. In reality, they
      often continue to behave (and dress) more like military vassals.
      Monk
        Monks are clergymen who retire from the world. They no
      longer owe obedience to the bishop, but to an abbot. A man who
      enters a monastery leaves the world and his family behind, and is
      supposed to belong to a new family, that of the monks of his new

home. Some men flee to monasteries to escape taxes, military
  service, or punishment.
     Monks swear oaths of stability, chastity, and obedience. A
  monk’s mission is to lead a truly pure and religious life, based on
  withdrawing from society. They live in a community to study
  and meditate; care for the sick; pray for the king, the people, and
  the dead; and fight the invisible enemies of the Franks. Singing
  liturgical songs is an important skill for a monk. Monks are not
  allowed to possess personal wealth.
     Most monasteries follow Saint Benedict’s rule, which is found-
  ed on spiritual and economic independence instead of charity.
  Benedictines must perform manual labor (gardening and farming)
  as well as intellectual occupations (praying and copying books).
     Spiritual and intellectual training does not include reading
  classical literature, which is distrusted even if education neces-
  sarily involves Latin and pre-Christian authors. To Alcuin, read-
  ing these pagan texts is an act of slothfulness. In monasteries for
  women (mostly in Ireland), the nuns are intellectually skilled.
     The reputation and pride of a monastery are founded on its
  relics, its library and scriptorium, and its teachers. Manuscripts
  are rare and precious, written on parchment made from sheep-
  or goatskins. Several works are often bound into one volume.
  Scribes copy manuscripts by hand, but do not produce entirely
  new texts themselves. The sale of copied books is a good source
  of income. It takes about two or three months for a monk to
  copy a manuscript of normal size. Borrowing and not returning
  books can lead to serious disputes between abbots.
     Unfortunately, many Bibles contain errors and show wide di-
  vergences. Alcuin and Theodulf come up with one standardized
  and flawless Bible edition, to be copied out and sent all around
  the empire. For clarity, Alcuin invents a standard way of writing
  letters: the Caroline minuscule, as he noticed that scribes cannot
  not always read each other’s writing. Punctuation is added in 800.
     Certain grand monasteries are rich enough to educate talented
  children for free. It would be sinful to ask money to open the way to
  the understanding of holy books. But only very rich monasteries are
  free for oblates, who are usually of noble origin. Often only mem-
  bers of the family of the founder can enter a monastery, which may
  remain a part of the landed property of that particular family.
     Monks interpret all sorts of signs (comets, weird births,
  miracles) in order to reveal God’s plans as it is laid down in the
  Bible. They do this by studying comparative history, looking for
  parallels and premonitions or prophecies.
     Monks are not yet bound to their cloister; they are free to
  travel from one monastery or abbey to another to exchange mes-
  sages and books, study, or buy grains for their gardens — garden-
  ers are always on the look-out for better seeds.
  Priest
     The job of a village priest is to help the bishop in his duties
  by administrating a small area called a parish. Priests live in their
  church, which should have a bell. To be efficient, a priest must know
  Latin and the liturgy and be able to deliver an understandable ser-
  mon to his flock (Reading & Writing, Religion, Eloquence).

title: Church Organization
leftColumn:
Christian priests keep concubines and maintain families
      until Phase 2, but they cannot marry. This separation allows a
      better distinction of the clergy from the other social classes (no-
      bles and peasants).
        In practice, most rural priests are completely illiterate,
      speak a mock-Latin (some baptize In nomene Patris et filia — in
      the name of the Father and the Daughter) and pervert the rites.
      Many rural priests perform animal sacrifices in response to folk
      demands. Others perform rituals in connection with the winter
      solstice, act as soothsayers, and bless amulets or perform sacrific-
      es for the dead, much like sorcerers and medicine-men.
        Charlemagne is well aware that such endemic ignorance
      among local priests is as dangerous as the occasional heretic
      movement, like adoptionism or iconoclasm.
       That priests and the other lesser clergy, whom they have
       to help them in their ministry, shall altogether show
       themselves subject to their bishops, as the canons de-
       mand. As they desire our favor and their own advance-
       ment, let them consent fully to be taught in sacred sub-
       jects by these their bishops. The secular clergy, moreover,
       ought to lead a completely canonical life, and be educated
       in the episcopal palace, or also in a monastery, with all
       diligence according to the discipline of the canons. They
       shall by no means be permitted to wander at large, but
       shall live altogether apart, not given to disgraceful gain,
       not fornicators, not thieves, not homicides, not rapists,
       not quarrelsome, not wrathful, not proud, not drunken;
       but chaste in heart and body, humble, modest, sober,
       merciful, peaceful; that as sons of God they may be wor-
       thy to be promoted to sacred orders: not like those living
       in towns and villages near or adjoining the church, with-
       out master and without discipline, reveling and fornicat-
       ing, and also doing other wicked deeds the consenting to
       which is unheard of. Priests shall carefully pay heed to
       the clergy they have with them, that they live according
       to the canons; that they be not given to vain sports or
       worldly feasting, or songs or luxuries, but that they live
       chastely and healthfully. Moreover, any priest or deacon
       who after this shall presume to have women in his house
       without permission of the canons, shall be deprived at
       once of his position and of his inheritance until he shall
       be brought into our presence.
           — Capitulary, anno 802
        The livelihood of the rural clergy is precarious. Many of
      them are less the subjects of the bishop than of the owner of
      the local manorial church. Nobles often install a priest under
      their control and usurp a part of the tithes. Priests are usually
      of humble origin, and sometimes a lord frees a slave to have him
      ordained as a priest in his service. Such a priest shares the life
      and pleasures of the peasant community he lives in: he keeps a
      woman who tends his house, and he is invited to taverns and
      wedding feasts.
        In general, there is a substantial lack of ecclesiastical super-
      vision by the bishops. A local land owner may obtain a relic and
rightColumn:
set aside a piece of land for a church or a chapel to be built on
  it, but he will continue to regard both the land and the ecclesi-
  astical buildings as his own private property. It is one thing to
  acquire merit in the eyes of God by building a church, but few
  want to carry religion so far that it becomes an impediment to
  ordinary pursuits and lusty appetites. Local priests are therefore
  expected to remain servants loyal to their lay lord.
     In short, an ordinary cleric is the illiterate servant of an
  illiterate noble. He serves at table, prepares the wine, leads the
  dogs to the hunt, and holds the ladies’ horses. If he has learning,
  his patron uses him as a secretary or steward. If he performs his
  functions badly, he can be beaten like any servant. Priesthood
  does not yet lead to social promotion.
  Missionary
     The duty of a missionary is to preach Christianity in order
  to convert pagans. Many missionaries are sent into the pagan
  lands (Saxony, Slavia, Denmark, Avarland) to Christianize them.
  A major task of missionaries is to destroy idols, cut down holy
  trees, baptize wells, and put crosses along the roads and in sacred
  sites. However, as missionaries in Saxony are “assisted” by aggres-
  sive and vengeful knights, their preaching is often ineffective.
     Monasteries at the frontiers of Christianity (like Fulda) be-
  come centers of learning for future missionaries. Charlemagne’s
  ancestors encouraged them to evangelize the German pagans:
  Willibrord in Frisia, Boniface in Germany, and Pirmin in
  Allemania. During Charlemagne’s reign, his soldiers are tasked
  with protecting the churches and monasteries founded by mis-
  sionaries and their disciples.
     After 785 the Saxons are officially Christianized, but in re-
  ality many of them are still pagans. The missionary priests are
  simply too few and too poorly trained. Alcuin even names them
  “predators, not preachers” as they insist more on the payment of
  tithes than the teaching of the Gospels.
     Some cynical Saxons let themselves be baptized more than
  once, claiming a gift (usually a white cloak) each time. Still,
  the Saxons are slowly converted and feudalized by the Franks,
  who reorganize the Saxon lands into large estates supervised by
  counts and bishops.
  Hermits
     Lone monks or nuns, called hermits, are quite numerous.
  They are examples of purity and often regarded as saints by the
  local population. They usually go barefoot, dressed in animal
  skins, and have a “magic” staff. They often live at places where
  travelers can get lost: in forests near bridges or fords, where — in
  return for small gifts — they take confession and give blessings
  and counsel. A simple hermit’s cell can provide safe harbor to all
  who go in fear of brigands, the cold or the dark.
     At the end of their military career, paladins usually retire
  from the world to live as hermits. Such a retirement can also be
  the result of a vow, a voluntary penitence or a fit of madness after
  a severe emotional shock.

  the result of a vow, a voluntary penitence or a fit of madness after
  a severe emotional shock.

title: Angels and Saints
leftColumn:
Angels and Saints

        The Franks venerate angels, like the three archangels
      Michael, Gabriel and Raphael. They pay a particular worship to
      saints and relics. A saint is a spiritual protector: the patron of a
      town, an abbey, a prince, a family, or all Christians.
        Saints are holy men or women whose lives exemplify the
      virtues taught by Jesus. They are perfect models of purity and pi-
      ousness who are rewarded after death for a lifetime of dedication
      to God. Many saints suffer a violent death for their faith, and are
      called martyrs. Saints who die a normal death are called confessors.
        People pray to saints for support, as they have the power to
      intercede with God on behalf of common mortals. Many saints
      are important in Carolingian Christianity, including the apos-
      tles, but one of the foremost is Saint Mary, the Mother of God.
        Some men or women living in Charlemagne’s time come to
      be reckoned as saints during their lifetimes, like Saint Benedict
      of Aniane, Saint Ludger, and Saint Fulrad.
      Relics
       He had brought from the church the arm of Saint Peter,
       from its gold and silver cover torn free,
       the count kissed the main joint, then the priest

       blessed him with it, over his helmet of steel,
       over his heart, before and behind, as was meet.
       Those jewels would serve him soon in his need:
       there was no man who might cause his defeat
       or inflict harm more than a coin’s width deep.
           — The Coronation of Louis, XIX

        Almost all churches have one or more saintly relics of virgins,
      hermits, bishops, or martyred missionaries as their religious focus.
      The possession of relics constitutes an assurance of efficient pro-
      tection against natural, human or demonic evil. People call on rel-
      ics for help, and they are often taken to a place where help is most
      needed, like newly founded churches or monasteries in missionary
      lands like Saxony. Welcoming a relic is always a serious ceremony,
      where a solemn translation scene is played out in public.
        The most common relics are bones of the saints. Some oth-
      er relics are such objects as pieces of Christ’s sandals, bread dis-
      tributed by the Apostles, milk of the Virgin, hair of St. John the
      Baptist, strands of St. Peter’s beard, or the bloody stones with
      which St. Stephen was crushed.
        Miraculous events, like healings, are all scrupulously noted
      down in official registers. Hoax healings are sometimes financed
      by unscrupulous clergy to increase the reputation of their relic
      or pilgrimage site.
        Since they are so dearly desired, greedy abbots sometimes
      engage thugs to steal holy bones for their own abbey. Robber
      knights may pretend to enter the service of a monastery, only to
      make off with the relics. The churches and cemeteries of Rome
      are the primary sources for relic hunters. Stealing bones from the
      ancient tombs is a dangerous, but very lucrative, business.
rightColumn:
On the other hand, stealing relics from pagan places is a pi-
  ous act and often divinely inspired by dreams or visions of angels
  or saints.
  Canonization
     The office of sainthood is officially conferred posthumously
  to recognize the greatness of an individual’s life. Only dead people
  may be canonized. Canonization requires that the candidate must
  have performed three miracles while alive, and three more must
  have occurred after death, preferably at their grave or through the
  use of a relic. While living, the person may have founded or led a
  monastery or church, where his or her remains usually rest. When
  a churchman recognizes the miracles and assigns a feast day, the
  process is complete and a saint has been made.
     Saintliness depends almost entirely on popular response.
  A local bishop or archbishop may informally approve the can-
  onization, which is usually the case. Only if the Pope himself
  confers sainthood is the canonization formal. This confers no
  special status except the increased honor of papal observances.
  Many paladins die as saints and are canonized.
  The  Church  and War

     The Bible’s fifth commandment seems to prohibit war when
  it says: “Thou shalt not kill.” So what should a good Christian do
  when faced with cruel overlords, foreign oppressors, or heathen
  invaders? The answer lies in three interesting doctrines: The
  Peace and Truce of God, the Just War, and the Crusades.
  The Peace and Truce of God
     This doctrine, the Treus Dei, calls for all men to lay down their
  arms at specific times. The Church claims that knights owe pro-
  tection to churches and clerics, especially; but also to merchants
  and peasants, including their property, whether mills, vines, cattle,
  or trade goods. Charlemagne subscribes to this chivalric view and
  confirms the knight’s duty of protecting the weak:
    That no one shall presume through fraud to plunder or
    do any injury to the holy churches of God, or to widows,
    orphans or strangers; for the emperor himself, after God
    and his saints, has been constituted their protector and
    defender.
       — Capitulary, anno 802
     The concept clearly pits the Church against the morality of
  its times, and stands as an outstanding example of the church’s
  positive influence during the horrors of the Dark Ages.
     Fighting is forbidden on all great festival days, from dusk on
  Friday to dawn Monday, and on all religious feasts. It expressly
  forbids harming church members or property, and protects peas-
  ants and merchants, and their livelihoods.
     The truce suggests that all knights in war undergo a 40-day
  penance after battle, to cleanse themselves of the taint of death.
  During this time, prayer and fasting should replace martial pur-
  suits. Unfortunately, enforcement is impossible outside the royal
  army. Noblemen are expected to be self-policing, which is asking
  a lot of them. Until Phase 2, there are only a few occasions when

title: Church Organization
leftColumn:
hostilities are suspended for a holy day, and sometimes this is
      only a ruse to make one side relax their defenses.
        The world of Paladin provides many opportunities for
      well-meaning knights to enforce this truce upon themselves, and
      possibly others. Such an act is one of piety, and deserves an expe-
      rience check in Love [God].
      The Just War
        The concept of the Just War was established in the late 4th
      century. A Just War is a war whose morality is approved by the
      Church. Strict criteria must be fulfilled. Only if all the condi-
      tions are met the war is acceptable.
       n
        Is the cause just? Is there clear injury to be redressed?
        The wrongful action must be perfectly clear or else
        risk being judged unjust. A supposed harm is not
        enough. Some lords pay their legal advisers hand-
        somely to discover the justice in their causes.
       n
        Has every reasonable attempt been made before re-
        sorting to bloodshed? War is the final option. All oth-
        er peaceable means must have been sought before a
        war can be considered just.
       n
        Will war be declared by a legitimate authority? A le-
        gitimate authority usually means the king, or at least a
        ranking nobleman considered to have the right to de-
        clare war. He might be a bishop, prince, duke, or count.
       n
        Will the war be waged solely by honorable and moral
        means? This clause only insists that the usual honor-
        able means be followed. The Treus Dei is expected to be
        honored, the 40-day truce expected to be offered, etc.
        Hanging a garrison that did not surrender is still ac-
        ceptable behavior, however; no requirement demands
        doing more than the common morality of the times.
       n
        Is the damage likely to be incurred less than the orig-
        inal injury? After all, if the war does nothing but in-
        crease the expenses to the combatant, there is no rea-
        son to pursue it.
       n
        Is success likely? Failure is a measure of God’s judg-
        ment. If the odds are impossible, God has apparently
        prejudged the event.
        Saint Augustine attempted to clarify the position for those
      still uncertain about this. He says that, in killing, what really
      matters is the intention in the combatants’ hearts. If they love
      their enemies as they slaughter them, anything is excusable.
        Charlemagne’s mission is to support and foster Christianity.
      His military campaigns against the Saracens and pagans of cen-
      tral Europe are as much religious as political expeditions. Before
      doing battle against the Avars in 791, the whole army prays and
      fasts for three days. Charlemagne hopes to enlarge the domin-
      ion of Christ and to establish the Augustinian City of God (his
      favorite book, together with the Bible) as an earthly reality. The
      expansion of Christianity is the motive for the wars in Saxony,
      Slavonia, Avarland and Spain. The wars against the pagans also
rightColumn:
carry the promise of many riches: lands, slaves and treasure, mak-
  ing them rather popular.
     As a rule, defeated pagans must be given the opportunity
  to accept baptism. If they refuse, they may be killed or reduced
  to slavery. On the other hand, it is possible to offer baptism to
  an unconquered enemy. Charlemagne conquers to convert, and
  converts to assure his conquest and the unity of his empire. Note,
  however, that some Frankish knights with a high Hate [Saxons]
  refuse to work for the conversion of the Saxons, so as not to find
  them as neighbors in Paradise!
  Crusades
     Charlemagne is invested with a sacred mission: the defense
  of Christianity. He inherited the title of “Patrician of Rome,”
  which means he is the official champion of Rome and the Pope
  and, after 787, of the Holy Land.
     A Crusade is a holy war which aims to liberate Christianity
  from the domination of unbelievers. Christ himself invited all his
  followers to spread the good news (the Gospel) to all peoples in
  order to offer them the possibility of salvation. The Carolingian
  Crusades into Spain are based on this idea, combined with the
  simple truth expressed by Roland: “The pagans are wrong and the
  Christians are right.”
     The Pope is in favor of crusade, since it causes the warring
  Christian princes to cease hostilities against each other and work
  harmoniously to liberate the Christian Visigoths from Moorish
  oppression. The king supports it because it rids the lands of trou-
  blesome warring lords. Common folk are happy for much the
  same reason. The knights and lords look forward to the lands
  they will conquer.
     The Carolingian crusades begin in 771, when Charlemagne
  launches his first Spanish campaign in order to liberate the tomb
  of Saint James at Compostela. After a short lull, the Crusades
  spring back into life with the second Spanish campaign, result-
  ing in the disaster at Roncevaux and the subsequent Reconquest
  in which the House of Narbonne plays a leading role.
  The Pope declares a Holy War:
    “God help us then,” said the pope so wise;
    “if the keeper of souls, Saint Peter, inspire
    you on this day in his service to strike,
    you may eat flesh all the days of your life
    and take women, as much as you like, to wife.
    There is no sin so bitter, no vice,
    but for treason, that you can devise
    that can balance this deed the rest of your life.

    (…)
    Whoever in battle on this day dies
    will live forever in paradise
    with all who love God in eternal delight.
    Saint Gabriel there will be your guide.”
       — The Coronation of Louis, XVIII

      His military campaigns against the Saracens and pagans of cen-
      tral Europe are as much religious as political expeditions. Before
      doing battle against the Avars in 791, the whole army prays and
      fasts for three days. Charlemagne hopes to enlarge the domin-
      ion of Christ and to establish the Augustinian City of God (his
      favorite book, together with the Bible) as an earthly reality. The
      expansion of Christianity is the motive for the wars in Saxony,
      Slavonia, Avarland and Spain. The wars against the pagans also

carry the promise of many riches: lands, slaves and treasure, mak-
  ing them rather popular.
     As a rule, defeated pagans must be given the opportunity
  to accept baptism. If they refuse, they may be killed or reduced
  to slavery. On the other hand, it is possible to offer baptism to
  an unconquered enemy. Charlemagne conquers to convert, and
  converts to assure his conquest and the unity of his empire. Note,
  however, that some Frankish knights with a high Hate [Saxons]
  refuse to work for the conversion of the Saxons, so as not to find
  them as neighbors in Paradise!
  Crusades
     Charlemagne is invested with a sacred mission: the defense
  of Christianity. He inherited the title of “Patrician of Rome,”
  which means he is the official champion of Rome and the Pope
  and, after 787, of the Holy Land.
     A Crusade is a holy war which aims to liberate Christianity
  from the domination of unbelievers. Christ himself invited all his
  followers to spread the good news (the Gospel) to all peoples in
  order to offer them the possibility of salvation. The Carolingian
  Crusades into Spain are based on this idea, combined with the
  simple truth expressed by Roland: “The pagans are wrong and the
  Christians are right.”
     The Pope is in favor of crusade, since it causes the warring
  Christian princes to cease hostilities against each other and work
  harmoniously to liberate the Christian Visigoths from Moorish
  oppression. The king supports it because it rids the lands of trou-
  blesome warring lords. Common folk are happy for much the
  same reason. The knights and lords look forward to the lands
  they will conquer.
     The Carolingian crusades begin in 771, when Charlemagne
  launches his first Spanish campaign in order to liberate the tomb
  of Saint James at Compostela. After a short lull, the Crusades
  spring back into life with the second Spanish campaign, result-
  ing in the disaster at Roncevaux and the subsequent Reconquest
  in which the House of Narbonne plays a leading role.
  The Pope declares a Holy War:
    “God help us then,” said the pope so wise;
    “if the keeper of souls, Saint Peter, inspire
    you on this day in his service to strike,
    you may eat flesh all the days of your life
    and take women, as much as you like, to wife.
    There is no sin so bitter, no vice,
    but for treason, that you can devise
    that can balance this deed the rest of your life.

(…)
    Whoever in battle on this day dies
    will live forever in paradise
    with all who love God in eternal delight.
    Saint Gabriel there will be your guide.”
       — The Coronation of Louis, XVIII

title: Discipline
leftColumn:
The Crusades are a military pilgrimage for knights, consist-
      ing of penitence, adventure, and the possibility to earn plunder or
      even land (particularly appealing to young, un-landed knights).
      The idea is to give a common goal to all Christian knights, who
      should fight pagans rather than each other. Knights find the idea
      of fighting in the defense of Christ attractive for different rea-
      sons: adventure, glory, riches and eternal salvation.
        Indeed, warriors are encouraged to view death for a holy
      cause as a likely means of entering Paradise, enforcing the notion
      of holy war. In the words of Pope Leo IV: “Whoever dies faithful
      in this struggle will not see himself refused entry into the heaven-
      ly kingdom.” So, according to the Pope, a hero who dies in the
      defense of the faith is automatically granted access to Paradise.
       “For our king we must be prepared to die.
       Help us now to sustain the Christian faith.
       You will have to engage in battle, as you well know;
       For you see the Saracens with your own eyes.
       Confess your sins, pray for the grace of God;
       To save your souls I shall absolve you all.
       If you die, you will be blessed martyrs
       And take your paradise on high.”

       The Franks dismount and kneel upon the ground;
       In God’s name the archbishop blessed them.
       As penance he orders them to strike.
           — Song of Roland, LXXXIX
        A war for God warrants special rules of combat. Because it
      is a religious cause, different conditions apply. Most important
      is that a religious cause allows no compromise with the enemy.
      Furthermore, dishonorable means are excusable against unbe-
      lievers. A holy war exempts men from ordinary morality.
        Since the army is the hand of God, the troops pray before
      doing battle. The troops do not eat meat nor drink wine, and
      barefoot priests sing psalms. The king asks his chaplains, bish-
      ops, and the Pope to pray for his success.
        A recurrent moral problem was the explanation of de-
      feat. For how can Christians lose if they are fighting with God
      on their side? Franks attribute such failures to sinful behavior
      among their ranks, or in the words of Saint Jerome: “Our sins
      give strength to the Barbarians.”
      Warfare

      Annual Royal  Campaigns
      A
          lmost every year, the Frankish king demands some of
          his counts to mobilize their men and come to the May
          Field. This annual call to arms is sent out in March or
      April, the actual gathering is in the first part of May.
       Be it known to you that we shall hold our general assem-
       bly this year in [place]. Wherefore we command you to be
       present there on [date] with your men well-armed and
rightColumn:
equipped. You should come with whatever arms, imple-
    ments, provisions, and clothing may be needed to proceed
    from there with the army whichever region we shall com-
    mand. Each horseman is to carry a shield and a spear,
    long sword and short sword, bow, quivers and arrows,
    and your carts are to contain implements of various kinds
    — axes and stone-cutting tools, augers, adzes, trench-
    ing tools, iron spades and the rest of the implements an
    army needs. And provisions in the carts for three months
    following the assembly, weapons and clothing for half a
    year. Your men should proceed to the appointed place by
    the shortest route, commandeering nothing along the way
    except for grass, firewood and water.
       — Capitulary, anno 806
     All free men, commoners and nobles alike, owe their lord a
  military service of three months. Both lay and ecclesiastical lords
  must muster their men for the king’s army. “A bishop or abbot is to
  leave only two of his enfeoffed knights at home.” Free men living in
  newly conquered lands must also serve in Charlemagne’s army.
     The royal army is between 10,000 and 50,000 men strong, but
  not everybody is called upon every year. Only in case of a foreign
  invasion do all free men have to assist their lord in the defense of the
  domain. The size of one’s property determines how often a man is
  called up for military service. Generally, up to one free farmer out of
  ten on an estate should join their count on a campaign.
     These men often regret leaving their families and the pursuit
  of agricultural activities. The levy of free men diminishes the ag-
  ricultural performance of a domain. Some cynical landlords call
  upon smaller farmers often in order to ruin them and confiscate
  their lands. In theory, the lands, wife and family of a free man who
  goes to war with the king are under the king’s protection.
  Discipline
     Not all troops arrive on time for the May Field. Bad weath-
  er, the conditions of the roads, and the difficulties of communi-
  cation often frustrate the best intentions. The punishment for
  late arrival is a wineless and meatless diet for a certain amount
  of time. Drunken soldiers are condemned to drink water for the
  rest of the campaign.
     Numerous ways of avoiding military service exist: entering
  the clergy, paying the count or abbot for the privilege to stay
  home (which is a frequent, though illegal, way for the lord to
  make some extra money). Some freemen even seek to avoid mil-
  itary service by becoming serfs. They surrender their freedom
  and their plot of land to a nobleman. As serfs, they then receive
  the land back as a tenancy.
     Noblemen sometimes train slaves as soldiers to replace their
  freemen in the levy. After 790, some vassals pay money (scutage)
  as a replacement of military service, which leads to the creation
  of professional mercenaries.
     Failure to meet the May Field without a valid reason is pun-
  ished by heavy fines (heribannum). Those guilty of desertion
  (herisliz) are put to death and their lands are confiscated.

title: Camp Followers
leftColumn:
As regards the punishment of anyone returning from
       the army without the leave and permission of the
       prince — which action the Franks call herisliz — it
       is our will that the ancient ruling be observed, namely
       sentence of death. And if someone from among those
       holding a benefice should fail his comrades-in-arms
       when the king is going on campaign against public en-
       emies and refuse to go or stay with him, he is to lose his
       honor and benefice.
           — Capitulary, anno 811
        Once the army starts moving, discipline becomes critical.
      Pillage and stealing forage is forbidden until enemy lands are
      reached. Breaches can be brought to justice by the count whose
      domain has been wronged.
        Charlemagne’s army can be a surprisingly sober and religious
      institution. Indeed, to the Frankish mind it is the army of God.
      Knights

        Poor knights who can afford a good war horse, but not ar-
      mor or helmet, are degraded and must join the sergeants. Not
      to lose the loyalty of his knights and vassals, a lord may donate
      equipment before a battle. Sometimes, he takes back the weap-
      ons and armor afterward and keeps them in a central armory,
      such as his own castle or a monastery.
      Freemen  Soldiers

        Most of the freemen serve as foot soldiers in the army. Most
      of them know how to use a bow, a spear and a dagger. These
      cheap hunting weapons are a part of everyday life. Though most
      foot soldiers fight with a heavy spear, they may use throwing
      axes, scythes, slings, and (in later Phases) pole-arms and ham-
      mers to unhorse enemy cavalry. The most expensive weapon is
      the sword. Good bows are hard to come by.
        Armor consists at best of heavy leather shirts studded with
      metal plates, conical helmets, and large round or oval wooden
      shields. The total cost to equip a footman is around 40d.
        The rare freemen who are rich enough to possess a horse
      form a contingent of mounted sergeants. They wield javelins or
      a spear and use felt or quilted fabric as light armor.
      Baggage-Train
        The main problem of long-distance warfare is not mili-
      tary might, but logistics (transport, food supplies and infor-
      mation). A band of warriors has to bring along a wagon to
      carry all their food and equipment, such as axes, hatchets,
      crow-bars, slings, carpentry and cooking tools. Most luggage
      is transported on two-wheeled carts pulled by oxen. The
      roads are often in very bad condition and horse fodder is
      sometimes hard to find. The army attracts merchants selling
      food at prohibitive prices.
        The men do not come only with weapons and armor, they
      must also supply the army with livestock, food, carts and oxen.
rightColumn:
Knights bring spare horses, because their mounts usually suffer
  badly during a long campaign or a forced march.
     Apart from food and animals, the baggage train contains
  weapons, treasure, and even small mill stones. To cross riv-
  ers they are equipped with small boats and amphibious carts
  covered with leather and their joints sealed with wax, pitch
  and tow. These can be used to create removable bridges of
  tethered pontoons.
     Depending on the goal of the campaign, the king may de-
  mand siege equipment (or the metal parts to make them): bat-
  tering rams, assault ladders, mangonels, catapults, rolling towers,
  and later even trebuchets.
  Camp   Followers

     With the baggage train marches an army of merchants.
  Their toughness in defense of their merchandise is recognized
  by all! Thieves and whores accompany the army, mixed in with
  servants and wives, children and slaves.
     Monks and priests with relics accompany the army as a spir-
  itual force. The clergy pray before a battle and afterwards ab-
  solve the Frankish warriors and baptize defeated pagans.
     The royal family sometimes accompanies the king on his
  annual campaign, staying in the camp when a battle is fought.
  Noblewomen sometimes accompany their husbands.
  Tactics

     The effectiveness of Charlemagne’s army depends less on
  size than on armament, skill, morale and, to a great extent, rap-
  id mobilization and movement and the concentration of force.
  Quick decision making, discipline, troops whose morale is al-
  most consistently superb, fast strong horses, and a good commu-
  nication system are the key to many Frankish successes.
     The Frankish army is designed primarily for attack,
  not defense. Sieges are rare, as war consists mostly of rapid
  strikes. Speed and night marches are very characteristic of the
  Frankish tactics. This enables Charlemagne to aim directly
  at the enemy’s heart. He combines political pressure, seeking
  to subvert the foe’s political elite, with invasions heading for
  their capital or religious center. The royal army usually at-
  tacks along two or more fronts, with a frontal attack by foot
  soldiers, and cavalry on flanks to out-maneuver the enemy.
  Thus the Franks make use of their numerical superiority to
  force the enemy to divide his forces or retreat in defense of
  his heartland.
     Threatening battle, rather than actually fighting one, is a
  very common and effective strategy. Charlemagne often wins
  wars without actual fighting. These victories are attributed to
  the massive religious ceremonies which precede the battles, or
  by the intervention of angels or saints. Still, when a battle must
  be fought, Charlemagne does not stay at the rear. He fights with
  his troops.
     The king rarely organizes raids for booty, but when he does
  he uses swift mounted troops. These also serve in ambushes or

segments.text:
As regards the punishment of anyone returning from
       the army without the leave and permission of the
       prince — which action the Franks call herisliz — it
       is our will that the ancient ruling be observed, namely
       sentence of death. And if someone from among those
       holding a benefice should fail his comrades-in-arms
       when the king is going on campaign against public en-
       emies and refuse to go or stay with him, he is to lose his
       honor and benefice.
           — Capitulary, anno 811
        Once the army starts moving, discipline becomes critical.
      Pillage and stealing forage is forbidden until enemy lands are
      reached. Breaches can be brought to justice by the count whose
      domain has been wronged.
        Charlemagne’s army can be a surprisingly sober and religious
      institution. Indeed, to the Frankish mind it is the army of God.
      Knights

Poor knights who can afford a good war horse, but not ar-
      mor or helmet, are degraded and must join the sergeants. Not
      to lose the loyalty of his knights and vassals, a lord may donate
      equipment before a battle. Sometimes, he takes back the weap-
      ons and armor afterward and keeps them in a central armory,
      such as his own castle or a monastery.
      Freemen  Soldiers

Most of the freemen serve as foot soldiers in the army. Most
      of them know how to use a bow, a spear and a dagger. These
      cheap hunting weapons are a part of everyday life. Though most
      foot soldiers fight with a heavy spear, they may use throwing
      axes, scythes, slings, and (in later Phases) pole-arms and ham-
      mers to unhorse enemy cavalry. The most expensive weapon is
      the sword. Good bows are hard to come by.
        Armor consists at best of heavy leather shirts studded with
      metal plates, conical helmets, and large round or oval wooden
      shields. The total cost to equip a footman is around 40d.
        The rare freemen who are rich enough to possess a horse
      form a contingent of mounted sergeants. They wield javelins or
      a spear and use felt or quilted fabric as light armor.
      Baggage-Train
        The main problem of long-distance warfare is not mili-
      tary might, but logistics (transport, food supplies and infor-
      mation). A band of warriors has to bring along a wagon to
      carry all their food and equipment, such as axes, hatchets,
      crow-bars, slings, carpentry and cooking tools. Most luggage
      is transported on two-wheeled carts pulled by oxen. The
      roads are often in very bad condition and horse fodder is
      sometimes hard to find. The army attracts merchants selling
      food at prohibitive prices.
        The men do not come only with weapons and armor, they
      must also supply the army with livestock, food, carts and oxen.

Knights bring spare horses, because their mounts usually suffer
  badly during a long campaign or a forced march.
     Apart from food and animals, the baggage train contains
  weapons, treasure, and even small mill stones. To cross riv-
  ers they are equipped with small boats and amphibious carts
  covered with leather and their joints sealed with wax, pitch
  and tow. These can be used to create removable bridges of
  tethered pontoons.
     Depending on the goal of the campaign, the king may de-
  mand siege equipment (or the metal parts to make them): bat-
  tering rams, assault ladders, mangonels, catapults, rolling towers,
  and later even trebuchets.
  Camp   Followers

With the baggage train marches an army of merchants.
  Their toughness in defense of their merchandise is recognized
  by all! Thieves and whores accompany the army, mixed in with
  servants and wives, children and slaves.
     Monks and priests with relics accompany the army as a spir-
  itual force. The clergy pray before a battle and afterwards ab-
  solve the Frankish warriors and baptize defeated pagans.
     The royal family sometimes accompanies the king on his
  annual campaign, staying in the camp when a battle is fought.
  Noblewomen sometimes accompany their husbands.
  Tactics

The effectiveness of Charlemagne’s army depends less on
  size than on armament, skill, morale and, to a great extent, rap-
  id mobilization and movement and the concentration of force.
  Quick decision making, discipline, troops whose morale is al-
  most consistently superb, fast strong horses, and a good commu-
  nication system are the key to many Frankish successes.
     The Frankish army is designed primarily for attack,
  not defense. Sieges are rare, as war consists mostly of rapid
  strikes. Speed and night marches are very characteristic of the
  Frankish tactics. This enables Charlemagne to aim directly
  at the enemy’s heart. He combines political pressure, seeking
  to subvert the foe’s political elite, with invasions heading for
  their capital or religious center. The royal army usually at-
  tacks along two or more fronts, with a frontal attack by foot
  soldiers, and cavalry on flanks to out-maneuver the enemy.
  Thus the Franks make use of their numerical superiority to
  force the enemy to divide his forces or retreat in defense of
  his heartland.
     Threatening battle, rather than actually fighting one, is a
  very common and effective strategy. Charlemagne often wins
  wars without actual fighting. These victories are attributed to
  the massive religious ceremonies which precede the battles, or
  by the intervention of angels or saints. Still, when a battle must
  be fought, Charlemagne does not stay at the rear. He fights with
  his troops.
     The king rarely organizes raids for booty, but when he does
  he uses swift mounted troops. These also serve in ambushes or

title: Battaille
leftColumn:
in pursuit. When the Franks capture a foreign city, it’s usually
      plundered, unless it’s a Christian city — though Frankish lords
      often have trouble preventing their men from sacking Christian
      towns as well.
        The hardships of the march, where forests, bogs, and
      mountain favor enemy resistance, encourages Frankish com-
      manders to practice a scorched earth policy. They take few
      or no prisoners and burn down many hostile villages. In this
      manner, Aquitaine, Brittany, Saxony, Septimania, and many
      other regions are ruined for decades. In the Spanish March,
      warfare consists of almost continual raids and counter-raids.
      In the face of this persistent looting, small castles and village
      fortifications spring up everywhere. Frankish troops in this
      region may include dissident Moors, who act as light and very
      fast cavalry.
      Battaille
        Armies are organized into three sections. Each section is called
      a battaille or battalion, and has a fixed place in the march and battle.
      Each is labeled by the order in which they march on the road.
        The Vanguard marches first, commanded by the sec-
      ond-highest leader. On the battlefield the vanguard lines up on
      the right side of the battle line.
        The Main battaille marches in the center, led by the highest
      commander of the army, and assembles for combat in the center
      of the battle line.
        The Rearward battaille is commanded by the third ranking
      noble, marches at the end of the line, and assembles on the left
      side of the field of combat.
        Frankish war banners are often the head of an animal carried
      on a pole; sometimes burning oil is placed in the animal’s mouth.
      Troop Types

        Several kinds of troops accompany a lord into battle.
        Knights — well-trained and well-outfitted — form a core of
      the professional, mounted warriors. They are the heart of the army.
        Infantry are unmounted troops used to do the foraging, gar-
      rison castles, assault walls, and build and protect camps. Infantry
      isn’t very useful in attacks, but has a role in consolidation after
      the battle. Infantry are armed with shield and spear, long knives,
      bows, crossbows, or axes. They usually wear leather armor, often
      augmented by miscellaneous bits of real armor plundered from
      the dead.
        Archery is of major tactical importance. Some very skillful
      archers manage to shoot their arrows from horseback, imitating
      the Huns. Short flat bows of simple construction are the most
      common, but the late Roman double-convex composite bows
      are not unknown.
        Sergeants are professional mounted troops, decently armed
      and trained, but generally lacking the skill, confidence, and first
      rate horses of knights. Poor knights without a liege, unattached
rightColumn:
squires, and ambitious men-at-arms with good equipment and a
  horse count as sergeants. Many mercenary units are composed of
  sergeants. These light cavalry troops thrust with the spear, rath-
  er than holding it firmly beneath the armpit to deliver a lance
  charge. Since the force of the cavalry is its mobility, they serve as
  rapid plunderers.
     Hobilars are mounted but unarmored troops used as scouts
  and messengers, but not mustered for battle as a unit.
     Engineers are men who can build and work the mighty
  engines used in siege, such as trebuchets, mangonels, and bel-
  freys. They oversee the making of siege works and digging
  tunnels. Without engineers it is hopeless to besiege a city or
  castle. They are also responsible for building castles able to
  withstand engines.
     Insufficiently-equipped warriors are ill considered and used
  as ordinary laborers for the army.
     Other people accompany the armies, though they are
  worthless as combat troops. Knights bring girlfriends, wives,
  and servants. Spectators, suppliers, well-wishers, and hangers-on
  congregate to trade with or cheat the soldiers. These followers
  are a constant nuisance on the march and are always a great trou-
  ble to feed.
     Heralds, because of their special status, play an important
  part in battle between Franks and civilized enemies. Heralds
  are recognized as neutral messengers and may not be attacked.
  Prior to a battle they carry messages back and forth between
  commanders to plan where the armies will meet. Just before the
  armies engage the heralds from both sides withdraw to the same
  hilltop, steeple, or silo to watch and record events of the fight.
  They help each other to identify combatants.
  The  Aftermath
     The victorious side chooses the name of the battle. Heralds
  carry messages between the combatants, commonly to make a
  temporary truce for burying the dead and exchanging ransoms.
  Frankish prisoners made during a war with a pagan enemy are
  not always ransomed. Victims of Saracen raids are sometimes
  sold as slaves in Toledo, for example. Children of nobles may be
  sold to a pagan court to be raised as that lord’s champion in fu-
  ture judicial combats.
     The night is used to collect the bodies of the dead and the
  dying from the field and give them a Christian burial. As the
  warrior-poet Angilbert wrote:
    The night was especially terrible,
    A night mingled with complaints and suffering
    When some died and others groaned in dire straits.
    O grief and lamentation! The dead are stripped naked,
    Vultures, crows and wolves greedily devour their flesh,
    They grow stiff, and their corpses lie there, unburied,
     helpless.

title: Fortifications
leftColumn:
Fortifications

      S
         ome cities still maintain their surviving Roman city walls,
         possibly with stone towers to strengthen the defensive ring
         around the habitations. Apart from these, the only military
      architecture in Frankland consists of castles and fortresses.
      Castles and Fortresses

        Castles are the abode of lords and the ultimate expression of
      power. They are both homes and tools of war. They offer refuge
      from danger and serve as a base for cavalry raids and major ex-
      peditions. Extraordinarily expensive to build and maintain, cas-
      tles are nonetheless essential for controlling the land, and gain
      the owner great prestige. Without a castle, a lord would be just
      another knight. Note that to build a castle, a noble has to ask
      permission from his lord or from the king himself.
        A second type of defensive work is the fortress. This is not
      the home of a nobleman, but a royal castle occupied by a perma-
      nent garrison in order to pacify or secure a certain region. Though
      Charlemagne conquers many lands, he doesn’t fortify much. True
      fortresses — like the ones in Fronsac or Eresburg — are rare.
        In frontier regions, fortifications consist of motte-and-bai-
      ley castles. The defense of frontier marches relies on a levy of free
      men, though the important fortifications are garrisoned by scara
      units. These wooden hill fortresses are meant less to defend the
      hinterland against invasions than to keep an eye on recently con-
      quered territories, and can be built rapidly in case of rebellion.
      The king holds the exclusive right to erect and garrison fortresses
      anywhere in his kingdom.
      Motte and  Bailey Castles
        The most common castle is a simple wood and earth struc-
      ture, called a motte and bailey. Such castles are of a style known for
      many decades. They are relatively easy and inexpensive to build.
        The motte is a hill, often artificially constructed, atop
      which sits the lord’s stronghold — a great log, or sometimes
      stone, tower. The bailey is a large courtyard that contains the
      buildings for the followers of the lord, including the stable,
      blacksmith, servants’ quarters, and cattle pens. A log stockade
      and ditch surrounds the bailey, which can be crossed only by
      means of a drawbridge.
      Stone Castles
        At the heart of small stone castles is a central keep that is the
      lord’s stronghold. The keep is three floors high, with a basement,
rightColumn:
and can be entered only through a door on the second story.
  A courtyard, still called the bailey, surrounds the keep. A tall,
  thick stone wall surrounds the bailey, and encloses many wood-
  en buildings. A moat (either water-filled or simply a dry ditch)
  outside the walls can be crossed only by the drawbridge.
     A medium stone castle is like a small castle, but with towers
  on the walls. Square towers stand at two or more of the corners
  of the walls, while a third overlooks the drawbridge, creating a
  gate tower.
     A large castle is like the medium castle, but with taller walls,
  towers at every corner, a large gatehouse, and a larger keep. The
  buildings in the bailey are probably built of wood, or perhaps
  even stone.
  Coastal  Defense

     By the turn of the century, the Danes begin to plague the
  Frankish coasts, but the defensive war that is necessary to re-
  sist them is of no interest to the nobles, as there is no land or
  booty to gain. Coastal defense therefore remains problematic.
  Lighthouses are built in Boulogne and near Hamburg, and some
  counts erect defensive earthworks for the local population to flee
  to.
     The freemen’s military service is often used for home de-
  fense instead of sending them to the royal army. The local foot
  soldiers are generally well motivated to fight off the invaders, in
  contrast to the nobles, who often hold domains in numerous dis-
  tant provinces.
     Some counts build castles along the coast not only to de-
  fend against raiders, but to affirm their own private power.
  Others take advantage of the incursions to attack their neigh-
  bors, or buy off the danger with heavy tribute and encourage the
  Danes to raid their rivals.
     The king and his counts possess almost no war ships. It isn’t
  until 800 that Charlemagne orders the construction of fleets at
  the mouth of rivers to defend the land against pagan raiders.
    Charlemagne ordered the building of a fleet to ward off
    the attacks of the Danes. For this purpose ships were con-
    structed near to the rivers which flow into the North Sea.
    Charlemagne also placed strongholds at all ports and at
    the mouths of rivers considered large enough for the entry
    of ships. He did the same in the south, along the shore of
    Septimania, Provence, and along the whole coast of Italy
    as far north as Rome, against the Saracens who had re-
    cently begun pirate attacks.
       — Einhard

         ome cities still maintain their surviving Roman city walls,
         possibly with stone towers to strengthen the defensive ring
         around the habitations. Apart from these, the only military
      architecture in Frankland consists of castles and fortresses.
      Castles and Fortresses

Castles are the abode of lords and the ultimate expression of
      power. They are both homes and tools of war. They offer refuge
      from danger and serve as a base for cavalry raids and major ex-
      peditions. Extraordinarily expensive to build and maintain, cas-
      tles are nonetheless essential for controlling the land, and gain
      the owner great prestige. Without a castle, a lord would be just
      another knight. Note that to build a castle, a noble has to ask
      permission from his lord or from the king himself.
        A second type of defensive work is the fortress. This is not
      the home of a nobleman, but a royal castle occupied by a perma-
      nent garrison in order to pacify or secure a certain region. Though
      Charlemagne conquers many lands, he doesn’t fortify much. True
      fortresses — like the ones in Fronsac or Eresburg — are rare.
        In frontier regions, fortifications consist of motte-and-bai-
      ley castles. The defense of frontier marches relies on a levy of free
      men, though the important fortifications are garrisoned by scara
      units. These wooden hill fortresses are meant less to defend the
      hinterland against invasions than to keep an eye on recently con-
      quered territories, and can be built rapidly in case of rebellion.
      The king holds the exclusive right to erect and garrison fortresses
      anywhere in his kingdom.
      Motte and  Bailey Castles
        The most common castle is a simple wood and earth struc-
      ture, called a motte and bailey. Such castles are of a style known for
      many decades. They are relatively easy and inexpensive to build.
        The motte is a hill, often artificially constructed, atop
      which sits the lord’s stronghold — a great log, or sometimes
      stone, tower. The bailey is a large courtyard that contains the
      buildings for the followers of the lord, including the stable,
      blacksmith, servants’ quarters, and cattle pens. A log stockade
      and ditch surrounds the bailey, which can be crossed only by
      means of a drawbridge.
      Stone Castles
        At the heart of small stone castles is a central keep that is the
      lord’s stronghold. The keep is three floors high, with a basement,

and can be entered only through a door on the second story.
  A courtyard, still called the bailey, surrounds the keep. A tall,
  thick stone wall surrounds the bailey, and encloses many wood-
  en buildings. A moat (either water-filled or simply a dry ditch)
  outside the walls can be crossed only by the drawbridge.
     A medium stone castle is like a small castle, but with towers
  on the walls. Square towers stand at two or more of the corners
  of the walls, while a third overlooks the drawbridge, creating a
  gate tower.
     A large castle is like the medium castle, but with taller walls,
  towers at every corner, a large gatehouse, and a larger keep. The
  buildings in the bailey are probably built of wood, or perhaps
  even stone.
  Coastal  Defense

By the turn of the century, the Danes begin to plague the
  Frankish coasts, but the defensive war that is necessary to re-
  sist them is of no interest to the nobles, as there is no land or
  booty to gain. Coastal defense therefore remains problematic.
  Lighthouses are built in Boulogne and near Hamburg, and some
  counts erect defensive earthworks for the local population to flee
  to.
     The freemen’s military service is often used for home de-
  fense instead of sending them to the royal army. The local foot
  soldiers are generally well motivated to fight off the invaders, in
  contrast to the nobles, who often hold domains in numerous dis-
  tant provinces.
     Some counts build castles along the coast not only to de-
  fend against raiders, but to affirm their own private power.
  Others take advantage of the incursions to attack their neigh-
  bors, or buy off the danger with heavy tribute and encourage the
  Danes to raid their rivals.
     The king and his counts possess almost no war ships. It isn’t
  until 800 that Charlemagne orders the construction of fleets at
  the mouth of rivers to defend the land against pagan raiders.
    Charlemagne ordered the building of a fleet to ward off
    the attacks of the Danes. For this purpose ships were con-
    structed near to the rivers which flow into the North Sea.
    Charlemagne also placed strongholds at all ports and at
    the mouths of rivers considered large enough for the entry
    of ships. He did the same in the south, along the shore of
    Septimania, Provence, and along the whole coast of Italy
    as far north as Rome, against the Saracens who had re-
    cently begun pirate attacks.
       — Einhard
